author: Manuel São Bento
content:
Check out my full review @ movieswetextedabout.com/spider-man-brand-new-day-movie-review-destin-daniel-cretton-delivers-peter-parkers-most-personal-story-yet

Rating: A

SPIDER-MAN: BRAND NEW DAY had every excuse to become a bloated victory lap for the MCU’s biggest names, and instead it turns out to be the most emotionally mature, personal Peter Parker story we’ve gotten yet — one that treats its sprawling cast as tools in service of a single, aching question about isolation, identity, and what it costs to keep pretending you don’t need anyone. Tom Holland has never been better, Sadie Sink announces herself as a genuine star, and Destin Daniel Cretton proves that even inside Marvel’s most crowded corner, a story can still belong entirely to one person. With some of the best Spidey action I’ve ever witnessed, a standout Michael Giacchino score, and terrific performances across the board, this is definitely top-tier MCU.

author: Brent Marchant
content: When I watch a movie, I expect to be entertained, enlightened and/or informed (not necessarily in that order or all at once). But what I *don’t* want is to be treated like a marketing prospect. And that, unfortunately, is one of the problems with many of the releases in the Marvel Universe, including this latest installment in the Spider-Man franchise. Given the studio’s intricate web of properties (no pun intended) in this overlapping assortment of superhero franchises, there are considerable character and storyline cross-overs in virtually all of its film projects. Now, because of that, some cross-pollination of the narratives is bound to occur. But, when this practice becomes a key element in developing the plots of these offerings, it begins to feel more like marketing manipulation than bona fide storytelling, as is the case here. I don’t particularly appreciate using existing efforts to purposely promote upcoming productions. It tends to make these movies somewhat formulaic and cookie-cutter in nature. And, even though that’s not carried to an extreme in this release, it’s present nevertheless, no matter how much director Destin Daniel Cretton may try to enliven whatever other distinguishing characteristics might have been incorporated into the script. In essence, the film continues the current Spider-Man mythology with protagonist Peter Parker (Tom Holland) working largely as a solo undercover crimefighter in New York going after bad guys in a world where he and his past accomplishments have been intentionally forgotten as part of a selfless protective initiative. Only he retains recollection of what came before, leaving him alone where this knowledge is concerned, since old colleagues, including his onetime love interest, M.J. (Zendaya), retain no personal memory of him. It causes him a certain sense of emotional weariness, but it’s also something that he doesn’t have the luxury of time to focus on, given his workload and the fact that he’s going through transformations of his own while battling a menacing new nemesis (Sadie Sink). True, he secures some assistance from past superhero kindreds (Mark Ruffalo, Florence Pugh), but they don’t remember him either, compromising their effectiveness. Can he overcome all of these challenges? That’s a question as much for viewers as it is for Spidey himself, given that, in telling this story, multiple narrative threads are introduced (and not especially clearly), a problem that plagues the flow of the material in the opening half. This could potentially hamper viewer understanding until the picture’s back end, when it finally finds a firmer footing to tell its tale (even if some of it isn’t always adequately explained). Judicious editing may have helped here, but then that may have meant trimming some of the marketing material for future releases (and we can’t have that now, can we?). In short, “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” is probably best seen as a mediocre Marvel offering that features some modestly entertaining enhanced character development but that nevertheless covers a lot of action-adventure ground we’ve already seen before in countless other studio releases and that could certainly use some shrewd pruning of its overlong 2:24:00 runtime, too. Diehard fans of the franchise will no doubt love this (or virtually anything else that Marvel chooses to put up on the screen) no matter what, but I can’t help but take issue with that assessment. After all, there’s quite an undeniable irony here in the bold wording of the film’s title, which would seem to promise something new but doesn’t follow through on that pledge as well as it might have.

author: Max Borghetti
content:
SPOILERS AHEAD: I loved the movie, I’m not going to lie. It feels different, daring, and genuinely confident in its own identity. Jon Watts should be taking notes.

That said, I do feel that Hulk/Banner deserved a much larger role. The character had the potential to contribute a great deal to the story, but they never fully took advantage of him.

The Bad Bunny reference made me laugh, and honestly, it also made me happy. Whether you like him or not, he is a Latino artist and represents us. It even reminded me somewhat of the cultural energy and pride embodied by Miles Morales.

What didn’t I like? For starters: where the hell is J. Jonah Jameson?

The movie is packed with news broadcasts discussing Spider-Man and everything happening across New York. We saw Jameson at the end of *Spider-Man: No Way Home*, and here he simply vanished. Nothing. Not even a mention. Completely erased from the map.

The same applies to the references involving the inhibitor chip and Doctor Octopus. A single comment or joke delivered by the suit’s own artificial intelligence would have been enough to acknowledge that connection without interrupting the story.

And what about Daredevil? Exactly the same problem. I would have been satisfied with just a few frames of Matt Murdock sitting behind the bars of his cell, sensing that Spider-Man was nearby. It did not require a full scene or a gratuitous cameo. One carefully constructed image would have been enough to excite the audience and connect both worlds.

There is also a major problem during the final act.

Our friendly neighborhood Spider-Man risks his life to save Jean Grey from a shot fired by the Punisher, and Frank ultimately takes him to the hospital. Sometime later, we see Peter lying in a hospital bed while Frank explains that the doctors had to completely destroy the suit in order to save his life.

That means they necessarily saw his face and discovered his identity.

And that is where the plot hole appears: once they learned who he was, they should have discovered that Peter Parker practically does not exist in any recognizable public record as a consequence of what happened at the end of *No Way Home*. So what was the point of that entire storyline and everything Peter sacrificed?

The problem becomes even more obvious in the final scene, when Peter casually walks out through the hospital’s main entrance dressed as Peter Parker. If the doctors had to remove his suit and saw that he was Spider-Man, how is it possible that nobody recognizes him, questions him, detains him, or at the very least reacts to such an enormous revelation?

Anyway…

I did think that Ned unconsciously remembering Peter through their handshake at the end was a beautiful and emotionally intelligent detail. It subtly suggests that, even though his memory was altered, certain emotional connections remain buried somewhere inside him.

But it is time to move forward.

I want to see Harry Osborn. I want to see Gwen Stacy. I want to see Peter finally become a photographer and build a life of his own, rather than constantly depending on the legacy of the Avengers.

I hope *Spider-Man 5* has the courage to explore that stage of the character’s life with the maturity, drama, and cinematic ambition it deserves.

Peter Parker has already lost far too much. Now it is time to watch him grow, rebuild his life, and finally become the definitive version of Spider-Man.

author: CinemaSerf
content: "Peter Parker" (Tom Holland) is pining. After having to sacrifice everyone's memory of him to save the world in the last film, he now has to swing from building to building in his red and blue kevlar stopping crimes whilst the biggest of all - his loss of "MJ" (Zendaya) remains unsolvable. The poor fella is lonely and so is putting all his efforts into his work to the extent that his police pal "DeWolff" (Liza Colón-Zayes) is starting to worry about his wellbeing. Well it isn't long before he is too - his spidey-senses are all over the shop. What's occurring? Well a chat with the sauna-dwelling "Black Widow" (Florence Pugh) following an Azazel-like experience with an ostensibly malevolent creature that can jump from person to person to person - but that can't use him as a conduit - starts to really get him confused. On the personal level, he has learned that spiders have three stages to their lives, so perhaps this is just a natural readjustment? He reckons a chat with "Banner" (Mark Ruffalo) might help - incognito, of course, but that only seems to make matters even worse. Might he, too, need an inhibitor to stop himself turning into something altogether more dangerous as his internal symbiosis between human and arachnid looks compromised? Meantime, he does make progress in identifying his ruthless and powerful new nemesis, but that doesn't help him explain why she is so bent on destroying the city's enforcement bureau and exacting her vengeance on it's boss "Metzger" (Tramell Tillman). Can he sort this out before he is subsumed by his new-found nature and, of course, what can he do about "MJ"? It's ten years since Holland first donned the red mask and as much as with watching the actor, we can also watch how his characterisation of "Spider-Man" has evolved. There are certainly plenty of set-piece action scenes - usually in tandem with Jon Bernthal's entertaining "Punisher", but there is also a little more soul to this film. It's much more of a characterful look at the man behind the eyes, of a troubled soul - but not in any sort of melodramatic fashion; more a study of just how loneliness can effect a person, any person, and of how difficult it can be for them to admit the problem let alone reach out to anyone. Zendaya is anything but the damsel in distress here too. There's no high-pitched squealing or "save-me, save-me" tied to a scaffold by the baddie sort of stuff. Indeed there's actually a distinct lack of the traditional baddie here and as the story unfolds the messy carnage starts to look like someone else's manifestation of solitude, too. This is certainly a piece in the puzzle of the MCU - with "Avengers" and "X-Men" related threads, but it doesn't mess about with it's timelines and so we are presented with something enjoyable and quickly paced, but just a little more substantial too - quite an achievement for a man who can't get his sponsors to make him red and blue spidey-pants too!

author: RetroWill
content:
Not an absolute disaster, but 6.5/10 at best. It falls well short of the previous trilogy, and it baffles me how it’s breaking records and pulling top reviews. It felt like a tired, bloated movie riding purely on hype and pent-up demand for a Tom Holland outing. 

My biggest issue was the core supporting cast. The emotional weight of No Way Home relied on Peter's sacrifice so they could live safe lives. Bringing them back when they don't even remember him felt like a total cop-out. They served zero narrative purpose and were clearly included out of obligation. Reverting on that sacrifice undercuts the last film, and the story would've been far tighter without them taking up screen time. 

The pacing and stakes were just as frustrating. A weak central conflict left a 2.5-hour movie dragging with shockingly little happening. To mask the lack of momentum, shoehorned hero cameos were jammed in for fan service rather than Peter's arc, weighing the story down with broader MCU maintenance. 

The action and visuals were equally lacklustre. Instead of grounded, street-level acrobatics, set pieces felt generic and CGI-heavy, with a rushed third act trading emotional payoff for a noisy climax. 

Overall, a mediocre effort. It's fine for a casual evening out, but as a flagship release, it’s underwhelming. Fans expecting a sharp follow-up will feel the franchise is running on fumes. It should have cut ties with the past to stand alone or start a fresh trilogy. Admittedly a tough task, but it would’ve made a far better fourth film.

author: popcar2
content:
Easily the worst Tom Holland Spiderman movie. The plot is unambitious and leaves so many plot points hanging it feels like barely anything was resolved, and they were scrambling to create a third act where Spiderman has to fight anything.

Why would they introduce Jean and then not resolve her plot line… At all? She starts the movie on the run, looks for her sister, realizes she’s dead, then goes back to being on the run. It didn’t really feel like we accomplished anything. It didn't feel like she had any character arc because we still don't know anything about her, other than she's mad at the people who kidnapped her sister.

Also, the twist of her not being the villain is CRAZY to me because she was insanely evil and spent most of the movie messing with Spiderman, threatening to kill his girlfriend, possessing multiple people and making them attempt suicide, and causing untold damage… only for the movie to end with “actually she’s a really nice person deep down inside?” What??? She was blatantly evil and sadistic, and now she’s just cool and misunderstood?

So much of Jean becoming a villain was out of convenience so there could be something for Spiderman to fight. Why would Jean run a tank through the city and plant a bomb if she wants to keep a low profile? Why did she free Scorpion? You also can't just make EVERY action scene about fighting mind-controlled villains. Oh my god, it's Scorpion... But he's mind controlled! It's Hulk but he's mind controlled! It's The Hand but they're mind controlled!!! It's a bunch of security guards but they're...! Oh nevermind, they just wanted to fight Spiderman for fun.

Half of the plot is just Spiderman getting the confidence to re-introduce himself to his friends. I totally get *why* they’re doing it and it’s nice that they reconnect in a believable way… But it’s just such a boring plot idea. The whole emotional core of the movie is just “guy connects with characters he used to be friends with last movie”. It takes an entire movie to reset the status quo back to the previous movie. Imagine if they spent this time introducing any new fun characters instead of re-introducing ones we already know.

The Hand is also just hanging out in New York and it’s never explained or resolved. Spiderman’s powers freaking out is never resolved but I guess it’s just implied he gets over it now that he has friends again. Jean Gray baits you into thinking they’re introducing mutants to the MCU but they never do. The director guy was supposedly left alive but we never see if anything happened to him…? Did they just let him go with zero consequences?

So much wasted potential and wasted time. Everything was kinda half assed. The only thing I can really say I liked was the direction, it felt a lot more dynamic and less flat than the other Tom Holland spiderman movies. I loved the swinging scenes. Everything else? Bleh.

author: andrewtislercinephile
content: *Spider-Man: Brand New Day* is an example of why Tom Holland's Peter Parker / Spider-Man is my favorite incarnation of the character in live-action. The story is the most mature of the Sony/MCU Spider-Man films, showing how Peter navigates being a superhero in a world where people forgot his name. Because Dr. Strange had wiped people's memories with a spell at the end of the previous film, *No Way Home*, both Ned Leeds and MJ don't remember him, leading to a fractured relationship between the three of them, but at the same time, their dynamics are still in there somewhere, and the way they handle their reconciliation-ranging from MJ drawing Peter and Ned building Lego sets together to Peter and Ned recreating their handshake at the end-is poignant and poetically symbolic because it shows that their connections are still airtight, even if MJ and Ned don't know who Peter Parker currently is. Now regarding Jean Grey, I was a little bit skeptical at first of her being the antagonist, especially after having seen the Disney+ series *X-Men '97*, where her dynamic as a mom to who eventually becomes Cable is one of the most mature forms of storytelling in media, but giving her the tragic reason of losing her sister Sara to the Department of Damage Control's actions made her very sympathetic. And the plot twist the "V-Max" she was looking for is just a vent is brilliant writing because it shows that just like Jean, Sara was also delusioned by the DODC's actions, and it led to her own demise when they pushed her too far and killed her. The way they handled Peter's powers evolving was smart as it didn't take away from who he is as a superhero-that being a normal person with superpowers-but it also increased what his powers were capable of doing. Giving him organic webbing is also a fun callback to the Sam Raimi trilogy, and Peter even mentions it when he finds out that he no longer needs synthetic web fluid. Florence Pugh's role as Yelena Boleva was really funny because her using a bathhouse as an "office" is so inappropriate it's comedy gold, and having her be a comic relief character after her role in *Thunderbolts\** really shows how forming a new team of superheroes has made her loosen up a little bit. In addition, it made sense why Hulk would be in this movie, as like Peter, he is a normal person with a mutation and the idea of the "inhibitor" helped stabilize Peter's powers, but at the same time, it also limited what he could do. I would say something about Michael Giacchino's musical score, but A) I don't need to talk about the music in every review I make on here, and B) We all know how amazing of a composer he is. In conclusion, *Spider-Man: Brand New Day* delivers a lot of what I love about MCU Spider-Man while bringing a rich, mature new story that continues the timeline of Tom Holland's iconic superhero and pushes him to the absolute extreme.

author: Nick
content: Zach Cregger takes Capcom's zombie-outbreak survival horror and does exactly what a video game adaptation should do: capture the *feeling* of the games instead of slavishly recreating cutscenes. Rather than shoehorning in Leon or Claire, he builds an original story around Bryan (Austin Abrams), a hapless medical courier who stumbles into an outbreak near Raccoon City — and it works because Cregger clearly loves this world rather than just licensing it. The tense, blood-soaked gore is offset by moments of levity and humor, that signature Cregger tonal whiplash from Barbarian and Weapons — genuinely unsettling dread punctuated by "what the fuck" comedic beats that shouldn't work together but do. It's easily the best live-action Resident Evil yet. Only real complaint: the ending. Hard swerve that undercuts the tension built for two hours. Docking half a star for that alone — everything before it is a near-perfect survival horror movie.

author: TheFilmCritics.org
content:
The best kind of survival horror knows that darkness is not merely a lack of light—it is a promise that something is waiting just beyond it. That instinct serves *Resident Evil* remarkably well, delivering a film that finally understands the eerie isolation and creeping dread that made the games so enduring.

The atmosphere is easily one of the movie's greatest strengths. Dark corridors, quiet stretches and an almost oppressive sense of isolation give the film the texture of survival horror rather than generic creature-feature action. The story's emphasis on being alone and cut off from safety captures the essence of the games, often making the viewer feel as though they are navigating the next room alongside the protagonist.

That commitment to suspense pays off. The film knows when to hold back and when to strike, and its jump scares are generally effective because they are built around genuine tension rather than simply being loud interruptions. There is a satisfying uncertainty to many sequences, with the audience constantly wondering what might emerge next.

The movie's original story may divide longtime fans, particularly those expecting a more direct adaptation of established Resident Evil lore. Yet setting an original narrative alongside the events of the games proves to be a sensible way to reboot the franchise. After so many previous films, a clean entry point for newcomers feels overdue. More importantly, the filmmakers clearly understand the source material: the weapons, video-game-like level structure, expendable side characters and various franchise tie-ins all feel deliberately designed rather than randomly inserted.

The practical effects are another highlight. The blood, gore and grotesque creature work have a convincing physicality that makes the horror considerably more satisfying. Unfortunately, the CGI is less consistent. Some effects blend reasonably well, while others are conspicuously digital, creating an uneven visual experience. The monsters themselves also suffer from the film's eagerness to showcase them. Their progression can feel suspiciously convenient, while some creatures are dispatched almost as quickly as they are introduced. At times, it resembles a monster highlight reel instead of allowing individual threats to develop into memorable encounters.

Pacing is sometimes inconsistent. Certain scenes rush through moments that deserved more room to breathe and build suspense, while others linger when the story clearly needs to move forward. The subplot involving the protagonist's girlfriend is particularly frustrating because it ultimately is inconsequential. There are also moments when the protagonist's goofy, humorous behavior clashes with the seriousness or urgency of the situation, making his overall tone sometimes feel inappropriate.

The ending may leave some viewers wanting more, although expectations matter here. *Resident Evil* has never been primarily about delivering profound narrative closure; audiences come for the monsters, scares, tension and grisly spectacle. On those terms, the film generally delivers. Viewers unfamiliar with the games will also miss some of the more specific references, but that does not prevent the movie from functioning as an accessible horror story in its own right.

Considering the franchise's uneven cinematic history, this *Resident Evil* is an effective return to its survival-horror roots with a story that deserves being told. It is not without rough edges, but the atmosphere, suspense, practical effects and understanding of what makes the games work give it a distinct identity. The movie is an imperfect but genuinely entertaining reboot that truly captures the essence of *Resident Evil* rather than feeling like it only wears the name.

author: CinemaSerf
content: Courier "Bryan" (Austin Abrams) is charged with delivering a vital organ through snowy conditions to a distant city hospital whilst arguing with his girlfriend on the phone about what to do about her recently discovered pregnancy. Next thing, he's clouted a woman wandering the woods at night with his car, and that's just the start of things going perilously wrong for this young man as she appears to have certain traits of lithe and nimble immortality and - well maybe she isn't alone? Abrams holds this together really quite well, and his dead pan delivery is really pretty engaging. Sure, the plot itself isn't that original and it's not really so similar to the 2002 version, but the wintry conditions set the scene darkly and a little claustrophobically and there's some fun to be had from a dialogue that tells us amidsts all his perils, that his socks are wet! The visual effects used to conjure up his nemesis are used sparingly but still quite effectively and the traditionally accumulating elements of the video game shoot'-em-up that we find here are actually acknowledged as part of the humour. The ending wasn't my favourite - it has something of the gory slapstick to it and maybe suggests a sequel, but Abrams holds the film together entertainingly by characterising his "Bryan" as an adaptable and cheeky character that - unusually for me - I actually did want to root for rather than see gobbled up by any monster. It's really hard to be fresh with this genre - same old, same old, week in, week out - but this spent more time on the writing and on a lead actor who leaves out the histrionics and brings us something that's really quite good fun.

author: Sierbahnn
content: As a adaptation of the Resident Evil franchise, this is really, really good. It beats the last movie, Welcome to Raccoon City, and is far more in line with the feeling of playing a Resident Evil game. The main protagonist isn't a skilled operative or military, he's just a guy who happens to get tangled up in extraordinarily gory and scary circumstances. He therefore acts accordingly. He struggles with things that action heroes take for granted, and it makes him far more interesting to watch than the protagonists of the last movie, for instance. The effect work is, of course, superb, as it would need to be in a movie like this, and it is a fun time overall. I recommend this wholeheartedly.

author: Manuel São Bento
content:

Rating: B

I went into RESIDENT EVIL having never played or watched a single entry in this franchise, and I still had a blast. Zach Cregger turns a video game he clearly loves into a horror-comedy that's relentlessly gory, genuinely funny, and stuffed with jump scares that actually worked on me. It's predictable once the machinery kicks in, and it doesn't carry the thematic weight of his last two films, but as a purely fun night at the movies, this delivers exactly what it promises.

author: kevinzhang87
content:
Resident Evil 2026 discards survival horror to deliver an relentless comedy special masquerading as an apocalyptic outbreak. Director Zach Cregger trades genuine dread for punchlines, turning bio-weapon chaos into an arena for cynical, rapid-fire banter.

Instead of claustrophobic tension, characters treat flesh-eating abominations like mild annoyances, tossing off mean-spirited quips faster than spent shotgun shells. While die-hard franchise purists seeking atmospheric dread will end up disappointed, fans of black comedy will relish the absurdity. It’s brutal, deeply sarcastic, and utterly uninterested in scaring you.

In short, this is not a Resident Evil movie. This is a stand-up show packed with cynical gags.

author: The Fixate & Binge Podcast, w/ Joe Curdy
content:
Zach Cregger's **RESIDENT EVIL** is this year's most terrifying—and humorous—horror film. Cregger's take on the storied video game-turned-film franchise refreshingly charts its own terror-strewn path into body horror and well-executed jump scares.

After the critical and financial success of last year's **WEAPONS**, the announcement of Cregger's plans to write and direct his next film from video game source material was not entirely met with universal optimism. The track record of video game film adaptations is enough to give anyone pause—as a literal graveyard of predecessors still serves as an awkward reminder of poor choices and poorer intentions, from 1993's risible **SUPER MARIO BROS**. to the embarrassment that is 2005's **DOOM**.

More concerning, the **RESIDENT EVIL** film franchise has already worn out its welcome with moviegoers, both critically and financially, with six (yes, SIX) films starring Milla Jovovich, and even a failed seventh film in 2021, **RESIDENT EVIL: WELCOME TO RACCOON CITY**, that served as a reboot.

This is the equivalent of hearing Judd Apatow wants to make a **POLICE ACADEMY** movie. No one could be more relieved to be wrong to ever doubt Cregger's decisions and instincts as a writer and director. Mea culpa, Mr. Cregger, mea culpa.

And what makes Cregger's take on the intellectual property so refreshingly new is his understanding of horror when balanced against humor. Cregger seems to know exactly when his audiences need to come up for air after terrifying moments of tension and atmosphere, with humor serving as the necessary oxygen to give audiences a breather before lurching forward into some new fresh hell.

Austin Abrams stars as Bryan, an underachieving, hapless medical transport delivery driver who accepts an offer of double compensation to deliver a medical package outside of his normal delivery zone, in the infamous **RACCOON CITY**. Careening through the snow-strewn mountain roads at night, one terrifying encounter after another ratchets up the growing sense of dread as Bryan draws closer and closer to his destination.

Abrams is deserving of praise for leaning into the anxiety of his experiences, fumbling with a First Player perspective hilariously into one moment of terror after another with very relatable naïveté. 

This is Cregger's best film as a horror director—and despite the ambiguity of the film's WTF ending (and no mid- or end-credits secret scene to slake the appetites of fans)—one can only hope Cregger agrees to take audiences on another ride through Raccoon City with the same anarchy and fun as his **RESIDENT EVIL**.

author: CinemaSerf
content: We discover from fairly early on that the young "Gemma" (Charli Penton) is usually left to her own devices by her clearly distracted mother, so it's no surprise when we spin forward a generation and discover that she (now Amelie Eve) has had to deal with a fairly traumatic experience before going on to becoming a dentist and raising her own daughter "Maya" (Island Austin) in the very same house. She's been dating, on the quiet, the hunky cop "Nick" (Brandon Perez) and all in her life seems stable until a visit to the basement with her child unearths some old family memorabilia - and then things start going bump in her dreams. A terrifying experience in a pillow fort and an even more gruesome one in her own dental practice encourages her to seek advice from "Clare" (Maisie Richardson-Sellars) who acts as a conduit to the world of the benign "Elise" (Lin Shaye) who explains something of the evil that is trying to escape from the "Further" realm and invade the world of the living with a population of zombified and hungry corpses. It seems that "Gemma" has a special gift that has attracted this menace and that it won't stop until she stops it. How? Well that's going to involve convincing "Maya" and her boyfriend that she's not lost the plot and that the dangers are real. There are a few genuinely affecting scenes here - especially amidst the ostensible safety of cushions and sheets, but the rest of this lacks much by way of jeopardy. Regular watchers of these films will probably agree that the supposedly insurmountable barriers between the malignant, the nefarious, the past and the present all appear to be wafer thin with an all too familiar surfeit of connecting two-way red doors. The acting is all fine and some of the photography does help to craft a certain sense of peril, but this isn't so much insidious as straightforward and though it does have it's moments, it's a franchise that has had it's day and ought now to be put in a box of it's own in the cellar with a label saying "open in fifty years".

author: Dean
content:
*Insidious: Out of the Further* isn't reinventing the wheel on its sixth go-around, but it delivers enough legitimate chills to earn its keep. Directed by Jacob Chase, the film shines brightest when it leans into surreal visual set pieces—including a nauseatingly tense dental-chair sequence and a claustrophobic, spatial-warping couch fort. Amelia Eve gives a strong, grounded lead performance, and Lin Shaye’s return as Elise Rainier provides the usual warm, ghostly nostalgia that ties the franchise together.

Movie relies a bit too heavily on loud, predictable jump scares though. It doesn't reach the heights of James Wan's original films, but with solid lead performances and a few standout sequences, it’s a fun, spooky ride that lands at a comfortable **7/10**.

author: Manuel São Bento
content:
Check out my full review @ https://www.manuelsbento.com/the-odyssey-2026-christopher-nolans-most-faithful-epic-is-also-his-most-ambitious-one/

Rating: A+ (updated after second viewing)

THE ODYSSEY is a maximalist, deeply faithful adaptation of Homer's poem that somehow ends on a quiet, contemplative note despite everything it throws at you along the way. Completely unafraid of its own scale and scope, it's ten years of war, myth, and horror (!) woven into the story so tightly that the whole thing paradoxically feels more grounded, not less. An astonishingly stacked ensemble led by a phenomenal Matt Damon, deceptively convincing practical effects, and filmmaking craft firing on every level. Ludwig Göransson's score alone is worth the ticket. Easily one of the best theatrical experiences of the year. This is Christopher Nolan at his most alive.

SECOND VIEWING:

Just rewatched THE ODYSSEY and somehow loved it even more the second time around. Knowing the whole story only made certain scenes hit harder, especially the moment Odysseus finally opens up to Penelope about what the Battle of Troy really cost him. Cried through most of it. The film moves with even more confidence once you already know where it's headed, and I can't find a single scene I'd cut. This is my first A+ since Dune: Part Two.

author: AlphaLucifer
content: The hype was massive, the crowd was packed, but the boredom in the theatre at the end credits said it all. A 172-minute film felt like it was a 6+ hour watch. This isn’t a respectful adaptation of Homer’s epic; it’s a bloated, self-important disaster that butchers the source material, erases Greek identity, and rams woke DEI nonsense down your throat while delivering some of the worst big-name acting I’ve seen in years. Right from the opener, it was clear Nolan had zero interest in Homer’s actual text. Instead of going back to the original Greek or a faithful classic translation, he based the whole thing on Emily Wilson’s modern, feminist-slanted version, that crappy, agenda-driven reinterpretation that twists the poem’s language, downplays traditional heroism, and injects contemporary gender politics. No wonder the soul is missing. **_The Odyssey_** is the foundational poem of Western civilisation, cunning, nostos, divine meddling, human endurance, told in sweeping oral poetry. Nolan reduces it to mere nothingness. Matt Damon as Odysseus is the biggest miscast of all; he sleepwalks through it like a tired Jason Bourne in a chiton, delivering flat quips with zero charisma or bronze-age king energy. No wit, no depth, just brooding stares. Zendaya’s Athena is wooden and out of place, Tom Holland’s Telemachus is hyperactive but empty, Anne Hathaway’s Penelope feels phoned in, and Robert Pattinson’s turn is lost in the gloom. Charlize Theron as Calypso, Jon Bernthal, walked and looking like he's out of a Robin-Hood film, and John Leguizamo all feel awkwardly shoehorned in with zero chemistry or gravitas. Worst of all is Elliot Page as Sinon (replacing Achilles after backlash); he runs around like a marionette doll with stiff, unnatural movements that kill every action beat. Lupita Nyong’o as Helen of Troy (and Clytemnestra) is completely out of place and entirely misrepresents the characters. The entire main cast is miscast to hell. Bad acting across the board sinks what little soul remains. The zero Greekness is unforgivable. This is the profoundly Greek cornerstone of Western literature, the first great literary piece of our civilisation, and Hollywood turned it into a generic fantasy IP. Greece helped fund this thing with taxpayer money, yet there’s not a single Greek actor in a major role. No olive-skinned warriors, no Mediterranean fire, no authentic Mycenaean aesthetics, let alone authentic period costumes. In fact, the landscapes and costumes look like leftover Nolan dark fantasy. Even worse, they loaded it with actors in roles that directly contradict the Homeric descriptions and classical imagery of ancient Greek heroes and gods... what the hell was Travis Scott doing in this film! It is a cultural erasure at its most blatant, profiting off Greece’s heritage while replacing the people it belongs to. The premiere didn’t even happen in Athens because they were scared of the backlash. Smart move, because Greeks are rightly outraged. The woke DEI casting is peak insult. Lupita as Helen, the face that launched a thousand ships, really? Homer's text depicted her with golden hair and fair beauty, but Nolan decided to 'modernise' the text to fit into today's woke-DEI agenda. Zendaya as Athena... with her usual dull facial expressions? Elliot Page’s tiny 'man-playing-woman-playing-man' Achilles stand-in? The rainbow ensemble screams committee quotas over truth. It’s not “inclusive”; it’s dishonest revisionism that strips the story of its European roots and historical context. On top of that, Nolan’s signature grim, dark tone, all brooding shadows and moral ambiguity, feels completely wrong for this story. **The Odyssey** belongs to bright Mediterranean sun, blue seas, blue skies, and passionate Hellenic vitality, even amid tragedy. Slapping his Batman/Dunkirk gloom over it makes everything feel oppressive and mismatched, like forcing a Nordic winter onto the Aegean; indeed, he even included Viking-style ships, of course completely unrelated to the period! The music doesn't fit in any scene, and the rap at the end credits was another WTF moment. Visually watching some scenes in IMAX is impressive, but it’s an empty spectacle. Feels like there was not even any climax to the point I thought by the middle of the film, when will it end? Save your money and don't bother. Reread the original **Odyssey** instead, **Homer's Odyssey**. In fact, go ahead and reread **Homer's Iliad** too while you're at it to see how much the actors and Nolan himself knew nothing of the actual original material. Nolan’s _The Odyssey_ is a one-star, two-star mess at best, with terrible acting, cultural disrespect, reliance on a politicised translation, 'modernised' like Nolan himself said, for the public, while in truth it was for the critics and Oscar voters, and it is also total proof of everything that is wrong with modern Hollywood, wrapped in expensive packaging.

author: Brent Marchant
content: As one of the 2026 summer movie season’s most anticipated releases, writer-director Christopher Nolan’s screen adaptation of Homer’s literary epic, The Odyssey, has generated more than its share of reactions and for a variety of reasons. So I’ll come right to the point on my view of this release: I liked it, but I didn’t love it. This retelling of the diverse experiences of Greek warrior Odysseus (Matt Damon) on returning to his Grecian home of Ithaca after fighting in the Trojan War explores the many adventures and profound soul-searching of his 10-year journey, the second half of a 20-year-long absence. Waiting for him back home are his devoted wife, Penelope (Anne Hathaway), who has long been courted by a band of would-be suitors like Antinous (Robert Pattinson) who believe her husband is dead, and Telemachus (Tom Holland), the son who’s never met his father and stands to succeed him as King of Ithaca should he be officially declared deceased. This historic drama, a common reading selection in many high school English lit classes, thus follows the intrigue and adventures from the perspectives of the trip and the homefront, many of which viewers are likely to find familiar in this cinematic depiction. However, not everything works in this adaptation. For starters, the film is too long with its 2:52:00 runtime, especially during the picture’s languishing, talky opening hour. Then there’s the writing, which incorporates more than its share of ill-fitting contemporary dialogue, material that should have never made its way into the final script. And there are noticeable exclusions and underdeveloped sequences from the source material that could have been included and/or tweaked in the film narrative with the removal of overlong, extraneous material. For example, despite frequent references to the Greek gods, their presence in the film is largely absent save for a few conversations between Odysseus and Athena, the Goddess of Wisdom (Zendaya). A similar fate befalls Helen of Troy (Lupita Nyong’o), “the woman who launched a thousand ships” and prompted the Trojan War in the first place, and Calypso (Charlize Theron), the mysterious caregiver who loves an ailing Odysseus and nurses him back to health for seven years in the midst of his journey. With those shortcomings aside, however, “The Odyssey” has its share of strengths, too, such as the picture’s decidedly engaging second half, as well as its fine performances, especially those of Hathaway, Pattinson, Holland and Samantha Morton as Circe, a witch whom Odysseus encounters during the trip home. Those looking for action-adventure segments will find plenty of those here as well, although the special effects depicting them are noticeably inconsistent – great in sequences like the Greeks’ ambush of their opponent’s stronghold with the ploy of the Trojan Horse and the soldiers’ dangerous encounter with the massive, menacing whirlpool Charybdis, and not so great during their contacts with the seductively voiced Sirens, the one-eyed giant Cyclops and the multi-headed cliff-dwelling monster Scylla. It’s difficult to pinpoint exactly how and why this production failed to live up to some of the high expectations that had been set for it, though it’s a safe bet that it might have fallen prey to believing its own pre-release hype, especially coming off of the impressive and well-earned success of Nolan’s previous effort, “Oppenheimer” (2023). Obviously, viewers will have to make up their own minds, but keeping the foregoing impressions in mind may prove helpful in formulating those opinions as audiences wend their way through their own personal odysseys.

author: Nick
content: Homer's epic has endured for thousands of years, and Nolan's adaptation reminds you exactly why. Superb acting, cinematography, and seeing it in IMAX just adds to everything that makes it epic. The year's best film, full stop.

author: CinemaSerf
content: With a production design worthy of Sir Ridley Scott, Christopher Nolan takes us into antiquity for his take on the second instalment of Homer's Trojan War stories. I have to say it's maybe not the most impressive of wooden horses that is left as a tribute for the maybe just a little too gullible Trojans, but now we know that this decade-long siege has all ended in a mighty conflagration and that Odysseus (Matt Damon) is keen on returning to Ithaca where his wife and son await him. On that island, though, strife is rife. Penelope (Anne Hathaway) is being besieged by an army of suitors like Antinous (Robert Pattinson) and the young Telemachus (Tom Holland) isn't really best equipped to step in and protect his mother from their machinations. Now flitting between the island's domestic issues and the legendary trials of the returning husband, Nolan tries to weave the two threads together in quite a compelling fashion. The snag for me throughout this epic drama is that we spent too much time on Ithaca with the family issues and not enough time with Odysseus and his crew as they faced a plethora of deadly foes and evil temptations as they traversed the Mediterranean. Too many of their adventures are too tightly compressed and involve a few scenes of menace before everyone rushes back to their ships - usually fewer than arrived - before continuing on their dangerous travels. Much is told thanks to his memory-provoking conversation with the lotus peddling Calypso (Charlize Theron) but again, we don't really get to grips much with who she is or what he is doing on her beautiful island. Charybdis and the Sirens, even the Cyclops are all given a little too much short shrift as we dwell more at the other end of his voyage on the issues facing the young Telemachus as he travels to Sparta to find news from Menelaus and his now restored wife Helen. The visual effects are pretty spectacular and Damon manages quite well to craft a character who is brave and ingenious but also troubled by both the destruction of Troy and by his behaviour whilst participating in that. What we also avoid here is much involvement from the Olympians. Barring some regular references to Zeus's laws of hospitality and a few scenes with Athena (Zendaya) who appears to be acting more as his psychiatrist than a goddess of war and wisdom whose statue was unceremoniously decapitated during the assault of the city, and whose temple was unceremoniously defiled - we don't really involve them. If you've read even the briefest of adaptations of the novel, you'll know that many of his difficulties getting home were due to the anger of gods like Poseidon and Apollo - yet those characters remain somewhat omni-absent. Perhaps, and I don't write this lightly, three hours simply isn't long enough to do justice to the characterful complexities of the story? I did enjoy this and it flew past, but I really wanted much more of the fantastic, the horror and the terror and maybe just a little less of the troubled souls presented here, and I was just a little bit disappointed as I left. Perhaps he's saving more for the director's cut?

author: MonksFilms
content:
So I went to see this one 2x because I had to confirm if I was tripping because my reaction just wasn't what most people felt when they saw The Odyssey according to the reviews here. The second viewing only confirmed my initial reaction, it's a good enough film but it not a mastepiece.

On a technical filmmaking level The Odyssey puts foot to ass and delivers some hard hitting moments like the cyclops encounter and the battle with the giant Laestrygonians. It's also immersive watching Odysseus and his crew on thier ship as they're traveling about the region, you feel like you're on the ship's deck. It's a film that excels at visual spectacle many times, combined with some inventive sound design and there are many moments that will stick with you.

So then there's that other half of the film and it's mostly were I felt the biggest disconnect from the material. Half of this film is spent with Penelope and Telemechus and how they navigate Odysseus' absence. These stretches are clunky and poorly written IMO. I wanted to groan out loud at their final confrontation before the last feast. Anne Hathaway's eyes and forhead veins bulge as she utters poorly written line after poorly written line in the strangest cadence. There's so many moments like this. 

I think Tom Holland and John Leguizamo seemed the most comfortable and natural while saying the dialogue. It wasn't even the modern language that bothered me. I just ask, why go through the effort of stacking this cast and then turn around and give them crumbs to work with in terms of a script? It really made it hard to connect with these characters on an emotional level. I think that's why the dog was added, so folks could feel something. Make a little effort so we can have some energy in these exchanges and John Bernthal doesn't just sound like Frank Castle in a robe. I think probably the most consistent group was Telemechus vs the suitors in the dining hall, and that's thanks more to Corey Hawkins and Robert Pattison's abilities than what was written for then. Tom also did a great job of being pissed and taking jabs at them. They made me laugh a few times, I genuinely wanted to fight them. Also I do give a lot of props to the Cerce scene. That was one of the few times where the dialogue and acting were in sync and cooking. Outside of that, memorable bars and exchanges were few and far between. Zendaya, Lupita, and Charlize just felt wasted. So many of these moments I just didn't care for and their blandness really stood out a second time. The average Game Of Thrones episode plays better than this dramatically.

Overall I think it's a technial marvel, but there's too many films that have come out this year that I've enjoyed so much more that prevent me from putting this one among them.

author: ℛ.
content:
After watching this in IMAX, I’m not surprised why people are talking about this movie. 

I’m not someone deeply versed in Greek mythology, but I can say that this film is an absolutely insane masterpiece. The way the storylines gradually converged kept me fully engaged, allowing me to watch this nearly three-hour film without ever feeling drowsy. Not to mention the visuals and cinematography—it felt like a real feast for the eyes. Although for the first dozen minutes or so I kept wondering, "Where is Odysseus?", my curiosity was ultimately satisfied once he appeared on screen.

I don't know about others, but I was thoroughly impressed by the performances of Matt Damon and Anne Hathaway.

I mean, Anne Hathaway—you are a true queen. Absolutely stunning. I loved how she conveyed all those "suppressed" emotions; she made me feel that same sense of stifled anguish, even though I wasn't the one playing Penelope.

And Matt Damon—his portrayal of Odysseus’s regret made it impossible not to feel the sting of the betrayal he suffered at the hands of those he trusted.

I know how confusing Greek mythology can be and how chaotic the conflicts are (even if I haven't delved too deeply into them), but this film strikes the perfect balance.

Last but not least, I like you, Robert Pattinson, but I felt like punching you when you played Antinous. And one more special shout-out to Tom Holland and Zendaya—you two absolutely cooked it as Telemachus and Athena.

author: karip
content:
Many viewers seem to criticize this movie for not showing “how it really happened” — that is, as Homer wrote it. But why should it?

The movie is not for people who couldn’t be bothered to read the book but still want to know the story, nor is it trying to retell Homer’s story exactly. And it probably wouldn’t make a very good movie for a modern audience if it did, given how different our worldview and experiences are.

Like every work derived from Homer’s original (including translations, or even a modern reader’s reading of the original) this is **one interpretation**. And a very good one, in my opinion.

Technically, the movie is extremely well made, and I think it captures the desperation and fragmented nature of the original story, as well as the sense that much of what happens is, in some way, bogus. There were a few minor things that weren’t to my taste, as there are in all Nolan movies, but still: 9/10.

author: luca1308
content:
# A movie made for cinemas, with some typical Nolan choices 

Great movie overall, just what you need to get people flocking to cinemas. Excellent cinematography, practical AND computer-generated effects. An immaculate immersive experience. Just the way you should put an epos on film. The approach is very different from what 300 did and a comparsion of those movies would be an innteresting topic from someone with more knowledge than me on movies. One is emphasizing legendary action at the cost of immersion, the other is emphasizing realism at the cost of memorable action scenes. I think that's intriguing, but now to the few "bad" things in my opinion:
 
Grade A acting from everyone except Tom Holand, who could've been switched out for a piece of wood that is making a concerned face. For the screentime he got, he earned no emotions. Jon Bernthal did more in his few minutes. The "controversial" casting choices would've stood out without the overblown controversy. As mentioned before, this is an epos, so essentially, a ancient fantasy story, maybe loosly based on real events. So by my taste, the director is free to interpret this story and put it into action in the way he wants. However, Ellen/Elliot Page doesn't sell as a man/young soldier. The scenes with her/him took me out of the immersion because the character feels off.

Secondly, I hate that ancient places are always displayed like someone went to a ruin today and restored it with minimum effort to make it barely livable. It's already bad in medieval movies, where everything is stone when we know castles had as much decor as possible (at least in the places where the important conversations take place), but I guess audiences are used to the "military" frugal, hard look of stone walls, that was establised through theatre and operas in the late 19th century and some stuck till this day. What a shame. Especially when knowing how colorful roman architecture was(inside and outside). This must have applied in some capacities to the mycenaean greeks as well. Nolan gave the inside of Ithakas palace some paint, but it still doesn't look like a place that's taken care off/people actually living in. It makes sense considering "the king has been gone for 20 years" and the general grim tone of the movie, but I still feel like it's a wasted opportunity to start a new trend of more realism. Especially since the non-methodological scenes appeared to be purposefully historically (late bronze-age) accurate.

And lastly, I simply hate Nolan combat scenes. I hate the shaky cam. Stop it. You didn't need it for this movie like you did with a stiff-neck batman or boring gun-fights. You have people going at each other with swords, at least tone down the shakiness by 50%. Please.

I will definetly buy this movie once it comes out. Probably worth more than a single rewatch for the cinematography alone.

author: misubisu
content:
**Score: 2/10    An Epic That Lost Its Way Home**

What did I miss? That's the question I kept asking myself throughout Christopher Nolan's *The Odyssey*. I was expecting so much more. The pedigree was undeniable: Nolan behind the camera, a staggering ensemble cast, a legendary source material that has endured for nearly three millennia. And yet, what unfolded on screen was, to put it bluntly, like watching a kids' movie.

**The Tone Problem: A Myth for Children**

Homer's *Odyssey* is not a children's story. It is a brutal, bloody, morally complex epic about a man who survives a decade of war only to spend another decade fighting monsters, gods, and his own flaws to get home. It deals with temptation, infidelity, vengeance, and the sheer, grinding cost of survival. Nolan's film, however, feels sanitised. The violence is bloodless. The monsters are cartoonish. The gods are reduced to plot devices. The moral ambiguities that make Odysseus a fascinating, flawed hero are sanded down into a bland, heroic archetype.

This is a film that seems terrified of its own darkness. It wants the prestige of Homer without the discomfort.

**The Coen Brothers Did It Better**

And here's the thing that kept nagging at me throughout: **the Coen Brothers did so much more with the material in *O Brother, Where Art Thou?*** Their 2000 film is a loose, Depression era adaptation of the *Odyssey*, and it crackles with wit, heart, and genuine thematic depth. It understands that the power of Homer's epic lies not in the monsters or the spectacle, but in the characters  their flaws, their longings, their stubborn, flawed humanity. The Coens took the bones of the story and built something alive, something that resonated with audiences who had never read a line of Homer. Nolan, by contrast, has taken the same bones and dressed them in expensive but lifeless armour. *O Brother* is a classic that grows richer with every viewing. This *Odyssey* will be forgotten before the year is out.

**The Performances: Wasted Talent**

The cast is extraordinary on paper. But extraordinary actors cannot save underwritten roles. The supporting players  and there are many  are given little more than extended cameos. They appear, deliver exposition, and vanish. There is no time to develop relationships, no room for chemistry to breathe. The emotional beats that should land with devastating force  the reunion with Penelope, the recognition by Argos, the slaughter of the suitors  pass by with a shrug.

**The Visuals: Spectacle Without Soul**

Nolan is a master of practical effects and large format cinematography, and there are moments of genuine visual grandeur. But spectacle without emotional investment is just noise. The set pieces feel disconnected, more like theme park attractions than narrative climaxes. The Cyclops is impressive in scale but lacks menace. The Sirens are beautiful but forgettable. The sea journeys that should feel epic feel episodic.

**The Pacing: A Slog and a Rush**

The film cannot decide what it wants to be. It rushes through key moments  Odysseus's time with Calypso, the encounter with Circe  while lingering on others that add little. The result is a film that feels both overstuffed and underdeveloped. It is, at times, genuinely boring.

**The Verdict**

*The Odyssey* is a profound disappointment. It takes one of the greatest stories ever told and reduces it to a shallow, sanitised, emotionally hollow spectacle. It is a kids' movie version of a myth that was never meant for children. It earns its 2/10 for the undeniable craft on display and the occasional glimpse of what could have been. But craft without soul is just a hollow shell.

**Watch if:** You want a visually polished but emotionally empty introduction to the story, or you're a completist for Nolan's filmography.

**Skip if:** You love Homer, you love epic storytelling, or you expect a film worthy of its source. This is not it. The Coen Brothers did it better with a fraction of the budget and a tenth of the self importance.

author: CinemaSerf
content: "Jax" (Harriet Slater) is disposing of the property of her recently deceased sister when she encounters her college friend "Luce" (Arsema Thomas) who encourages "Jax" to embrace some of the challenges sister "Shiloh" had intended to carry out before her untimely death. One such trip involves the pair travelling to Thailand and walking a precarious route four thousand feet above sea level to visit a sacred dragon that will eat all of their fears. Turning up, they discover that this route has been deemed unsafe by the authorities and that it's a no-go area. Foiled? Well, no - they meet "Jon" (Tom Brittney) who offers to guide them for $5k. A bit steep? Yes, but not as steep as the ladder up the cliffs to a rotting wooden path supported by scaffolding poles (allegedly built by monks decades ago!!). This area is prone to earthquakes, so guess what happens as they meander along towards the Devil's elbow? Actually, to be fair to this it's not it's predictability that lets it down. That has to be the responsibility of a writer who has produced some of the most banal dialogue ever to hit the silver screen and to some acting that, even when precariously perched on a plank of wood, doesn't convey any sense of fear or peril whatsoever. The last twenty minutes would actually be comical if they weren't so risible, and that sense of acrophobic menace that existed in the first film (2022) is distinctly lacking as the twist(s) in this story fail to resonate plausibly. Even the photography looks as if the camera had been turned on it's side and at no point did I actually believe that anyone had ever left the ground for this - even the drone pilot. This will look fine on the television on a winter's Friday night after some vino, but you'll never need to watch it twice.

author: CinemaSerf
content: The annoyingly verbose "Ben" (Owen Wilson) arrives in Brisbane aboard a private jet tasked with delivering a liver that could save the life of the young "Ellie" (Scarlett Crabtree) whose mother "Kate" (Leila George) is gradually climbing the walls. His ride to the hospital is to be provided by "Hank" (Alan Ritchson) who isn't best impressed that his passenger suffers from an excitable form of verbal diarrhoea - but that's just the start of his woes as they both discover that this organ is particularly rare and that the local branch of the Colombian drug-peddling mafia are determined to get their hands on it. What ought to have been a straightforward courier job quickly becomes an action-packed race across the country leaving wreckage, carnage and quite a few bodies in their wake. Naturally, as their battle for survival hots up, the two begin to bond a little - but what chance they can make it in time? Jeopardy? Well no, not really. Not with a young child lying in an hospital bed and this not sporting an "R" rating, but if you like shoot 'em up buddy movies with car chases, menacing grannies, plotting, scheming and a rare parakeet then this isn't the worst adventure movie you'll ever see. Indeed, it actually hits a little purple patch in the third quarter that is quite entertaining before a denouement that does drag things out a bit, but that doesn't actually deliver quite as expected. It's all forgettable fayre, but it killed ninety minutes in the cinema easily enough and I quite enjoyed it - even if I couldn't decide whether Wilson was simply annoying at being himself or just good at crafting a character that I'd have cheerfully fed to a large snake.

author: Brent Marchant
content: When it comes to summertime movies, many viewers expect fun thrill rides, escapist fare at its best. At the same time, though, as the summer movie season winds down, expectations tend to lower by the time August rolls around, when the dregs of its remaining releases are unceremoniously rolled out. But, every so often, audiences are in for an unexpected nifty little treat when a sleeper offering hits theaters. Such is the case with the latest effort from writer-director David Robert Mitchell, a Spielbergian sci-fi retrothriller that skillfully drops elements of the “Jurassic Park” franchise into 1980s suburbia, and it does so with a deft mix of heart-pounding action-adventure and raucous, often-campy humor. The film follows the adventures of the Platt family, mother Denise (Anne Hathaway), father Greg (Ewan McGregor), and teenage children Audrey (Maisy Stella) and Brian (Christian Convery), along with their mischievous but resourceful pooch, an Australian cattle dog named Starbuck. On the surface, everything seems fine, though, as soon becomes apparent, there are some simmering troubles in family household (marital discord, financial difficulties, potential problem drinking, the dashed dreams of adolescence). However, after a bright, intense light appears during a thunderstorm one night, the Platts’ world gets turned upside down as their neighborhood experiences a series of infrastructure collapses, along with the appearance of anomalous plant life, specimens that appear to belong to extinct prehistoric species. But that’s only the beginning, as these developments are followed by the presence of dinosaurs. Needless to say, the residents of Oak Street are stunned at what they find, and it’s not long before survival and escape become imminent concerns. But how? What’s more, how did all of this come about? Those are the questions the family and their neighbors face as their world crumbles around them. Admittedly, the premise of this story is a relatively simple one, and it occasionally turns repetitive and derivative as it plays out. However, these shortcomings are made up for by great action sequences and raucously funny laughs, many of them deliberately over the top and characterized by ample but restrained gratuitousness (though squeamish viewers may still wish to bow out). A number of typical Spielbergian tropes are also included here, such as the curmudgeonly neighbor (P.J. Byrne), the kindly old lady down the street (Anne Gee Byrd), the mild-mannered but unexpectedly tough, gun-toting mid-lifer (Emily Kuroda), the neighborhood bully (Hudson Meek) and the beautiful new neighbor girl (Jordan Alexa Davis), all of whose story threads figure into the flow of the narrative and are sufficiently wrapped up by the time the credits roll. But perhaps the biggest surprise here is the film’s integration of subtle but effective themes one might not anticipate from a production like this, such as messages related to second chances, redemption and forgiveness, which are skillfully incorporated without beating viewers over the head (credit the expertly penned script for this). Thankfully, while many critics acknowledge that there are numerous respectful nods to the “Jurassic” franchise, most astutely appreciate the big nostalgic fun in this, despite a cantankerously vocal minority of cynical peers who contend such attributes are out-and-out ripoffs of classic cinematic content. I suppose one could see things that way, but that spoils the fun, begging the question about the half-empty/half-full glass metaphor, one that ultimately comes down to your view/your choice. So what’s it going to be? Given the dearth of good, entertaining pictures at this time of year, in my view, “The End of Oak Street” is genuinely a welcome breath of fresh air in an otherwise-stale room, a late summer release that’s truly “dino-mite.”

"The End of Oak Street" is yet another fossilized production from an entertainment industry out of fresh ideas. This is essentially Jurassic Park in 1980's US suburbia. The lead in is overlong, rather boring, more than a little cliched, leaning heavily on 80's nostalgia to carry it. author: Manuel São Bento
content:
Check out my full review @ https://movieswetextedabout.com/the-end-of-oak-street-movie-review-a-stylish-amblin-style-spectacle-undone-by-tonal-indecision/

Rating: B-

THE END OF OAK STREET is a well-built summer blockbuster whose biggest obstacle is its own indecision about what it wants to be. The dinosaur spectacle is thrilling, Anne Hathaway anchors it with real gravity, Michael Giacchino’s score elevates nearly every set piece, and the Amblin-inspired craft on display is a genuine pleasure to watch unfold — but the moment the film tries to layer real emotional stakes onto a story built for popcorn thrills, the seams show, and they never fully close back up. Setting the right tone is a promise to the audience about how much to feel, and breaking that promise even once can undo a lot of goodwill a movie has otherwise earned.

content: Ok, so the whole premiss is fairly flawed. The idea that dinosaurs could roam the streets of an American town without the military - normally first on the scene if you drop your ice cream - taking centre stage with their missiles, tanks and helicopters is even more far-fetched than the idea that velociraptors and Tyrannosaurs might be gobbling up suburban citizens. But it's true! After some some very loud and unexplained noises and some brightly flashing lights, the "Platt" family awaken to find their dog missing. Perhaps "Starbuck" has gone for a coffee? Son "Brian" (Christian Convery) is very concerned but soon that's the least of his problems as with dad "Greg" (Ewan McGregor), mum "Denise" (Anne Hathaway) and sister "Audrey" (Maisy Stella) they find themselves holed up in a home with some seriously noisy and peckish neighbours. How can they possibly fight back with - literally - only a bow and arrow and a baseball bat? What now ensues is just good fun, and what's more all of the cast look like they are enjoying this daft Jurassic romp with shades of "Mysterious Island" (1961) thrown in for good measure. It's end-to-end stuff with plenty going on and although I could have done without some of the obligatory family dysfunction that always seems neccessary these days, I found this to be a great deal better than I was expecting and Hathaway proved to be something of an entertaining revelation.

author: UnexpectedCheese
content:
**A Great Premise That Never Quite Lives Up to Its Potential**

The End of Oak Street has one of those premises that immediately sells you on the movie: an ordinary suburban neighborhood suddenly finds itself surrounded by prehistoric wilderness and dinosaurs. Unfortunately, the movie itself never becomes quite as interesting as that setup.

There’s definitely fun to be had here. The dinosaur sequences are entertaining, Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor are good, and the movie moves along quickly enough that it never really becomes boring. I also appreciated that it feels more like an old-fashioned adventure movie than another attempt to build a giant franchise.

The problem is that it spends a surprising amount of time on fairly generic family drama when there’s a much more interesting story happening outside the house. The characters never become compelling enough to justify how much attention is given to their problems, and some of the emotional moments feel forced rather than earned.

It also wears its Spielberg influences very heavily on its sleeve. There’s nothing wrong with trying to capture that 1980s Amblin feeling, but at times it feels less inspired by those movies than like it’s deliberately trying to recreate them.

Still, dinosaurs attacking suburbia is a pretty difficult concept to make completely boring, and there are enough good sequences here to make it worth watching. I just wish the movie had embraced the weirdness of its premise a little more.

**6/10**

author: RealZero
content:
The movie series that would've had a perfect ending with Toy Story 3 manages to, once more, not screw up with another sequel.

So, yeah, I think Pixar once again managed to make a good movie and a good Toy Story with this one. Not the best or a totally awesome one. A safe one. But I'm still quite happy with it.

**Short summary (spoiler free):**
A good movie that, to me, feels more like an "Inside Out", where it heavily relies on the toys trying to steer Bonny's life and also has a much bigger focus on the human characters.
Jessie is a strong protagonist, but most of the other toys are actually not really important, especially the original "Andy's Toys" group.
Very nice and emotional depiction of the emotions of a child trying to make friends and the, sometimes hard, part the parents have in it, but less "toy adventure" than the previous movies.
I still recommend it, but it feels a bit different to me.


**Full review (contains basic "act" spoilers but no ending, etc.):**

Jessie does a great job as a new protagonist, and while Buzz's role isn't exactly too important for the main plot, I do think Jessie and Buzz's dynamic can work quite well. The same as Woody and Buzz did before.

The main plot is a quite nice idea: How do electronic devices influence how toys are seen and handled in the lives of kids? And I'm happy to see that it doesn't fully go the "electronic devices are bad" route.

Every Toy Story started off quite slow and tame before the emotional stuff hit. And the "how will the new toy influence our lives?" idea is once again the same that Toy Story 1 already used.
And that's actually a point where this movie feels a bit repetitive. And it's also what I mean with "it's a safe one".

The worry is the same. The reaction of the other toys is the same. And Jessie's and Buzz's tries to calm everyone down are also very much the same as Woody did about Buzz in the first movie.

In general, the big number of total toys means that the ones that are not Jessie, Bully, Buzz and the newcomers are really not important to the plot at all. Most of them sit around most of the movie and have no part in it, except for some lines at the beginning and the end.

And I think this is why especially the beginning feels much weaker than, for example, Toy Story 1. The group of Andy's toys felt more like a tightly-knit group, while this is very much a Jessie-movie.
Don't get me wrong! I like Jessie! It's a good Jessie movie! But I think this is why the first third of the movie feels slower and less impactful than Toy Story 1 despite using basically the same plot.

The second third is quite different then. ALSO showing how a child's life changes through new things, but with very different problems. The toys figure out more about the situation. Jessie's past is brought up again in more detail and how it caused trauma and made her who she is. It also introduces most of the new characters who, along with Jessie, actually are the main characters of the movie. They're not as funny and interesting to me as "Andy's toys", but they work nicely for the plot once the heavy getting-to-know phase is over.

The last third is then where the movie gets the most emotional, where all things fall together and all the newly introduced characters actually come together and show how their dynamic works. To me, this is also the strongest part of the movie in a pure sense of entertainment. It has most of the "action" part, obviously, as well.


So, what does the movie do well? I think many parts of this movie are actually "for adults/parents", because they show nicely how "fitting in" and "finding good friends" can be hard for young children. 
Parents try to help their children with it, and how they see them struggle and fail at times. Of course this can also show children how this is a normal part of life, but I think the movie "hits harder" seen from the point of the parents trying their best. But maybe that's just my perspective.

What's not so good?
The movie, to me, is far less "funny". There are no really fun gags, much more emotion comes from sadness and worry. This is not bad in itself! But I just feel that part of Toy Story was always the kind of humor that was possible because the toys are toys. Mr Potato Head being taken apart, Woody waving with Buzz's ripped off arm, stuff like that. This one does make one smile, but it wasn't a "laughing loud" one. Especially not compared to movies like "Hoppers" which were completely hilarious.

In fact, now that I think about it: The whole movie feels like "Inside Out", with the toys taking the part of the "emotions", and less than what made the other Toy Stories "Toy Story". Especially the much stronger focus on the humans, as well.

So, all in all: The movie feels like "Inside Out". It's a good movie, Jessie is a strong protagonist, emotions are shown really heavy and realistic, and I did feel for the main characters. But I also feel that thus the movie heavily relied on betting on sadness and our compassion towards Bonny instead of the adventures of the toys and the humor that used to come with it.

I think it's a good movie, but not among the best "Toy Stories".

Visually, it's really impressive, of course. I think Pixar really tried to go all-out on plants and realistic animals this time.


I originally rated it 10% better, but writing this I feel it gets most of its "positive memory" from the emotional last part, which doesn't really make up for the beginning.
But yeah, hard to say. Still a good one!

author: CinemaSerf
content: Even though there is a pretty clear and potent message here, this isn't my favourite from the franchise - in fact, in many ways it reminded me of what I felt was the much more engaging "Ron's Gone Wrong" (2021). "Bonnie" is a lonely little girl who still plays with her toys. This earns her the ridicule of her more tech-savvy classmates at school and so, despondent, her parents buy her a "Lilypad". This promises to be her route to inclusion and popularity and soon she is even being invited to a sleepover. She takes "Jessie" and "Blaze" with her and next day returns crestfallen, realising that her love for them is the source of her misery. "Lilypad" decides that action must be taken so starts to manipulate her messages so that the toys are confined to a box in the garage. That's when they send for "Woody". He and his friends must now find a way to free their boxed up companions and help them recover their place in her heart before "Lilypad" has them consigned to a charity shop. Crucial to their success might be "Smarty Pants". This is an early digital gizmo that has also been consigned to the back of a drawer as it'd been superceded and so in a sorry state with no battery power, these unlikely allies realise that they must work together to find "Bonnie" a real and much less fickle friend. Perhaps it's just the slightly over sentimental characterisation of "Bonnie" but this film seemed to take an age to get going and then when it did it forgot to remember that growing up involves a shedding of skins - physically and metaphorically. We all have favourite toys, records, clothes that we are joined at the hip with until we ultimately discard - and the emotional heart-strings this tries to tug all ran just a bit counter-intuitively for me. Sure, it offers us an indictment of a prevailing trend amidst society at large to rely on technology to do more and more for us, and to insulate us from the fun and perils of actually growing up with real people, but the ending maybe just diluted that a little too conveniently and I found there to be quite a lot less humour for us here, too. It's still good fun with plenty of adventures but maybe it's not just "Woody" et al that need to be put to bed, now?
