author: andrewtislercinephile
content: Pixar has always made some of the best sequels in history, and the *Toy Story* franchise is no exception. This fifth entry-all about "toys vs tech"-is easily the franchise's best in my opinion, and the most relatable. I really liked how the movie handled the conflict with a level of nuance, where the toys' fear of technology stems from being there for various kids for years (including their current one, Bonnie) and not wanting technology to take away that attention from them. The "villain", Lilypad, is also portrayed as a somewhat menacing character, but in reality is just doing her job, and the toys' point of view is why she is portrayed as a villain, with the movie's ending where the toys and her come to an understanding and work together being the perfect resolution. I also really loved Woody's role in this movie, where he used his past experience with Andy to try and help Buzz and the others out, but in the process, he continued acting like a control freak. This is a very common characteristic of him, where he frequently tries to take control of a situation and not let someone else handle it, and in this movie, that is his arc: learning to let Buzz and Jessie handle some of the scenarios themselves and step back. The animation is also phenomenal, showing Pixar's technology having evolved in the last 40 years or so to the point where their movies look just like real life, but with stylized character designs. The way they animated Lilypad is particularly creative, having her eyes and mouth be 2D-esque while the rest of her is all 3D. I also loved the cel-shaded, painterly look of the playtime scenes, as they added color and vibrant visuals to this otherwise grounded franchise. While I don't think an entire *Toy Story* movie can be animated this way, I do think there can be more sequences that use this technique besides the few playtime scenes this movie gives us. This movie, of course, was also very funny, and every joke landed really well, with my favorite being when Buzz told a bunch of drones that look like him that Zurg is their father. At the same time, this joke also hints at something deep: Even though Buzz and Zurg are enemies, they're still family, and Buzz still cares about him, likely after seeing him bond with Utility Belt Buzz in *Toy Story 2*. It was also refreshing that while Randy Newman did the instrumental score, he didn't return to sing "You've Got a Friend in Me". That song is 30+ years old, so it's bound to be repetitive. Taylor Swift's new song, "I Knew It, I Knew You", is a breath of fresh air, keeping the lighthearted vibes of the franchise intact while adding modern pop artists to this timeless franchise's music. *Toy Story 5* overall is easily, in my opinion, the franchise's best entry, and the most relatable to its time period, and I cannot wait to see what else Pixar does with this iconic franchise.

author: Brent Marchant
content: You won’t often see me review animated films. That’s because I remember what cartoons were like when I was growing up as a Baby Boomer, and I loved them (especially Looney Tunes). In fact, in my view, most of today’s headache-inducing animation is overly manic and overly silly, releases that pale in comparison to those classic old school offerings. For those who agree with me, however, there’s a new release out there that serves as a fitting homage to those works of days gone by that pays a fitting tribute to them while simultaneously incorporating fresh, contemporary material that does justice to its source material, “Coyote vs. Acme.” Based on the long-running comical desert conflict between the Road Runner and the bird’s perpetually unsuccessful nemesis, Wile E. Coyote, this feature-length tale brilliantly fuses animation and live action (in the same vein as “Who Framed Roger Rabbit?” (1988)) in an inventive new story. When the Coyote realizes that all of his efforts to entrap his target using an assortment of inherently faulty products from the infamous Acme Corp., he decides to try a new tactic to fulfill his goal: sue Acme in court, with the Road Runner serving as a firsthand witness to all of the product failures, thereby granting him ready access to the bird – and putting him one step closer to realizing his long-hoped-for dinner. He gets the idea after seeing a television commercial for shady Albuquerque accident attorney Kevin Avery (Will Forte), a lawyer known for bringing (and settling) many cartoon product injury cases against Acme and its chief legal counsel (and boastful law school rival), Buddy Crane (John Cena). But can Avery at last best his old foe through this lawsuit? What ensues is a smart, insightful corporate satire and lawyer parody in which the two attorneys battle one another surrounded by a host of beloved Warner Bros. cartoon characters presented in ways viewers have never seen them before, including Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Sylvester, Tweety, Granny, Porky Pig, Elmer Fudd, Foghorn Leghorn and the Tasmanian Devil., among others. The result is a delightfully humorous tale strategically peppered with memorable “Easter Eggs” from the franchise source material in a present-day narrative that’s unquestionably unusual but that never feels forced or implausible (comparatively speaking, that is). Admittedly, the picture isn’t rip-roaringly funny, but it’s definitely modestly amusing and successfully avoids the aforementioned pitfalls that weigh down most contemporary animated features. Director Dave Green’s third big screen effort will nostalgically warm the hearts of audiences who grew up with these flawed but familiar characters, evoking moderate chuckles as they’re showcased in a largely new light, quite a nifty trick to pull off as successfully as the filmmaker has done here. Yet, if nothing further comes out of this release (though, given its box office success, I doubt that will happen), one likely won’t be sorry when it ends, having deservedly earned the celebrated “That’s all, folks” sign-off that viewers have come to associate with this cherished body of work.

author: TheFilmCritics.org
content:
The Acme Corporation has finally met an adversary it can’t flatten with an anvil: a courtroom, and the result is an unexpectedly charming Looney Tunes comedy in *Coyote vs. Acme*.

The premise is inspired: after yet another Acme product goes spectacularly wrong, Wile E. Coyote takes the company to court with the help of a down-on-his-luck lawyer. It is exactly the kind of ridiculous escalation that feels appropriate for a character who has spent decades ordering increasingly elaborate devices to catch one very fast bird. Better yet, the film actually makes something of the idea, turning Acme’s absurd catalog into the basis for a surprisingly effective corporate satire.

Most importantly, the movie feels like Looney Tunes. The slapstick is broad, the visual gags come fast, and the dialogue occasionally has the same mischievous snap as the cartoons. Not every joke hits its target, but there are enough genuine laughs to keep the comedy firing. The satire is similarly effective, poking fun at corporate indifference and legal maneuvering without becoming so self-important that it forgets this is, fundamentally, a movie about a coyote suing a cartoon company.

The live-action and animation are also blended impressively well. There are a handful of moments where the seams show, but for the most part the cartoon characters inhabit the live-action world naturally. It helps that the film doesn’t treat the Looney Tunes characters as museum pieces. They are allowed to be funny, chaotic and occasionally ridiculous in precisely the way they should be.

John Cena is another highlight. As the smug corporate attorney, he plays the increasingly absurd circumstances with such complete seriousness that it becomes a joke in itself. Additionally, there is also more heart in the film than one might expect, giving the story some emotional weight beneath all the courtroom theatrics and exploding Acme merchandise.

Unfortunately, the film’s biggest strength is also its biggest weakness. The premise is so clever that it creates expectations the movie doesn’t entirely satisfy. What could have been a wonderfully strange, unpredictable collision of courtroom comedy and Looney Tunes madness often settles into a fairly conventional underdog legal story. The subplot involving Acme selling its products specifically to cartoon characters feels particularly unnecessary, adding complication without much payoff.

The pacing is another problem. *Coyote vs. Acme* isn’t exactly slow, but it is uneven. The first half has a lively rhythm and plenty of personality; somewhere around the midpoint, however, the story may start to feel like a bit of a slog. Some of the acting doesn’t help either, particularly with Lana Condor as Paige Avery, proving less convincing than the stronger performances around her. The legalese may also make the movie somewhat harder for younger viewers to follow than its Looney Tunes packaging suggests.

While *Coyote vs. Acme* is quite entertaining, it feels like it doesn’t realize its full potential. The premise promises something wonderfully creative, and the film delivers just enough of that promise to make the missed opportunities frustrating. There is a genuinely funny, affectionate Looney Tunes movie in here, along with a terrific central idea and a welcome amount of heart. It just needed to be a little bolder and more consistent.

author: Nick
content:
Coyote vs. Acme is a genuinely fun surprise. The gimmick — Wile E. author: andrewtislercinephile
content: *Coyote vs. Acme* finally got released after Warner Bros. tried to shelve the project for a $30 million tax write-off. It is exactly as I expected it to be: Funny, action-packed, emotional, and self-aware. The blend of live-action and animation is really cool because the real humans use animated props in the same vein as *Who Framed Roger Rabbit*, but the reason it feels more believable here is because instead of puppeteering the animated props, the human actors hold stand-ins that get replaced in post-production before release. Yes, I honestly believe actors holding real props and then replacing them in the editing is more believable than puppeteering because how do you puppet an animated prop? Anywho, the characters' roles in the movie, specifically the *Looney Tunes* characters, felt like an homage to classic crime films, like how Bugs Bunny's role as a whistle blower is similar to Deep Throat from *All the President's Men* (1976). Will Forte and John Cena's live-action acting was also great, delivering some funny moments together, while Forte also provides some emotional scenes between him and Wile E. Coyote. My only issue is that Wile E. Coyote still doesn't talk. This might come as a shocker, but I'm actually getting sick of these types of movies not letting the silent character talk. While Wile E. Coyote's signs and mute expressions works for a 22-minute cartoon, for a 90-minute movie, dialogue is necessary to ensure proper character interactions. Even in *WALL-E*, the title character doesn't entirely not talk. He just talks LESS. *Coyote vs. Acme* is still a pure delight despite this, and I really wished Warner Bros. decided to release this any sooner.

author: misubisu
content:
**Score: 8/10   A Triumphant, Hilarious, and Surprisingly Heartfelt Return to Form**

After years of studio limbo, cancellation drama, and fan campaigns, *Coyote vs. Acme* has finally arrived and thank goodness it did. This is a film that understands exactly what it is and executes it with confidence, wit, and genuine heart. It is **great storytelling** wrapped in a **great and believable blend of animation and film**, proving that the Looney Tunes can still deliver the goods when handled with respect and intelligence.

**The Premise: A Courtroom Comedy with a Wild Heart**

The story follows Wile E. Coyote as he finally snaps and takes Acme Corporation to court after decades of malfunctioning products have left him battered, bruised, and perpetually humiliated. Enter Kevin Avery (Will Forte), a down-on-his-luck lawyer who takes the case, and corporate fixer Buddy Crane (John Cena), sent by Acme to make the problem go away by any means necessary. What follows is a hilarious, surprisingly moving courtroom drama that explores justice, corporate greed, and the enduring power of never giving up.

**The Blend: Seamless and Believable**

The integration of animation and live action is flawless. The Looney Tunes characters exist in the real world with a tangible, physical presence that makes the absurdity feel grounded. The animation is vibrant, energetic, and faithful to the classic style, while the live action elements are shot with a playful, almost cartoonish sensibility that bridges the gap beautifully. It's a **great and believable blend** that serves the story rather than distracting from it.

**The Performances: Cena and Forte Go All In**

**Cena and Forte were 'all in' with their performances.** Will Forte brings his signature blend of earnest desperation and comedic timing to Kevin, making him a genuinely sympathetic protagonist. John Cena continues to prove himself a comedic force, delivering lines with deadpan precision and physical comedy that recalls his best work in *Peacemaker*. Their dynamic the hapless hero and the relentless corporate enforcer is the film's engine, and they play off each other brilliantly.

**The Looney Tunes: Still Ageless**

**It was so good to catch up with all the memorable Looney Tunes characters and see that they hadn't aged a day!** Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Porky Pig, and the rest are all present and accounted for, each one rendered with love and respect for their classic personas. The film understands that these characters are timeless, and it treats them accordingly no cheap updates, no cynical reboots, just pure, unfiltered Looney Tunes energy.

**Eric Bauza: A Vocal Tour de Force**

**Eric Bauza's Foghorn Leghorn was outstanding as were the multitude of other voices he did.** Bauza is a revelation, seamlessly inhabiting multiple iconic characters with such skill that you'd swear Mel Blanc himself was back in the recording booth. His Foghorn Leghorn is a particular standout pompous, verbose, and utterly hilarious, capturing the spirit of the original while making it entirely his own. His voice acting was superb. He is the film's secret weapon.

**The Verdict**

*Coyote vs. Acme* is a triumph. It's funny, smart, and surprisingly emotional a film that respects its source material while finding something new and meaningful to say. It's a testament to the enduring appeal of the Looney Tunes and a reminder that good storytelling, great performances, and a genuine love for the characters can overcome any production turmoil.

**Watch if:** You grew up with the Looney Tunes, appreciate clever courtroom comedy, or want to see John Cena and Will Forte at their comedic best.

**Skip if:** You have no patience for animated chaos or you're immune to the charms of a determined coyote and his eternal quest for a decent meal. (If so, what's wrong with you?)

author: Brent Marchant
content: An old saying maintains “Never put the cart before the horse,” an observation whose implications should be obvious. That applies in filmmaking, too: When a standalone production is thought to be the inspiration for a new franchise, the creators need to be careful not to get ahead of themselves. That’s to say that the first film in the proposed series absolutely must be a knock-out to earn the right to a sequel (or sequels) (“Star Trek” notwithstanding). But, if those behind the initial effort are so focused on what lies down the road in a potential franchise that they don’t get the first release right, it’s the equivalent of shooting themselves in the foot. And that is precisely what undermines this latest release from writer-director Na Hing-jin. In essence, this sci-fi action-adventure follows the improbable, occasionally strangely madcap attempts by a small town South Korean police force and others to hunt down a mysterious monster that’s wreaking all manner of havoc in their community and the surrounding environment. The problem, though, is that little is explained as the story unfolds, with an array of tropes that seem unconscionably thrown together – virtually no back story, a disjointed, poorly constructed narrative, woefully cheap CGI, a plot based almost entirely on clichés, frenetic action sequences, and absurd, sometimes patently inappropriate comic relief, and more overused expletives than seen in “The Wolf of Wall Street” (2013). While the film admittedly gets off to a reasonably well-managed start, coming across as a fusion between the “Godzilla” movies and the folksy, homespun nature of “Fargo” (1996), it’s an opening act that’s ultimately unforgivably drawn out (building suspense is one thing, but knowing that a big reveal is coming and taking 45 minutes to get there is a bit much). And, sadly, things go downhill from there, with a story that makes little sense stretched out to a stunning 2:39:00 runtime, overstaying its welcome by nearly an hour. My only “hope” for the picture at that point was that it was mercifully heading to wrap things up with some kind of coherent explanation that, unfortunately, never comes. And that’s where the focus of what’s to be included in future franchise installments intrudes upon the credibility and integrity of this release. What’s even more mystifying here is the high praise that this overlong saga has received both in critics’ circles and at the prestigious Cannes Film Festival, where “Hope” was inexplicably awarded a Palme d’Or nomination, the event’s highest honor. Moviegoers looking for entertaining scary fare along these lines have so many other, better choices to draw from, such as “Jaws” (1975), “Jurassic Park” (1993) and the recently released “The End of Oak Street” (2026). Please, watch one of those titles instead.

author: CinemaSerf
content: The discovery of a badly mauled cow is quite perplexing for the local police chief (Hwang Jung-min), especially when a few of his wise-cracking citizens suggest it might have been caused by a marauding tiger! It doesn't take him long to realise that whatever it is, it's a great deal bigger and more menacing than a cat as he returns to town and finds scenes of death and destruction with gunfire sounding regularly. What are they shooting at? Meantime, out in the woods his group of mischievous tiger-hunters are finding themselves embroiled in something altogether more mysterious, extra-terrestrial and perilous too! Ok, so it is far too long and for much of the later stages it reminded me of an hybrid of that lacklustre "65" (2023) and "Predator" (1987) - only with some added semi-slapstick comedy, but the first hour is quickly paced and entertaining end-to-end stuff. There's a bit of comedy horror; some welcome sarcasm delivered front and centre of the pithy and earthy script and the fact that we don't encounter their powerful new foe for almost all of that phase of the film manages to build an enjoyable sense of anticipation. Just what could be tossing people and cars so effortlessly? Once we meet their new nemesis, however, this plot quickly starts to lose it's sharpness and actually, despite a lively effort from the feisty "Sung Ae" (Hoyeon), becomes just a little too repetitious. Seemingly endless supplies of ammunition and never ending empty roads start to give the film a distinctly video-game feel supported by some CGI that can be a little ropey at times. The really quite disappointing conclusion left me wondering whether they just ran out of filming days or whether there might be plans for a sequel if this does well enough at the box office, but in any event it doesn't really satisfy and the few clues we are given about their visitors and their motivation are oblique at best. There's no denying that it's good fun to watch, though, with plenty of action, explosives and even a few horses - but it could have lost forty-five minutes and been none the worse for it.

author: The Fixate & Binge Podcast, w/ Joe Curdy
content:
For lack of a better word, Na Hong-jin's return to the big screen offers a hopeful premise and nail-biting tension—only to squander both with bloated screen time, cut-rate CGI, and a frustrating fifth act that awkwardly attempts to lay the foundation for a future franchise after failing to stick the landing.

Na's talents as a filmmaker are not in dispute—the brilliance of his 2016 film **THE WAILING** is testament to that. The ability to bring to life small, sleepy South Korean communities with their rich tapestry of characters on the big screen remains one of Na’s endearing charms—and this ability carries over seamlessly into **HOPE**.

This is Na's biggest strength as a writer and director, and it helps draw audiences into the chaos of the first half of **HOPE**, as a fishing village discovers something monstrous and devastating has ambushed the town, leaving a trail of destruction in its wake.

Local police chief Beom Seok (played by Hwang Jung-min) meets with some local hunters (including his nephew Sung-ki, played by Zo In-sung) who have discovered a horribly mutilated cow discarded in the middle of a country lane. The wounds look too severe to have been the work of any indigenous animals in the area—and in attempting to rule out a more understandable and manageable threat, Chief Beom Seok circles back into town to discover they truly have no idea what they're dealing with.

Whole quarters of the town look to have been fed through a woodchopper, with bodies strewn across the streets in horrible, disturbing ways. Director Na does a superb job of keeping audiences in the dark, with careful editing and action sequences that give viewers the feeling they're just as clueless as the locals are.

With heart-pounding action sequences racing through the dilapidated town streets, there is almost no opportunity for viewers to catch their breath. Na achieves this nerve-shredding tension by wisely prolonging the creature reveals until absolutely necessary.

However, the second half of the film begins to drag, especially as Na clearly tries to set up a wider scope for the film with additional creatures with mysterious motives and shoddy CGI renderings—as the 2-hour-and-40-minute film stumbles to an abrupt ending on a cliffhanger.

Ultimately, **HOPE** is a letdown because it appears to take its eye off the ball of just telling a standalone story, as it clearly is looking ahead to create more films. That kind of excess makes the film overstay its welcome in ways that will test audiences' patience.

Nevertheless, there are some truly unforgettable action sequences, a humorous story of diarrhea, and great performances from Hwang, and Hoyeon (last seen in Netflix's SQUID GAME) as deputy Sung Ae -- but all in all, this is a mixed bag.

content:
Watched [08](https://letterboxd.com/fixateandbinge/diary/for/2026/09/08/) [Sep](https://letterboxd.com/fixateandbinge/diary/for/2026/09/) [2026](https://letterboxd.com/fixateandbinge/diary/for/2026/)

With **ONSLAUGHT**, Adam Wingard's follow-up to his slick 2014 actioner **THE GUEST**, the magic — as is so often the case with sequels — fails on nearly every level to connect.

Even the addition of Dan Stevens in a supporting role as septuagenarian Hans Kimmler — a character who appears to be an amalgamation of Josef Mengele and Dr. Strangelove — fails to land. In fact, given the character's parodic underpinnings, he might have worked better in a comedy.

The set-up seems oddly familiar: genetically engineered super soldiers escape a nearby military bunker and go on a pointless killing spree, murdering everything that moves in their path. It's 1992's sci-fi actioner **UNIVERSAL SOLDIER**, except without the charm of Van Damme or the psychotic menace of Dolph Lundgren.

Co-written with Simon Barrett, Wingard's film appears to have fallen prey to an overzealous final cut that strips away some necessary exposition. (Why exactly does Rebecca Hall's character inexplicably have literal blood on her hands during one interstitial telephone scene that comes with zero set-up?)

MMA fans who recognized Alex "Poatan" Pereira in the opening credits are likely to be equally underwhelmed, with his zero dialogue and brooding stares amounting to little more than physical presence as one of three super soldiers who bring an orgy of death to a small New Mexico desert town.

Seemingly caught in their path of destruction is a rundown trailer park managed by single mom and military vet Celeste, played by Adria Arjona. As the super soldiers turn the mobile home park into Swiss cheese for the crime of simply being in their way, Celeste — with the help of Reginald VelJohnson's Josiah — fights back.

Wingard and Barrett seem more committed to developing Arjona's character at the expense of more interesting characters such as Stevens' Kimmler and his wife, Hanna Kimmler (Hall) — which is a shame, as the film ends with an end-titles sequence suggesting a follow-up could be in the works.

Heaven help us.

A flimsy plot, a paint-by-numbers action set-up, and — dare I say it — the wasting of Arjona's considerable talent make **ONSLAUGHT** a muddled, lifeless mess that proves all the blood, bullets and body count in the world can't resurrect a movie with no pulse.

author: CinemaSerf
content: Getting on for three decades after their first outing, the "Owen" women are still struggling too keep the loves of their lives alive. Now, though, the effects of the family curse have spread to the next generation and to "Kylie" (Joey King) who has fallen love with school sweetheart "Gideon" (Xolo Maridueña). Her mother (Sandra Bullock) had long since sworn her sister (Nicole Kidman) to secrecy about their broom-wielding provenence, so "Kylie" and sister "Antonia" (Maisie Williams) know nothing of the potential threat - until, that is, poor old "Gideon" comes a cropper. Now with him in intensive care, and armed with a mysterious book left by grandma "Jet" (Dianne Weist), "Kylie" heads to a quaintly depicted and almost Edwardian Britain where the "Hogwarts Express" appears to still be still in service, where she hopes to find a way to smash this evil once and for all and so save her beau from being buried under a pile of liberally sprinkled salt. I don't know if maybe it's just the time having passed, but there really isn't any sparkle to this. Bullock and Kidman have their moments, but the mischievously maternal efforts of Weist and the sparingly used Stockard Channing are largely missing and there is a distinct lack of joy throughout this. It's more of a family soap - Iike a feature-length episode of "Buffy" and though the assembled actors do just about enough, I left the cinema thinking this was nothing I'd ever remember and that it was almost entirely devoid of magic.

author: Chris Sawin
content:
Curry Barker has crafted something mostly special for an almost non-existent budget. author: CinemaSerf
content: "Bear" (Michael Johnston) has a crush on his pal "Nikki" (Inde Navarrette) but it's a love that dare not speak it's name. He hasn't the courage to even ask her out! When she decides that she has had enough of their two-horse town and wants to move away, he decides to buy her a gift and alights on a "make a wish" toy. Make your wish and it will come true as surely as if it were rubbed out on that lamp of "Aladdin". Well he gives her a lift home, but their parting is a bit wobbly and so in a fit of pique he snaps the gift and makes his wish after she has gone. What he doesn't expect is that it will come true, but that's just the start as the consequences of his hastily considered prayer begin to take over just about everyone's lives - and not necessarily for the better, or the safer, either. Things don't improve much for him when he discovers that his options to reverse his heart's desire are limited in the extreme. It's a toss up between the pair at the top of the billing here, but I reckon Navarrette might just have edged it on the acting front as both deliver positively visceral performances with this horror as it takes on an whole new perspective of maniacally tempramental behaviour and turns any sense of romance into something positively hysterical, menacing and at times quite menacingly gory and funny too. I really did enjoy the denouement and I reckon this is the best I've seen from this genre in 2026 so far. Never mind careless talk, just beware what you wish for?

author: James Berry
content:
Full Review: aisleseatreviews.com

"Waking up in the middle of the night with the eerie sense that you’re being watched, only to look down and see your kid standing pitch-black next to your bed staring at you. That is the exact level of visceral dread this movie locks you into."

Obsession is one of those rare, deeply unsettling horror films that doesn't just want to jump-scare you—it actively wants to get under your skin and suffocate you. You get about 15 minutes of relative safety at the start, but the exact second that One Wish Willow snaps, the air is completely sucked out of the room. You could literally hear a collective wave of tension ripple through the theater.

Inde Navarrette is phenomenal. Her ability to instantly pivot from an obsessed, psychotic girlfriend back to a normal, completely terrified Nikki who realizes she's trapped, and then snap right back into the madness is chilling. The bedroom scene where she watches Bear sleep is going to stick with me for a long time.

Massive props to director Curry Barker for making a flawless leap from YouTube horror to the big screen. He relies on old-school atmosphere rather than cheap audio cues, masterfully weaponizing camera placement, shadows, and lingering silence. There is a shot of her just standing there smiling that goes on for so long it made the entire crowd audibly uneasy.

With all the respect in the world, this is a "one-timer" for me because I am in no rush to put myself back through this emotional meat grinder. But it is an absolute must-experience with a theater crowd.

Verdict: Front Row (An Absolute Must-See)

author: Dean
content: Curry Barker’s feature debut is a flawless, deeply unsettling masterpiece that takes the classic "be careful what you wish for" trope and turns it into a relentless nightmare. The film centers on a music store employee who uses a supernatural trinket to force his longtime crush to love him, unleashing a wave of horrifying, unhinged consequences. Visually striking and meticulously paced, the movie keeps you completely locked in from the opening frame to its devastating conclusion.  What elevates this psychological horror film to absolute perfection are the phenomenal acting performances from Michael Johnston and Inde Navarrette. Johnston is brilliant as Bear, capturing a desperate, tragic vulnerability that makes his downward spiral incredibly painful to watch. Navarrette delivers a tour de force performance as Nikki, flawlessly shifting between heartbreaking torment and a chilling, vacant fixation that anchors the entire film. It is an intense, unforgettable ride that stands out as one of the absolute best entries in modern horror.

author: druscilla_of_old
content:
I know I'm supposed to say I love this movie and it's the best thing I've seen this year (cause, for some reason, it seems to be the current movie fad among White audiences) but I'm gonna be real: Obsession is a mess of a rag doll strewn up with overused clichés and age-old literary and movie tropes. Like, for instance, the use of wishes to weave a "be careful what you wish for" cautionary tale is a centuries old literary trope. So is the "crazy woman" trope.

Yet, even if one chooses to ignore this, the movie is haunted by numerous other problems that are impossible to igore: pacing issues, poor dialogue writing, poor audio quality, and choppy editing, to name a few. The only saving graces for the movie seem to be a couple of well-timed jump-scares and the relatively well-done "boys night out" scene.

Those aside, I've seen some people, bafflingly so, tout this movie as a "feminist" movie. Like, what?! In what world exactly is a movie made by a White man (Curry Barker), led by a White man (Michael Johnston), and whose main lesson seems to be cautioning White men to avoid getting into relationships with "crazy" women, feminist?? Also, the fact that Inde Navarrette is a fan of a court-adjudged wifebeater and rapist in real life (Johnny Depp) should be a massive red flag as to the kinds of people and work she'd be involved with. Speaking of Navarrette, I've seen lots of people praise her acting - even billing her for an Oscar [*eyeroll*] - but if you pay close attention to her scenes, special effects and editing do a tonne of work to help her achieve the kinds of emotions that may have moved audiences. 

In all, I wouldn't recommend this one to most people except avid horror fans whose interest in it would extend beyond pure entertainment. The 4-star I gave it were mostly due to the couple of positives I've mentioned above as well Michael Johnston's (sometimes) outstanding performance.

author: The Fixate & Binge Podcast, w/ Joe Curdy
content:
Writer/director Curry Barker’s leap from YouTube viral fame to the big screen is one of the best success stories in Hollywood, and Kane Parsons’ **BACKROOMS** for A24 later this month appears to be further proof that the road from YouTube to Hollywood — while still less traveled — can make all the difference.

The viral success of Barker's [**MILK & SERIAL** (2024)](https://letterboxd.com/fixateandbinge/film/milk-serial/) showcased enormous potential and a natural instinct for low-budget horror filmmaking, making his transition to the big screen feel like a well-earned graduation.

In **OBSESSION**, Barker has crafted a slow-burn psychological horror film that steadily builds careens towards its shocking conclusion.

While the deliberate pacing occasionally tested my patience, once Barker’s story fully unfolds, it seeps into the viewer’s psyche in ways few recent horror films have managed — provoking deeply uncomfortable questions about consent and free agency, while possibly making you think twice before blowing out candles on your next birthday.

**OBSESSION** presents a seemingly innocuous setup centered on the lovelorn Bear (Michael Johnston), who literally wishes to escape the friend zone with his longtime pal Nikki (Inde Navarrette). After stumbling upon a “One Wish Willow” collector’s item in a new-age curio shop — one that wouldn’t feel out of place beside the Zoltar machine in the Tom Hanks smash hit BIG (1988) — Bear makes a wish without understanding the terrifying power he has unleashed.

Encouraged by his best friend Ian (frequent Barker collaborator Cooper Tomlinson), Bear initially appears to get everything he wants when Nikki suddenly develops a romantic interest in him.

But soon the wheels start to come off as Bear's happily-ever-after spirals into a nightmare after the possessiveness of Nikki becomes increasingly unhinged. Navarrette delivers a terrifying performance that has echoes of **FATAL ATTRACTION** and **SINGLE, WHITE, FEMALE** -- with additional layers of psychological torture for her loss of bodily autonomy

With shocking moments of terror, expertly sustained tension, disturbing imagery, and a fearless performance from Navarrette, **OBSESSION** stands as one of the year’s best horror films.

author: Vinicius Monteiro
content:
There’s a fine line between genuine affection and possession, and horror movies usually thrive when crossing it. I went into *Obsession* expecting a psychological deep dive into emotional dependency, but what we actually get is an experience that violently swings between brilliance and frustration. Directed by Curry Barker, the film swings big in its attempt to show toxic masculinity and the loss of free will. The first thirty minutes are genuinely suffocating, doing a great job of making you feel trapped. But while Barker takes huge risks for his debut feature, the movie stumbles trying to keep that momentum going.

The real trouble starts when the story needs to stretch past its initial premise. The second act drags hard, trapping the viewer in a repetitive loop of jealousy and chasing that goes nowhere. They could have easily chopped at least twenty minutes in the editing room. On top of that, the indie budget really shows; scenes meant to be psychologically oppressive are ruined by amateurish lighting and set designs that break the immersion. Worse still is the jarring mix of tones. Right when the discomfort peaks, the script throws in bizarre dark humor. A badly timed joke or a goofy reaction completely kills the dramatic weight, making it clear the director hasn't quite learned how to trim the fat from his own ideas.

The whole plot with the mystical artifact hooks you at first, but it loses steam once the curse actually kicks in. Instead of building tension, the narrative just stalls. This makes the interactions suffer, too. Dedicated actors are stuck delivering stiff, unnatural dialogue, forced to spell out feelings that their body language was already showing perfectly. It makes some of the more dramatic scenes feel like a bad teen soap opera draft.

Following the protagonist, Bear (Michael Johnston), for almost two hours is a tough pill to swallow. He’s a pathetic guy whose harmless neediness quickly turns into a sick, one-dimensional selfishness. While the movie doesn't shy away from exposing the ugliest sides of possessiveness disguised as romance, Bear has zero redeeming qualities, making the watch tedious since there's no one to root for. If the movie survives its structural flaws, it’s almost entirely thanks to Inde Navarrette. Tasked with playing a character who gets psychologically beaten down by both the male lead and bad writing, she delivers an incredibly mature, visceral performance. Her subtle shifts in posture and gaze anchor the whole movie, making her the only real emotional core in the story.

Using folk horror to talk about toxic masculinity is the coolest idea here, but the execution completely lacks subtlety. The movie talks down to the audience, hammering its message home so hard that it feels more like a lecture than an organic psychological study. This also exposes a major flaw in how it handles its female lead. In trying to call out abuse, the narrative reduces her to a mere tool for suffering, tortured just to push the bad guy's arc forward. It leaves you wondering if it's genuinely critiquing misogyny or just exploiting women's trauma for shock value.

The film's early strength is its grounded tension, relying on everyday paranoia rather than monsters in the dark. But by the third act, the director throws all that out the window and goes full grotesque. Instead of feeling earned, this sudden bloodbath of graphic violence feels like a desperate crutch to shock an already bored audience. The sound design also fumbles; they went for an eerie lack of music, which works at first, but ends up making long scenes feel empty. When loud noises do happen, they're poorly mixed and feel like cheap jump scares.

After racing through a chaotic, blood-soaked climax, the movie just ends. An abrupt cut to black rolls the credits without explaining the artifact or the rules of the curse. It doesn't feel like a thought-provoking open ending; it just feels like the writers painted themselves into a corner and didn't know how to wrap things up, leaving you waiting for a payoff that never comes.

In the end, *Obsession* is a tough, uneven watch. Curry Barker has the guts to poke at the painful wounds of toxic relationships, and Inde Navarrette’s amazing acting keeps things afloat. But the pacing issues, weird tonal shifts, and the rushed, gory climax really test your patience. Still, it forces you to think. Horror is supposed to push us out of our comfort zone, right? If you want to feel that oppressive atmosphere, it's worth a watch. Just go in with a strong stomach, ready for the messy pacing, and see how you handle the sudden silence when those credits finally roll.

author: Martin Oaks
content:
**Emotional Hijacking**

Bear is a shy, introverted young man working in a music shop who is deeply and secretly in love with his friend and colleague, Nikki. Desperate over his unrequited romantic longing, Bear acquires a mysterious supernatural object called "The Weeping Willow," which has the power to grant wishes. Blind to the consequences, he wishes for Nikki to fall in love with him "more than anything else in this world." The spell works instantly, but the idyllic dream swiftly morphs into a nightmare: Nikki’s implanted love mutates into an irrational, suffocating, and deeply disturbing behavior. Her morbid devotion erases the boundaries of her sanity, unleashing a downward spiral of violence and obsessive possessiveness that threatens to destroy both their lives and everyone around them.

In certain aspects, "Obsession" stands out as the great revelation of contemporary horror cinema. Operating on a shoestring budget of just $750,000, director Curry Barker achieves what many Hollywood blockbusters can only dream of: building an atmosphere of tension relying strictly on the power of ideas, a fresh approach to staging, and raw storytelling.

Barker taps into 1980s cinematic references, taking the classic premise of magical manipulation (W.W. Jacobs' "The Monkey's Paw") and transplanting it into deeply uncomfortable psychological territory. The horror becomes visceral, psychological, and existential, confronting us with the terrifying facets of the human ego. It seeks to prove that forcing someone to love you does not stem from devotion, but rather from a craving for control and a pathological fear of loneliness or rejection.

Finally, a humble piece of advice for a talented Curry Barker, who will never read this review but is still in the budding stages of his career: the overreliance on jump-scare audio stingers is symptomatic of an endemic disease—one that blends narrative laziness, behavioral psychology, and the familiar commercial pressures of Hollywood. Do not fall into the temptation of mimicking the cheapest tropes of late-career Shyamalan. Instead, fully exploit that aesthetic and cinematic creativity currently flourishing within you. Flee once and for all from cheap, gimmicky chords, and lose your fear of silence. Remember that true horror dwells in the stillness of masterpieces like "Nosferatu", "Les Diaboliques" or "Rosemary's Baby", by Murnau, Clouzot and Polanski, respectively.

author: Yasmin J. Lee
content:
### My little food critic 🗒️

Just because Current Joys finally got justice for their underrated music doesn’t mean anyone else in this flick did. Long story short: Bear is the true villain of this story. I appreciated Curry Baker’s rom-com subversion. There were moments when Bear seemed like a guy trying to navigate romance in the age of disengagement and misunderstandings. However, at every twist and turn, he failed to correct his mistake. Ultimately dragging the cast of characters to a Shakespearean tragic ending.

Despite Baker not giving us insight into Nikki’s headspace, I assume she’s in a “Get Out”-adjacent sunken place. As a result of Bear’s haphazard wish, Nikki has become a passive viewer of her relationship with Bear. Frozen at her doorstep, an [obsessive](https://youtu.be/GrNt7Vz68oY?si=x1CsxLA6K-vGQt6X) (take a shot) spirit takes control of her body. Rather than connecting the dots, Bear is blissfully ignorant of the effects of his one wish.

I haven’t watched the few commentary videos explaining why he’s the villain in an effort to avoid unwarranted spoilers before watching this in theaters. Now that I’ve had my experience with “Obsession,” I understand why the “he’s the villain” phrase has come up numerous times. Bear expected Nikki to be his eager companion who lived predominantly in the heart of his home. However, his inner darkness is alluded to through the color grading and lighting. Taking a Coppola approach to lighting, shadows consume the rooms Bear and Nikki occupy. Naturally, the low lighting heightens our paranoia when Nikki hides in corners, wailing for Bear.

As the curse worsens, Bear refuses to acknowledge the severity of his situation. The boundaries he establishes with Nikki are slaps on the wrist, at best. His delusion clouded his judgment so intensely that he doesn’t recognize that he can’t reason with someone in this state of mind. This contradicts his initial concerns from the exposition. His concerns about denying Nikki access to consent and being fearful that she was inebriated all withered away the moment he confessed his feelings for her. He is so careless with the *actual* Nikki, so much so that he waits until the end of Act Two to get curious about how to reverse or contradict the One Wish Willow.

Secondly, Bear tells Nikki over dinner that he wants to become a food critic one day. Granted, these characters are young people who have a right to evolve and shift their interests, but why do we have ZERO clues about this hidden dream of Bear’s? The main set is his home. Mind you, there are no cookbooks, spice racks, or even elaborate cooking dishes. I interpret this as an intentional production design choice to reveal Bear’s disingenuous passion. Bear claims he’s in love with Nikki, but he never wanted her autonomy or actual demeanor. He wanted to be the center of her world without her input or personality. He wants to be a food critic, yet he couldn’t smell that Sandy-wich?

Bear’s dismal commitment to anything smothered the fire of the women in his life. Nikki had plans of moving out to pursue her writing career. Sarah waited anxiously for an acceptance letter from art school, hoping to be a tattoo artist. All this dissolved into nothingness so Bear could have Sarah and Nikki's enamored attention. (I’m convinced Bear relished knowing Sarah had a crush on him. This boosted his ego, especially since Nikki’s in love with him more than anyone else in the f#%king world.)

Considering the amount of passion I have about these characters and how invested I’ve become in their worlds, it’s safe to say I enjoyed this story. The themes about consent and free will were great, and the stakes rose at a decent rate. The pacing was a little off at times. The cinematography really outshone any other choices in this film. The costuming had a small-town alternative vibe we don’t see enough of in mainstream films. Dressing Nikki in red frequently throughout the story was a nice element as well. Inde Navarrette made this film beyond memorable. Her performance control is something to be marveled at. She embodied the mannerisms of a cat while simultaneously distinguishing the wavering boundaries of the real Nikki and the possessed spirit.

Even though the aesthetics of “Obsession” were well-rounded on screen, this film reminded me of too many other recent horror films to be immersive. The fact that Nikki was basically in the sunken place was a solid homage to “Get Out” (2017), but when Nikki started to say, “no, no, no, no,...” it felt too similar to that kitchen scene for me to feel the energy shift completely. Most of the locations reminded me of different movies (the house = Barbarian (2022), the party scene = Talk to Me (2022)), and the tone was a little too clean to make its voice unique.

All in all, I give this film 3.9 stars out of 5 stars. And HEY! We have a new scream queen ❤️‍🔥 

*Enjoyed this review? Subscribe to my Substack (Snowy Reviews, by Yasmin) and give me a follow (@yasminthewriter) on Letterboxd, and see what I review next!*

author: Angel Brown
content:
Curry Barker’s Obsession Is A Disturbing Supernatural Horror Film That Transforms An Innocent Romantic Desire Into A Grotesque Nightmare. When Hopeless Romantic Bear Uses A Mysterious Wish-Granting Object To Make His Longtime Crush, Nikki, Fall In Love With Him, He Discovers That Forced Affection Comes With Horrifying Consequences. Michael Johnston Delivers A Compelling Performance As Bear, While Inde Navarrette Is Particularly Memorable, Bringing Unsettling Intensity To A Story About Manipulation, Consent, And The Dark Side Of Romantic Idealization.



The Film’s Blend Of Psychological Tension, Gruesome Violence, And Dark Humor Makes It Both Uncomfortable And Captivating. Although Its Disturbing Premise And Increasingly Extreme Scenes May Alienate Some Viewers, Barker’s Direction Gives The Story A Distinctive Edge And Delivers A Chilling Reminder That Love Cannot Be Manufactured Without Consequences.

author: Stian Andreassen
content:
The poster (the dark one with Statham looking left) makes it look like *Die Hard* (on purpose, I'm guessing), and the plot synopsis makes it sound like *Under Siege*. It's both and neither, at the same time. 

Jason Statham has become a movie genre of its own right, and this one fits neatly into that genre. It's not philosophical, or interested in the human condition, nor can it be said the be a character study. There are no characters here, only "dossiers", that lets you know what kinda person this is – usually deadly, ex-military or mercenary. The plot is ultra-thin, there's just enough of it to justify Statham killing a metric fuckton of bad guys. Formulaic, sure, but we don't come to a Statham movie for the intricate plot with intelligent twists, do we?

Maybe not Statham’s best, but certainly good enough for fans to devour with relish. There's some really good mêlée choreography here, and while you can see Jason getting steadily older, he can still pack a punch.

author: MovieGuys
content:
There was a time when I looked forward to Jason Statham films. He fits the action genre comfortably, mixing man of action with enough depth and thoughtfulness to remain interesting. It's a shame, then, to see his films become as formulaic as "Mutiny". 

This is a deeply superficial action flick that sets up a basic human trafficking at sea scenario, backed by caricature mercenary bad guys facing off against an ex-military/police hero in the form of Statham. What comes next is predictable, repetitive, and frankly rather bland. 

No true insights into anyone's motives, no witty narrative or general creativity. 

In summary, a superficially watchable but also wholly forgettable action romp.

author: Sierbahnn
content: This is not Transporter. This is not the Beekeeper, but it is certainly better than the Mechanic and at least half a dozen other movies that are pretty much exactly like this. Jason does his Jason thing and he does so very proficiently and this time he's backed up by a functioning script and good antagonist and even a supporting cast that you can get behind. author: CinemaSerf
content: Disgraced British policeman "Cole" has landed on his feet looking after the personal safety of a kindly shipping magnate who runs an global operation from his home in Bangkok. Just as he is about to sell his company, though, "Tibu" (Ramon Tikaram) and his bodyguard find themselves ambushed, the former assassinated and the latter man framed for the crime and declared outlaw. One thing our hero does know is that some cops are in on the killing and that one of the now dead assassins was due to work aboard one of the company's freighters. Stowing away aboard the giant "Artemis", he quickly finds himself embroiled in some unsavoury nautical activites with only the recently drafted third mate "Ellis" (Annabelle Wallis) on his side. With the heavily armed crew under the command of the menacing captain (Roland Møller) bent on ensuring he goes swimming with concrete boots, what chance "Cole" can survive their pursuit and then hopefully avenge the death of his friend? No, jeopardy there isn't and I am afraid to say that this vehicle for Statham is really repetitive and actually quite dull. For a start, he seems to rapdily acquaint himself with this massive vessel and gets from bow to stern as if he were Grant Gustin (or Ezra Miller) - all whilst proving as bullet and knife-proof as a man with Kevlar skin. Møller isn't remotely intimidating - though there is some fun with an axe towards the end, and that conclusion is both rushed and leaves room for "Mutiny Too". This is all standard Sky television fayre that effortlessly passes ninety minutes but don't look for anything innovative or distinguishing or you'll be disappointed.

author: Brent Marchant
content: Some movies seem destined for mixed reactions. That may be somewhat apparent before their release, but it invariably surfaces once in distribution. And it would seem to be very much the case with the latest and long-awaited release from writer-director Alejandro G. Iñárritu, a project that has been heavily promoted for some time. To complicate matters, “Digger” is a film that could easily fall prey to spoilers if too much is revealed in advance (a point decisively driven home in a caution posted on screen before the picture’s start at press previews), so I apologize in advance if this analysis seems somewhat cryptic or evasive. The film primarily follows the wily exploits of Digger Rockwell (Tom Cruise in his first return to a character who essentially isn’t an action-adventure hero since “Magnolia” (1999)), an aging, loud-mouthed good ole boy oil tycoon who is one of the most powerful men in the world. He’s good friends with the equally boisterous President Compson (John Goodman in what is arguably the best performance of his career), a bought-and-paid-for politician who conveys an impression of independence but is nevertheless quietly beholden to the protagonist and the commodity his corporation controls. But, for all the power these two colleagues wield, even their considerable resources and responsiveness are taxed when an explosion on a Greenland drilling tract leased to Digger’s company triggers an environmental emergency – the detachment of an enormous ice shelf destined for collision with northern Europe. And, since Digger is responsible for the disaster and whatever fallout stems from the actions of his American company, how are he and Compson supposed to respond? But that’s only the half of what’s transpiring here, and that’s where those spoilers come into play. What’s more, this is also where the mixed reactions to this offering are most likely to emerge. Indeed, to say more would reveal too much, but suffice it to say that the movie takes a radical turn at this juncture, one that some may find hard to follow initially, even though this shift is not entirely unexpected given that it recalls similar changes found in some of the filmmaker’s previous pictures, like “Birdman” (2014) and “Bardo” (2022). While some of this could probably have been handled differently (and better), the overall narrative nevertheless makes for an intriguing story filled with insightful (if familiar) messages about environmental decline, the unchecked power of big business, greedy CEOs and compromised politicians, and a public that often complains but takes few meaningful steps to counteract any of the foregoing. The picture could have also used a little less shouting, not only in the characters’ dialogue, but also in the conveyance of its sentiments. The writing has its strong points (especially in its piercing one-liners and pointed contentions), and the performances are generally solid, including those by the leads and supporting cast members Riz Ahmed, Sandra Hüller, Michael Stuhlbarg and Jesse Plemons. But the biggest drawback in this satire is that there’s really no one to pull for, and that keeps me at least from giving this release a stronger endorsement. Perhaps it would take another viewing to recommend it more enthusiastically. But that would undoubtedly take some digging.

author: CinemaSerf
content: "Digger" (Tom Cruise) is an oil gazzillionaire who cares little for safety or the environment as he determines to milk the planet of as many of it's resources as he can before someone tells him to stop. It's his multi-billion dollar operation in the Arctic that is causing consternation after a massive methane explosion releases a part of the ice shelf and sets it en-route to the low countries of Europe where catastrophe looms. Quickly in cahoots with the president (John Goodman) and finally having to listen to the only scientist in his otherwise acolytic empire prepared to deliver some home truths - "Ganesh" (Riz Ahmed) they consider their options. Get in front of the news: tell the truth and own the problem; feign ignorance and let a now rather angry nature take it's course or do they get the bombers out? All the while this is playing out, we are aware that this is actually all part of a complicated stage play entitled "Fossil Fools" and that "Digger" is really "Curtis", an actor who is having some family troubles and who isn't entirely focussed on the job in hand. Now juggling both scenarios, we embark on quite a scathing satire of global geopolitics that culminates in probably the best performance I've ever seen from Tom Cruise. His animated soliloquy to a suitably gray/beige parliament towards the end about the extent of public complicity in the current environmental situation is potent, thought-provoking and is one of those monologues that has a lot more truth to it than we, watching, might care to acknowledge. Sure, it plays to many a stereotype along the way and it tends to exaggerate for theatrical effect now and again, but by blending satire into scenarios that might readily seem plausible - especially just about everything featuring the on-form Goodman, it hits the mark more often than not. It's not just aiming for the low-hanging fruit of corporate excess, but perhaps with rather more sophistry suggests that that greed is just as prevalent amongst the convenience culture masses who have, for generations, taken low-cost energy and travel for granted. Maybe it's more luck than judgement on the part of Alejandro Iñárritu but the substance of this film really does resonate strongly right now and with Cruise, Goodman, their make up artistes and some seriously poignant writing unafraid to take populist cinema firmly into the realms of hitherto largely avoided, but still quite darkly humorous, controversy - some of this is really quite profound and it makes few bones about speculating that the most powerful people in the world nowadays have rarely, if ever, been anywhere near any ballot papers.

author: James Rowland
content:
*May Contain Spoilers:*  
  
I *think* love Digger. It’s a beautiful, but bleak film. One which you only truly understand after letting it sit for a few days. As I have done.   
  
From the very beginning, Iñárritu does the unthinkable - daring you to dislike it. The sound design, cinematography, make-up - all stunning, but deeply uncomfortable. These first 30 mins are both exciting, and daunting; rattling by with little time for pause. Not giving us the chance to breathe. Then, just as we begin to settle into the chaos of it all… Iñárritu dares us once again - to sit through the most bizarre cinema experience I’ve ever felt.   
  
The entire 2nd act contains arguably the best scenes of the film, and carries the majority of the narrative… yet in the moment, you hate it. Once the projections drop, and the theatre is revealed; we are left with an overall feeling of “so?” Why should you care for the story anymore? It's fake! Sure, it’s funny, and impressive - but hollow.  
  
Fortunately, that’s only half the story. Just as Digger Rockwell - and Kenny later on - battle with "controlling the narrative”. Iñárritu completely alters our “perception” of the whole experience. When we get the final reveal. It all clicks… The foreshadowing of the leaking sets, Curtis’ daughter. That is why *think* I love this film. It’s not a quick shot of escapism, it’s a slow drag, of thought provoking mastery.  
  
I also said this was a bleak film; and it is. Only now does the final line - delivered over the credits - hit me. This is not a film about a play about historical events in the future, it is a film - about a film - about a play about historical events in the future. The final line, “level 4”, is delivered first to the audience of the play, and then to the audience of this film. In both cases it says: ‘The show is over. Leave. Go back to your miserable lives’. Digger does not deliver a cliched ‘make the world a better place’ message. To it, the world is beyond saving, and we’re left to pick up the pieces.  
  
Which is where the film’s most interesting character comes in: Kenny (Jesse Plemons). Because this is not a film about the climate crisis… It’s a film about storytelling (I see why Tom Cruise liked it). Kenny’s actions to rescue Curtis’ daughter bring a family together; Just as Fossil Fools brings a community together. But to do so… Managing a scarily effective surveillance company. Funding and handpicking the talent behind the play… Perhaps Kenny too is "controlling the narrative”. Just like Digger. Just like Iñárritu.  
  
This is a long review, for an elaborate film. I really would recommend watching it - even though it may pain you in the moment.  
  
Great Film.  
  
*(P.S. That score by Cosmo Sheldrake… Incredible. OSCAR worthy.)*

author: ianrathbone
The Fixate & Binge Podcast, w/ Joe Curdy
content:
Ignore the critical consensus and pay no mind to its dismal box office returns -- Alejandro G. Iñárritu's **DIGGER** is way out in front as the best film of 2026, featuring the finest performance from star Tom Cruise since Paul Thomas Anderson's **MAGNOLIA**.

And not to put too fine a point on it, but **DIGGER** may go down as Iñárritu's best film with its whip-smart blend of political satire underpinned by exemplary supporting performances from Riz Ahmed and John Goodman in this grandiose, meta-cinematic opus, wisely filmed on high-resolution VistaVision 35mm by cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki. The result is a sumptuous big screen epic that both awes and entertains.

Cruise's fully committed performance as the eponymous lead 'Digger' Rockwell is an audacious gamble that swings for the fences, and largely scores.

For decades Cruise has leaned into his larger-than-life movie star persona, and Iñárritu exploits it here, giving him a large enough sandbox to explore his character’s charisma, legendary intensity and limitless reserves of conviction. It is Cruise’s embracing of this meta-commentary on his own persona that helps carry the joke so seamlessly throughout the film.

As Digger, Cruise cavorts and carouses across the screen in a performance that crescendos gloriously with a seductive 10-minute speech in a single take that is utterly mesmerizing. We’ve never seen Cruise quite this magnetic before — a bloated oil man incapable of getting out of the way of his own insatiable greed. This is Les Grossman on beta-blockers and Metamucil.

Anyone interested in understanding the doomed American love affair with oil, wealth, power and moral corruption could hardly ask for a more provocative double feature than **THERE WILL BE BLOOD** and **DIGGER**. Where PTA plumbed the depths of insatiable greed that helped build the oil empire in America, Iñárritu shows us where such unbridled greed ultimately — and inevitably — leads our society.

Beyond its spectacle, gallows humor and over-the-top provocations, the larger impact of the film comes from its belief in art as therapy for a failed society that refused to save itself. In this respect, **DIGGER** plays like both a eulogy and an epilogue -- a reckoning with the depredations of end-stage capitalism and its inevitable conclusion.

To say more is to risk spoiling the film's larger surprise -- because another layer of **DIGGER** is hiding in plain sight. Once revealed, it doesn't simply reframe what we've been watching — it elevates the film's satire into something surprisingly poignant.

As **DIGGER** looks destined to fail at the box office -- a predicament that underscores the challenge of marketing Iñárritu's film without spoiling its overarching message -- one thing is for sure: this is Cruise's finest work, arguably the best from Iñárritu, and (at the time of this writing) the best film of 2026.

author: andrewtislercinephile
content: Tom Cruise is such an iconic actor, but *Digger* has to be his most unconventional movie yet. From its main conflict-which is about an oil tycoon dealing with rising pollution and a deadly flood-is not only realistic, but it also is high-stakes, and this movie is supposed to be a play-within-a-movie type thing, where Digger Rockwell himself is just a character an actor named Curtis Manson plays. It has a perfect blend of satire, black comedy, and powerful themes while still feeling like a proper storyline, where characters in the play have to deal with the circumstances themselves. Furthermore, the plot twist where the play's events are true makes the situation even more shocking as we did not expect that an exaggerated satirical farce on a stage could be predicting what's happening right outside the theatre's doors. I also gotta give props to the supporting cast, as they delivered a great combination of comedy and honest character emotion, particularly John Goodman as the President. I love John Goodman, so it was no shocker I found his acting in this movie to be just as good as in his other movies, if not better. His over-the-top reactions and responses were so funny I swear they were improvised. My only issue with this movie is how the owner of the theatre claims Digger is a real person, when Tom Cruise himself specified he didn't base Digger on anyone real. If the actor playing Digger specifies Digger isn't based on anyone, the movie shouldn't go and claim that Digger is a real person either. Other than that, I had a fun time watching *Digger* and I am very excited to get it on DVD next January/February.

author: CinemaSerf
content: Hot on the heels of the 14th century great plague that killed almost half of the English population, the young and troubled King Richard II (Woody Norman) is being governed by his greedy nobles and clergy. Their actions result in his people being left exposed to the cruelty of their taxation agents and often they are no longer left with enough to live on or to feed their families. One such farmer (Andrew Garfield) decides that enough is enough and violently rebels against the authority of the Chief Justice (Stanley Townsend). Pretty swiftly he discovers that he isn't alone. His Essex-men are sooned joined by many from Kent - led by Wat Tyler (Cosmo Jarvis) and John Ball (Jamie Bell) who determine to march to London to put their case before the King. That's quite a risky strategy as they have no idea if the King will manage to pull himself together enough to see and/or engage with them or will he, too, end up being manipulated by the likes of his Archbishop (Stephen Dillane - whom I could have sworn was Rupert Everett) and his duplicitious treasurer (Tom Hollander)? What takes over now is a rather pedestrian delivery of a turbulent period in history that I felt never quite hit the mark and the style of the photography also started to get under my skin a bit, too. Why did it constantly have to be moving? Much of this is shot as if we are up close and personal with the characters or amidst the conflict, but often I felt as if I was observing whilst hopping from foot to foot, or constantly moving around the object to no obvious or beneficial purpose and after a while I just wanted to get out of this particular wind tunnel and let the historical aspects more stably play out. On that front Garfield and Jarvis deliver competently and Norman quite ably presents something of the vulerabilities that Richard II later become famed for, but Bell was curiously out of sorts and though the production design does convince us of something of the lives of the poverty-stricken agrarian population, the film really never quite settles down to anything much more than a decently funded tea-time television costume drama - a bit like "The King" (2019). I was disappointed, but I did still quite enjoy it and it does need to been screen in a cinema if you're to get the full value from the set-piece scenes. It will look very ordinary on the television.

author: Brent Marchant
content: When times are tough and world-weary souls have looked for an avenue of escapism to retreat from their woes, worries and weltschmerz, they’ve often flocked to the movies to relieve that pent-up pressure. And, at a time when it feels like the world is going to you-know-where in a you-know-what (like now), that’s true more than ever. So it’s with that in mind that this much-anticipated sci-fi space adventure from directors Phil Lord and Christopher Miller enters the picture, a release promulgated with the hope of providing that much-needed and much-hoped-for entertainment remedy. Unfortunately, it comes up seriously short of the mark. When once-famous but now-discredited scientist Ryland Grace (Ryan Gosling) redeems himself by discovering the cause of a space-based catastrophe lying in wait with the potential to devastate the Earth, he’s “recruited” by an international panel of investigators (led by a regrettably miscast Sandra Hüller) to participate in a mission to resolve the issue. He’s reluctant to go, given personal misgivings and his lack of experience as an astronaut, apprehensions that are unsurprisingly confirmed when he wakes up from hibernation to find he’s the only member of his crew to survive. He’s thus left to teach himself how to pilot his spacecraft on his own and to look for a solution to the impending calamity, one that has apparently affected all of our neighboring solar systems but one. And, upon his arrival at that sole surviving locale, he encounters a stone-faced alien whom he names “Rocky” (voiced by James Ortiz) who has been dispatched from his home world to this same location for the same purpose. Perhaps working together will yield an answer for this unlikely duo, but first these two very different beings must learn how to communicate if they’re to collaborate successfully, a challenge almost as big as their scientific dilemma. While this may sound like a plausible premise for an escapist fantasy offering, problems arise not so much in the nature of the story but in its error-filled execution. For starters, at a runtime of 2:36:00, it’s too long to maintain viewer interest with what it has to work with. That’s because the treatment never takes itself seriously enough to make audience members want to care about the characters or the outcome. Instead of creating a thrilling and engaging space adventure, the film becomes more of a lightweight buddy movie (and a very silly, almost juvenile, one at that). Comic relief is one thing, but this production carries this idea way too far, and this ends up becoming a chief source of the picture’s desperate need for editing. On top of this, the narrative isn’t especially original, combining tropes found in releases like “Interstellar” (2014), “The Martian” (2015), and, even as unlikely as it may sound, “Cast Away” (2000), with visual elements that look like they were plucked from “2001: A Space Odyssey” (1968) and “2010: The Year We Make Contact” (1984). And, speaking of visuals, the special effects are a decidedly mixed bag of images, with some stunningly beautiful and others that unbelievably look like they’re 40 years out of date (talk about continuity issues). Then there’s the lead performance by Gosling, who carries much of the picture by himself, again portraying (or attempting to portray) his signature supposedly soft-spoken everyman, but who, in this instance, routinely steps out of character and goes over the top with displays that are unmitigatedly hammy and cloying (much like his extraterrestrial co-star). Consequently, when all is said and done, “Project Hail Mary” comes up an unexpected disappointment, failing to deliver the goods that its marketing team so fervently promised. I realize that I probably sound cantankerous and curmudgeonly in my assessment and that this will likely end up being an unpopular opinion that goes against what most critics and viewers say about it, but I truthfully came away from this one feeling unsatisfied. Nevertheless, if you’re still compelled to see this one any way, at least do yourself the favor of watching it on an IMAX screen for best effect. But, if I were you, I’d wait for it to come to streaming instead.

author: CinemaSerf
content: I think this might be my favourite sci-fi film since “Galaxy Quest” (1999) and like that, this is a solid and entertaining story led by an actor who is quite possibly getting better looking and more charismatic as he gets older. “Grace” (Ryan Gosling) is the kind of interactive science teacher that I’d have loved. Few text books, just gadgets, gizmos and beanbag factoids that appear to keep his teenage students interested and enthusiastic. When he leaves one afternoon he encounters the enigmatic "Eva” (Sandra Hüller) who knows of his more rebellious past amongst the scientific community and who invites him to participate in a crucial and global project. The sun is dying, and rapidly, and they have identified what they think might be the cause. Quickly identifying what he calls the “astrophage”, he is soon aboard an aircraft carrier in the middle of the ocean working on an antidote that might be sourced from a star light years from earth. A scientist he wants to be - an astronaut, well that's a different matter - and so after an unfortunate explosion that’s where “Eva” has a difficult decision to make. Running in parallel to this thread is one on a spaceship in a galaxy far, far, away - and where it’s lone astronaut has met and befriended another wanderer looking for a solution to this intergalactic plague. The two are pretty much polar opposites. They’ve no language in common and they don’t even breathe the same air - but some technical legerdemain, sign language, model making and good old-fashioned goodwill might just help them find a solution in time? Aside from a couple of quite sparing interventions from Hüller - and a mean bit of her karaoke, this is really just Gosling demonstrating that cardigans are cool as he hurtles through space. The writing provides him with some quite witty dialogue a well as just an hint or two of actual science; the visual effects are impressive too but ultimately it’s his amiable characterisation that makes us smile and tugs at our heartstrings almost simultaneously as their story races along for a couple of hours mixing jeopardy, humour and the power of friendship into it as it goes. It looks great on a big screen and I'd certainly be up for a sequel.

"Project Hail Mary stands as a triumph of narrative over technique, where the redemption of a man who believed himself a coward becomes the symbol of hope for an entire civilization. It’s a beautiful exploration of how genuine communication and personal sacrifice can tear down the most unthinkable barriers, uniting two beings from opposite worlds in a common purpose. Leaving the theater, my thoughts weren’t focused on orbital physics or alien chemistry, but on the profound lesson of altruism that Rocky and Grace leave to the real world. It asserts itself as one of the most immersive and emotionally rewarding sci-fi experiences in recent cinema, joining the technical grandeur of an IMAX production with the intimacy of one of the purest friendships ever seen on screen through a memorable performance by Ryan Gosling. It reminds us that, in the deafening silence of the cosmos, our greatest strength doesn’t lie in the problems solved, but in the courage to reach out to the unknown to discover that one is never truly alone. In the end, what really lasts aren’t the cutting-edge visual effects or the scientific rigor, but the soul of the story."

content: Project Hail Mary presents itself as a modern science fiction centered on the classic mission to save the world, or in this case, multiple worlds. author: Dean
content:
The film adaptation of Project Hail Mary is a masterclass in how to translate a high-concept sci-fi premise into a deeply moving cinematic experience. While the technical aspects and the scale of the cosmic mission are undeniably impressive, the true strength of the film lies in its profound emotional core.

The narrative goes beyond the "competence porn" of solving physics problems and instead focuses on the vulnerability of being completely alone—and the transformative power of finding a connection in the most unlikely of places. The relationship at the center of the story is handled with a delicate, genuine warmth that makes the stakes feel intensely personal rather than just global. It is a rare film that manages to be intellectually stimulating while simultaneously making you feel a deep sense of companionship and hope.

The performances ground the more fantastical elements, ensuring that the humor and the moments of quiet reflection land with equal impact. It’s a beautiful reminder that even in the vast, cold emptiness of space, the most important discovery one can make is the capacity for friendship and sacrifice. This movie is a resonant, soulful journey that stays with you long after the credits roll.
