author: Vinicius Monteiro
content:
Waking up in the absolute void, with no memory, and carrying the weight of saving humanity on your shoulders. This setup had everything to be just another generic sci-fi flick we forget about a week later, right? But "Project Hail Mary" tries to pull the rug out from under us by mixing the coldness of space with an unlikely tale of friendship. The result is a ride that hits a few narrative potholes but definitely won't leave anyone indifferent. Let’s break down what actually works and what got lost in orbit in this blockbuster.

Doing a movie where the lead spends most of the time alone talking to thin air is a trial by fire for any actor, and Ryan Gosling passes with flying colors. He delivers a near-perfect mix of constant vulnerability, sharp wits, and his signature sarcastic humor. Watching this guy transition from a scared teacher to the reluctant savior of humanity really hooks you. Gosling uses that blank stare and little nervous tics to show the panic he’s trying to hide behind jokes. We care about Grace’s headspace because his fear is palpable. He’s not a trained action hero; he’s just a regular dude trying not to lose his mind in the cosmic void.

This brutal isolation on the ship gets a lot heavier when the movie cuts to Grace’s memories. While the space setting is suffocating and tight, our planet, in the flashbacks, is a slow-motion picture of despair. Earth is freezing over. To show this, the script hits the bullseye by giving Sandra Hüller room to shine as Eva Stratt, the leader of the global task force. Hüller is chilling. She makes ruthless, almost cruel political decisions, bulldozing over laws and human rights to try and save the species. This cold government vibe perfectly justifies the protagonist's desperation. We get that there’s no way around it: either he pulls this off, or that freezing, militarized planet is simply going to cease to exist.

If Earth brings the human tension, it’s the interspecies friendship that injects real life into the story. When the character Rocky shows up, the movie reaches a whole new level. He’s not your typical humanoid alien. He’s an Eridian—basically a giant spider made of rocks that breathes ammonia and lives in the dark. And surprisingly enough, he completely steals the show.

Building this relationship is one of the script's highest points. They break through massive language and physical barriers, starting with suspicion, shifting into the scientific method, and arriving at a deep sense of empathy. It’s super rare to see mainstream cinema treat "first contact" with this much patience. No shooting, no invasion. Just two terrified beings from different galaxies trying to figure out how to help each other.

Speaking of figuring things out, fans of Andy Weir's book always talk about the insane amount of hard sci-fi in the story, and the movie doesn't shy away from that. A huge chunk of the communication and problem-solving between Grace and Rocky happens through math and physics. They draw makeshift graphs, build scale models, and put theories to the test. For anyone who loves a good science puzzle, watching these two crunch numbers so they don't burn to death or suffocate is a treat. The science here isn’t just window dressing; it’s the actual language connecting the two species.

But it’s exactly in this attempt to balance serious science with looming tragedy that my skeptical side kicks in. The movie tries to juggle too much at once. Directors Lord and Miller bring their trademark humor, but in the context of a global apocalypse, the mix sometimes turns sour. There are moments when the stakes are sky-high, the ship is falling apart, and suddenly Grace cracks a joke that feels straight out of a Sunday afternoon sitcom. It breaks the immersion instantly.

On the flip side, the movie leans so hard into optimism and melodrama that it borders on artificial. Some of the final scenes are so obviously engineered to make us cry—with the music swelling and lingering stares—that it kind of backfires. For viewers who aren't as prone to emotional manipulation, all this sweetness feels a bit too cheesy. It strips away the gravity and weight of a mission that, at its core, should be dirty, traumatizing, and practically a suicide run.

If the tone wobbles, the aesthetics grab the wheel tight. You really can't fault the art direction. The cinematography does a brilliant job contrasting the pitch-black universe with the yellowish, utilitarian interior of the Hail Mary. There’s a constant feeling of thermal claustrophobia—you can practically feel the heat of the engines and the cold of the glass.

Thankfully, the design team went for a fantastic balance of practical and digital effects. The textures of Rocky’s engineering, the way the Eridian ship looks like a giant mineral clock... all of it dodges that plastic, generic, weightless CGI we usually get in summer blockbusters. Things actually look like they have mass; they feel heavy.

And since we’re talking about the physicality of the ship, it’s impossible to ignore the sound design. Because Eridians communicate through musical tones, the soundtrack couldn't just be some sweeping background instrumental. The music is literally part of the dialogue. The movie uses chord progressions and vibrations that constantly talk back to the metallic clanks of the ship. It’s smart, immersive sound work. A lot of the time, we understand what Rocky is feeling—anger, joy, fear—just from the texture and frequency of the chords he plays, without needing Gosling to spoon-feed and translate the emotion every five minutes.

Going back to how it compares to the source material, the adaptation tried so hard to stay true to Weir's scientific detail that it forgot to watch the clock. This is the movie’s Achilles' heel: the pacing. Clocking in at over two and a half hours, the second act really drags. The script spends so much time on little lab experiments aboard the ship that the story runs out of steam. It lacks real thrills and emotional nuance in the middle of the journey; that classic gut-punch feeling that something irreparable might happen ends up feeling numbed.

Worse still, the overall structure leans on a pretty derivative skeleton. Putting the brilliance of the central relationship aside, the backbone of the plot is a bunch of tropes we've seen dozens of times in other space movies. The last-minute sacrifices, the engine failures, the race against time. The movie doesn't really innovate much there, choosing to lean on formulas that have already been tried and tested by the genre.

At the end of the day, Project Hail Mary is a cinematic experience with very obvious highs and lows. It knocks it out of the park with its stunning visuals, brilliant sound, and the patient building of a charismatic duo that you genuinely root for. The issue is when it trips hard over an overly long runtime and a melodrama that waters down the harsh reality of the end of the world.

It’s a movie with its heart in the right place—maybe even a bit too optimistic for its own good. Is it worth your time? Absolutely. Find the biggest screen and the best sound system you can, take the ride, and see for yourself. Just go in knowing you aren't going to get a narrative revolution in sci-fi, but rather a comforting, human-and-alien adventure looking to find warmth in the coldest part of the universe.

author: badelf
content:
Summary: 9/10: thrilling, funny, emotionally resonant sci-fi that uses its high concept to ask essential questions about cooperation, sacrifice, and whether we can save ourselves before it's too late.

I hadn't read Andy Weir's award-winning novel before seeing the film, so I wouldn't be disappointed by the adaptation. And I wasn't. The Lord-Miller team, Phil Lord and Christopher Miller, made this an exciting and rewarding sci-fi film that captures Weir's science-heavy problem-solving while never losing sight of its emotional core.

Ryan Gosling totally nailed the sardonic scientist, insisting on playing someone not good at being in space, someone who flips out and feels clumsy in zero gravity. His character arc, from isolated problem-solver to someone capable of profound emotional connection with Rocky, a sentient rock-shaped alien, is beautifully rendered. Gosling brings vulnerability and humor to a role that could have been purely cerebral, making Grace's transformation genuinely moving.

The premise of the film carries urgent relevance: we humans can survive only within a rather narrow temperature range. Project Hail Mary presents a cooling scenario, but the existential threat is the same whether we cool or overheat through global warming. The astrophage consuming the sun's energy becomes a metaphor for the forces draining our planet's capacity to sustain life.

According to a study published in Nature, almost two-thirds of global warming is caused by the wealthiest 10% of the world. Our time is running out, and this film functions as a call to action: we need many heroes like Grace and Rocky to step up and wrestle our future from the wealthy capitalists, monopolists, "kings," dictators, and other "astrophages" consuming resources without regard for collective survival.

Lord and Miller, working from Drew Goddard's screenplay, balance the novel's technical problem-solving with genuine humor and heart. The film understands that science fiction at its best isn't just about solving equations; it's about what we're willing to risk, who we're willing to become, to save each other.

author: MovieGuys
content:
Like a warm hug from the universe. That's how I'd characterise "Project Hail Mary". This is not an easy film to make, and yet its talented screenwriters give it laid-back, airy lightness, married up to a tale that's deeply humanistic and moving, even when it's being otherworldly. Action elements are present, but it's the story of two unlikely friends that really binds this wonderful film together.

In summary, it's rare for me to say "I loved a film", but "Project Hail Mary" is a film I won't forget. It's a reminder that it can be "good to be human" and, well, "not human," too! An instant classic.

author: The Fixate & Binge Podcast, w/ Joe Curdy
content:
Take the intergalactic splendor of **INTERSTELLAR**, mix in the humor and existentialism of **THE MARTIAN**, and what you get is **PROJECT HAIL MARY**, a masterpiece of filmmaking from directors Phil Lord and Christoper Miller, adapted for the screen by Drew Goddard from Andy Weir's 2021 novel (the latter of which collaborated on Weir's previous novel **THE MARTIAN**).

Featuring a strong central performance from Ryan Gosling as Dr Ryland Grace, a brilliant astrophysicist whose banishment from his science colleagues results in a rewarding, but secondary career as an unsung Middle School science teacher.

But the Earth is imperiled by a mysterious phenomenon affecting the literal source of life in our Solar System resulting in the incremental cooling of our Sun by a scientifically baffling occurrence -- and suddenly Dr Grace is called upon to test the very theory that resulted in his ignominious discrediting from the scientific community.

Helping the global project is Dr Eva Strait, played by Sandra Hüller, who assembles a Doomsday team of scientists alongside Gosling from around the world committed to unraveling this mystery.

Like **THE MARTIAN** before it, Weir's novels adapted for the screen in Goddard's capable hands achieve something few films within the genre ever attain -- a genuine interest in science and the awe of man's power to think through its most insurmountable challenges.

Narratively, Lord and Miller's film bounces between the past and the present with Gosling -- as his lonely mission comes into greater focus. As Gosling's spacecraft approaches an intergalactic sun which could holds clues to saving life back home, he encounters a fellow intrepid alien traveller seeking the same answers for survival.

It is this close encounter with alien life that improbably forms the heart of the film, as Gosling's interaction with his alien companion, affectionately (and aptly) named 'Rocky' highlights the value of friendship, sacrifice and the bonds of existence.

The emotions stirred from their heartwarming, compassionate pairing is the true surprise from the film, elevating it into esteemed cinema company alongside **CLOSE ENCOUNTERS OF THE THIRD KIND** (which gets a nice shout-out in the film) and **E.T.**

Practical effects and its very non-Green Screen rendering make this film a technological marvel of filmmaking -- as everything here fires on all the cylinders needed for pure cinema; expect multiple nominations at the 2027 Oscars for its technical achievements.

As for me and my family, we loved the film for its humor, determination, surprises and a very satisfying denouement. Who knew that at the edge of the universe Man might find its most meaningful friendship?

author: MovieGuys
content:
Colony is a marginal departure from your classic zombie flick. While intelligently written, there's not a lot on offer here, aside from a zombie hive mind proposition, that distinguishes this outbreak zombie horror disaster drama from others in the genre. That's not to say it's not worth a look if you like this kind of thing. The acting is excellent; the characters have a genuine depth, offering up predictably human responses, for better or worse, to the unfolding disaster that befalls them. Action is solid too, with lots of zombie thrills but little in the way of genuine scares, backed by solid choregraphy and cinamatics. 

In summary. Colony isn't doing anything overly new, but its script offers enough interest and excitement to make this film a worthwhile watch.

author: CinemaSerf
content: I wasn't inspired by the start of this film as it resembled a sort of foaming-at-the-mouth edition of the "Kids from Fame", but once it settles down it's actually quite a decent hybrid of a horror movie and a sci-fi thriller. It's following a presentation by a tech CEO (Kim Jong-tae) who is advancing the theories of communal communication and learning, itself quite a terrifying thought, that the disgruntled "Suh Yeong Cheol" (Koo Hyo-hwan) decides to seek his revenge on that man whom he accuses of stealing his revolutionary ideas and then firing him. He injects him with a serum that sees a remarkable effect on his ertswhile boss and proves contagious to just about everyone he comes into contact with - with this teeth!! This conference is taking place adjacent to a shopping mall so as these now rabid creatures spread that spells trouble for a disparate bunch of shoppers who manage to seek shelter in one of the shops. With the behaviour of the baying humans outside clearly adapting from the more moronic to something altogether more effective, they realise that help is staying firmly on the outside and that they are are going to have to save themselves. Luckily, all of their phones still work and amongst the group is a professor, "Se Jeong" (Jun Ji-hyun) who was at the seminar, so after a remote assessment with her peers they conclude that they must isolate "Suh" from his guardians and use him as some sort of vaccine. Easier said than done, but that's their task... This is quite a tensely constructed and well paced action adventure that benefits from some decent visual effects and from an ensemble cast working to create something of the claustrophobic to it: think "Poseidon Adventure" only with bloody-eyed savages pursuing them rather than rising water levels. It introduces and develops the concept that the infected masses aren't just wandering about arms outstretched, but that there is something more sophisticated behind their command and control processes and from that comes much of the menace here. Imagine an enemy that can reboot itself each time one of it's number learns something new? It also doesn't shy away from eliminating a few of the characters we are supposed to be cheering for - especially one young woman who convinced me that a building like this could actually serve well as a place to put some of our more obnoxious citizens for their just desserts. It does rather peter out a bit at the end turning into something akin to a video-game shoot 'em up, but the acting is all competent and the film raises quite a few questions about the dominating role of technology in our lives and at how ill-equipped humanity is to deal with it when it gets a mind of it's own.

author: Manuel São Bento
content:
Check out my full review @ https://www.manuelsbento.com/colony-2026-yeon-sang-ho-finds-a-genuinely-smart-idea-inside-a-familiar-zombie-formula/

Rating: B

Yeon Sang-ho returns to zombies with COLONY, trading a bullet train for a sealed-off Seoul high-rise and swapping fast infected for a hive-mind that evolves through communication. It's the smartest idea in the movie: these monsters understand each other better than the humans understand themselves, and that thesis about empathy and miscommunication genuinely lands. The cast sells it well despite mostly archetypal roles, but a few maddeningly avoidable plot mechanics keep undercutting the tension. Entertaining and tense, but derivative in almost every way except the one that matters most.

author: euron_legends
content:
Amazon MGM Studios seems to have found an area where it works pretty well: adapting young adult romances that already come with an established community behind them. The Love Hypothesis is another example.

The film, directed by Claire Scanlon, adapts Ali Hazelwood's novel, which also has a pretty interesting origin: it started out as fan fiction and eventually became a New York Times bestseller.

The story follows Olive Smith (Lili Reinhart), a brilliant PhD student who has a much clearer idea of where she wants to take her scientific career than what she wants from her love life. Everything changes after an impulsive kiss leads to a fake relationship with Adam Carlsen (Tom Bateman), a professor known for his difficult personality.

And from there, the movie knows exactly what it wants to be.

What I liked most is that it doesn't try to hide the fact that this is a romance. It doesn't seem embarrassed by its intimate scenes or try to make them completely sanitized just to fit a platform. The movie lets its characters be adults, lets there be genuine attraction between them, and gives that part of their relationship real weight within the story.

But above all, it works because of its leads.

Lili Reinhart and Tom Bateman have a chemistry that makes the relationship believable. There are moments when you simply buy the fact that these two characters are into each other, and that may sound basic, but in a romance, it's probably one of the most important things.

The critical reception has also been pretty positive, with 86% of reviews being favorable on Rotten Tomatoes at the time of writing.

I don't think The Love Hypothesis is reinventing anything. It doesn't need to.

It's a movie that understands exactly what kind of story it wants to tell and, for now, seems pretty comfortable telling it without apologizing for being a romance.

author: Manuel São Bento
content:
Check out my full review @ https://www.manuelsbento.com/moana-2026-stranded-on-a-soundstage-of-pure-nostalgia/

Rating: C

MOANA had every chance to expand on its animated predecessor, and it wastes almost all of it. Beat for beat identical to the 2016 original, this remake trades vibrant, sun-drenched color for green screen sterility, turning musical numbers that once felt joyously alive into stiff, mechanical spectacle. The lead performance brings real warmth to the title role, and the central chemistry has its moments, but neither is enough to disguise a film that never once asks why it needed to exist.

author: CinemaSerf
content: On a gorgeous Polynesian island where they all...speak...very...slowly, the young "Moana" (Catherine Laga'aia) is conflicted by her father's (John Tui) warning never to venture beyond the reef that protects their home and her grandmother (Rena Owen) who is embedded more in the tribe's ancestral and mystical roots and who has little fear of the open ocean and what lies beyond. When their crops all start to die, she is reminded of the legend of the demi-god "Maui" (Dwayne Johnson) who took the heart-stone from the benign goddess from whom all life sprang, and so she determines to find him and his magical hook and then restore the ornate stone to this font of all goodness. Perhaps that will reverse the process that is killing everything? Ten years on from the original animation and this doesn't really add very much to a story that was always a bit cheesy and thin. Here, it's at least forty-five minutes before the film really gets going and Johnson enters the fray and even then it's all just a little too formulaic. He does look like he's enjoying himself, but Laga'aia hasn't much by way of charisma to match and my favourites - the dart-blowing, sea-going, coconut critters - barely feature at all. The two songs that underpin this are familiar enough by now, but the rest of the music is borderline bland and by the rather hastily arrived at conclusion of this perfectly watchable but entirely forgettable rehash, I was wondering if they were already cannibalising the set from the "Lion King" on stage ready for the next iteration of "Moana" - the musical. It's pretty to look at but isn't much more than expensively crafted wallpaper, sorry.

author: Manuel São Bento
content:
Check out my full review @ https://www.manuelsbento.com/disclosure-day-2026-a-breathtakingly-human-paradigm-shift-in-modern-sci-fi/

Rating: A-

DISCLOSURE DAY is a fascinating, deeply hopeful return to sci-fi for Steven Spielberg, beautifully championing the concept of truth as a fundamental human right. Subverting the destructive tropes of typical alien invasion flicks, it favors radical empathy and genuine human connection over blockbuster chaos. Emily Blunt delivers a sensational, potentially career-best performance that anchors a truly incredible ensemble cast. Driven by exceptional camera work and a sweeping pace, it stands as one of my favorite films of the year so far. I cannot wait to see it again!

author: Brent Marchant
content: Director Steven Spielberg’s filmography is legendary, to say the least. Movies like “Jaws” (1975), “Close Encounters of the Third Kind” (1977), “Raiders of the Lost Ark” (1981), “E.T.: The Extraterrestrial” (1982), “Schindler’s List” (1993) and “Jurassic Park” (1993) have gone down as classics in the annals of filmmaking. And, even though some of his works in more recent years haven’t quite lived up to the quality of past efforts, it’s comforting to know that he’s still got what it takes when he gets behind the camera. This is where his latest release, “Disclosure Day,” comes into play, easily his best picture in years. This sci-fi/conspiracy theory/personal discovery thriller sports a multifaceted narrative that’s probably too complex to detail here, but that’s likely to be beneficial to viewers who walk into the theater knowing little, if anything about it in advance. In fact, I’d actually recommend approaching this offering from that standpoint to allow it to wash over you organically, to experience and wrap yourself up in the sense of awe and wonder it evokes without the hindrance of too many preconceptions. The one thing I will say about it is that it’s more than just another picture about UFOs and space aliens. While it’s true that formal disclosure about the coverup of an extraterrestrial presence on Earth over the past 80 years is at the core of the storyline, there’s much more going on here, imbuing the title with multiple meanings involving other subjects, including those of a personal and spiritual nature, adding depth to what might have otherwise been merely a more conventional science fiction movie. This becomes apparent through the film’s myriad story threads, which start out seeming disparate and unrelated, much like what happened at the beginning of “Close Encounters.” But, as this picture unfolds, connections develop showing how they all ultimately coalesce, just like in its predecessor. Some have called this kind of storytelling improbable and unrealistic, but many of us have undoubtedly seen this happen in our own lives, and, when that occurs, it doesn’t seem nearly so farfetched (so why should it be any different in a work of cinematic fiction?). Of course, grasping the connections, nuances and meanings in this requires devoting sufficient attention when watching the movie, so, if you’re unable or unwilling to do so for a film with a 2:25:00 runtime, you might want to skip this one. That would be regrettable, though, given that Spielberg is back at the top of his game here, telling a story with the same skills he has brought to so many other releases over the years in terms of depicting a compelling plot, building suspense, executing gripping action sequences and providing appropriately timed comic relief. He also provides a comprehensive palette of ufology-related topics, some of which are well known and others of which are more obscure (references that fans of Coast to Coast AM radio and The X-Files TV series will surely appreciate), but all of which are sufficiently explained without requiring ample viewer foreknowledge. And Spielberg has a lot of help bringing all this into being thanks to the insightful screenplay of David Koepp, the original score of composer John Williams (arguably his most mature work ever), and the superb performances of an ensemble cast featuring Emily Blunt, Josh O’Connor, Colin Firth, Colman Domingo, Eve Hewson, Wyatt Russell and Elizabeth Marvel. I’d heartily recommend watching this on as large a screen as possible (e.g., IMAX), and please pay no heed to the trolls voicing their uninformed opinions in trying to inexplicably tear this one down. “Disclosure Day” is about as nearly a perfect piece of filmmaking as one can envision. In fact, if I had to register a complaint of any kind here, it might be that the final act could be seen as being a little stretched out, but that’s such a minor criticism that it’s hardly worth mentioning. Savor all of the various forms of disclosure being served up in this release, as you may end up drawing upon them to discover aspects about yourself that you never knew before – and enabling you to walk out of the theater at the end a different person than who you were when you went in and into a different world than what you knew before.

author: dumasori
content:
**A Movie Made by Dinosaurs, for the Dinosaurs**

I wanted to like Disclosure Day. The premise—a government agent racing to expose classified alien contact—should be tense, urgent, relevant. Instead, what we get is a film so divorced from how the actual world works that it feels like it was written by people who've been in a bunker since 1987.

The core problem: when your protagonist needs to leak classified information in 2026 or whenever this is supposed to happen, why in God's name are we watching them scheme about getting it done through a news room? The movie shows thumb drives, AI, all this modern tech—and then treats a television newsroom like it's the only lever that matters. It's nonsensical. If you want to burn a government secret to the world, you don't need Walter Cronkite anymore. There are better platforms on the internet. The infrastructure exists. The filmmakers simply have no clue how modern information systems work.

And then there's the blandness. The villains have no depth—why do they actually care about keeping this secret? The heroes have no passion—what's driving them besides a vague sense of duty? There's no tension, no stakes that feel real, no reason to invest in anyone on screen. It's hollow. The whole thing is just hollow.

Disclosure Day isn't terrible. It's worse: it's boring. Please let it remain undisclosed!

author: CinemaSerf
content: I blame Christopher Nolan: this film is far, far, too long. The concept is quite interesting and complex, and the first half hour tees things up intriguingly but thereafter it just disappoints with a surfeit of dialogue and very little menace before delivering a conclusion that for someone who worked in live television for thirty years is implausible bordering on the downright preposterous. "Daniel" (Josh O'Connor) has a narrow escape from the nasty "Noah" (Colin Firth) who wants to get back a mysterious glowing device that he has pinched. Meantime, television weather forecaster "Margaret" (Emily Blunt) takes a bit of a turn. Inexplicably, she can now speak fluent Korean and then passes out at the prospect of telling Kansans that hail is looming. How could these two events possibly be connected? Well that's what we find out as the mother of all, very extended and somewhat repetitive, car chases gradually fills us in on a plan being co-ordinated by "Hugo" (Colman Domingo - the only man so far who actually needed to speak with an American accent) that isn't really understood by anyone - including himself! Is there something extra-terrestrial afoot here? All the while the world is facing another existential crisis over some military antics on the Korean peninsula and so maybe mankind is doomed anyway and all this burning rubber is for nought? This film is a wet dream for conspiracy theorists the world over, but with little by way of characterisation it's lacking in depth, detail, humour or soul. It's overly trading on the name of it's director/writer and relying on some visual and occasional animatronic effects that we've been getting more and more used to ever since "ET" forty-odd years ago. This isn't a bad film, it just isn't a very good one and I reckon nobody will remember it for long. It is a cinema must, though, if you do want to see it. It will look extremely bland on the television and after a while that fast-forward button might prove irresistably tempting.

author: MonksFilms
content:
I feel like i'm rating this film lower if it wasn't a Steven Spielberg production. For the most part it features his usual polish which is above average in most cases. The camera movement and staging is as good as ever. There's even some car chase sequences thrown in to break up the pacing and give this film a jolt of energy and remind us of how much fun Spielberg's action can be.

My biggest complaint is my disconnection with the characters. Everyone of the cast members do a great job with what they have to work with. Unfortunately there's not much to them. Perhaps Jane (Eve Hewson) is the character with the biggest arch but we don't get a lotta time with her. It makes the whole thing run like molasses at times in the middle as they just seem to be checking off the boxes of plot exposition. I also didn't like the cat and mouse play between Noah (Colin Firth) and our two main characters Margaret (Emily Blunt) and Daniel (Josh O'Conner). It's confusing at first, then it makes sense, and then they use it too much to the point it just drags.

The film somehow manages to come together for a roller coaster finale. The sloppy and seemingly rushed threads come together for something that definitely hits hard and is more concentrated and developed than the early parts of the film. I found myself at full attention as the film began firing on all cinematic cylinders for it's conclusion. Overall I'm happy I saw it but it's probably gonna be my only watch for Disclosure. This probably would have worked better as a series so the characters and ideas could be developed a bit more. We do get what could be John Williams' last score, I made sure I stayed for the whole credits roll.

author: misubisu
content:
**Score: 3/10 — A Fictional Misstep in a Moment Demanding Truth**

For the average movie-goer, this film would probably gain a higher score. It has the Spielberg pedigree, a solid cast led by the fantastic Emily Blunt, and a chase-thriller structure that delivers some entertainment. But for those of us who sit where we do on the precipice of actual disclosure, deeply invested in the reality of UAPs and Non-Human Intelligence (NHI), this film is an extremely flawed and very disappointing experience.

The most frustrating part is its premise. The film explores a "what if" scenario of a public unveiling of alien secrets, but given where we are in the world today, this is not the right time for a fictitious movie on this topic to be released. **Half the population of the planet believes that we are not alone, and are looking for answers.** The real world conversation is finally shifting, driven by congressional hearings, whistleblower testimonies, and a slow trickle of government acknowledgment. Releasing a heavily fictionalised, melodramatic thriller during this fragile moment feels not just unhelpful, but almost exploitative.

I can watch a movie like *E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial* and be thoroughly entertained because it is very clearly a film made for entertainment, with an entertaining plot. *Disclosure Day*, on the other hand, is not just entertainment for many people. It draws directly on real world themes; the "Tic Tac" sightings, the Roswell narrative, the 2023 congressional hearings using them as a launchpad for a film that one critic called "flimsy" and "outdated". The result is a film that feels caught between wanting to be a serious meditation on the topic and delivering a generic chase movie that "has no ideas about aliens that we haven't heard before" .

The plot is a mess. A whistleblower's plan to leak evidence depends on a local TV news broadcast, which feels like a plot device from the 1980s . There are seemingly pointless supernatural elements, such as "a crop circle magically forms around Daniel" with no explanation . The film's focus on the chase means the thought provoking elements are sacrificed for action that one review called "a drab X-Files episode" .

The ending, in which Margaret delivers the one word message "Listen" to the world, feels more like a pretentious cliffhanger than a profound statement. The hope is that we can separate the real, unfolding history from this reductive, fictional placeholder .

**The Verdict**

*Disclosure Day* is a film that misunderstands its moment. For those of us deep in the rabbit hole of UFOs and NHI, you're better off not watching this movie. The real story is far more fascinating and unfolding in real time. This film is a hollow echo of a conversation that has finally started to get serious.

**Watch if:** You are an average movie goer looking for an undemanding Spielberg thriller and can ignore the real world context.

**Skip if:** You follow the UAP topic closely. The sub plots and storylines are extremely flawed and very disappointing. The search for truth is better served by documentaries and congressional hearings than this reductive movie.

author: Martin Oaks
content:
**Spielberg’s fade to black**

Daniel (Josh O'Connor) is a cybersecurity analyst who stumbles upon classified video files proving the government has been capturing and torturing non-human beings ever since the Roswell incident. After becoming a digital fugitive, he joins forces with Margaret Fairchild (Emily Blunt), a TV meteorologist experiencing strange perceptual phenomena. Together, they launch a race against time to expose the existence of alien life to the world, all while escaping the clutches of an implacable government contractor played by Colin Firth, who is hell-bent on stopping the uncontrolled leak of these files.

"Disclosure Day" marks Steven Spielberg’s long-awaited return to alien-contact sci-fi—a genre where he previously gifted us absolute masterpieces like "Close Encounters of the Third Kind." Unfortunately, this piece of work feels way more like an exercise in self-indulgence than a fresh, modern take.

The first hour of the feature film works quite well as a corporate conspiracy thriller. The protagonists' pursuit maintains a tense pace, and the cinematography is, predictably, top-tier (complete with its fair share of absurd details and inexplicable plot holes, of course). However, as the plot drags on, David Koepp’s script gets tangled up in pseudoscientific nonsense about childhood trauma and the main characters' psychic abilities, completely draining the urgency from their very escape.

The film's fatal flaw lies in its high-and-mighty moral and philosophical pretensions. Spielberg gets so incredibly bogged down in emphasizing the importance of faith, communication, and humanity's place in the universe that he forgets to give the audience any sort of satisfying resolution. Deliberately cutting the climax short just to fade to black after the word "Listen..." is nowhere near a poetic, cinematic stroke of freaking genius—it’s just a cheap trick to avoid answering the questions we spent over two hours setting up.

author: Wuchak
content:
***What if those rumors about the Roswell incident are true?***

This comes in the tradition of Spielberg’s “Close Encounters of the Third Kind,” smacking of an X-Files story with focus on that show’s alien conspiracy, such as the 1998 film “Fight the Future,” just without Mulder and Scully. The 2008 version of “The Day the Earth Stood Still” is also comparable.

Way back in 1989 an episode of Unsolved Mysteries explored the Roswell incident with witnesses claiming that they saw the bodies of extraterrestrial beings as Feds cleaned up a crash site in New Mexico of debris made from unearthly material. The next year Megadeth released the song “Hangar 18,” named after the building at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Dayton, Ohio, and rooted in the Roswell incident. This movie simply expounds on the coverup with the revelation of the (supposed) truth to all humanity. My point is that the ideas in the movie aren’t anything new.

I heard a rather extremist response describing the film as “a psyop to convince the public that aliens (demons) are benevolent” but, if this is the case, the same argument could be made for the original version of “The Day the Earth Stood Still” from 75 years ago, not to mention dozens of episodes of Star Trek. I think I’ll go with the mundane possibility that this is merely a sci-fi story meant to entertain and provoke ideas, particularly about humankind needing to chill out since we’re closer to the brink of nuclear Armageddon than ever.

The second viewpoint is easier to embrace seeing as how the movie includes magic cylinders that enable holders to channel cosmic energy and perform superhuman feats. This isn’t far removed from the Cosmic Cube of the Marvel universe, the Tesseract, which Thanos breaks in “Avengers: Infinity War” to extract the Space Stone.

Emily Blunt is effective in the leading role, yet she’s outshined by Eve Hewson as Jane. Meanwhile Colin Firth does well as the antagonist. Others with key roles include Josh O’Connor, Colman Domingo and Wyatt Russell.

With Spielberg at the helm, the movie is well made and the story is compelling, augmented by a suspenseful action sequence in the second half involving a train and a couple of vehicles. I also liked how Margaret (Blunt) is uncannily able to read a person's mail, so to speak, which profoundly affects them and is pulled off in an almost reverent way.

Unfortunately, the flick’s hindered by at least one glaring sequence in which it’s impossible to suspend disbelief. I’m talking about the part where the male protagonist eludes several quasi-FBI agents at a farmhouse with the agents being either incompetent or blind since he fails to actually hide behind anything. Then there’s the car literally driving through a house no worse for wear. Why Sure!

Another issue is that I don’t see this working on repeat viewings. It’s a one-watch movie.   

It runs 2h 25m and was shot in three months from Feb-May 2025 across southeastern New York and the state of New Jersey (too many locations to cite).

GRADE: B-

author: CinemaSerf
content: When the yellow perils manage to gatecrash a film studio and cause havoc on the set of a film, the director is terrified that his two rotund bosses will want his head. Instead, though, they adore the chaos and commission him to make more films featuring the "Minions". Swiftly, they go from rags to riches and are hugely popular until... Sound. Silent movies have gone the way of the dodo and now there is to be audio. Yikes - who wants to sit in a drive-in and listen to lots of squeaking and squawking coming from these diminutive stars? Well, nobody really and so swiftly they are back out on poverty row once more with nowhere to go. "James" and his pal "Henry" conclude that their film-making days are not yet over when their erstwhile director gives them an old boxed Brownie, but they need a baddie. What better one than a monster, and when they stumble upon an ancient book of spells and arouse the mischievous "Goomi" they appear to have solved their problem - without realising that this isn't so much a big jelly of a stage beastie, it's one that is being controlled to absorb everything in it's path be that animal, mineral or solid concrete. Now it is the pretty urgent task of these "Minions" to reverse their spell before they, and all of their fellows, become extinct. Aside from this being quite an entertaining homage to the golden days of Hollywood it's all just a terribly predictable and dare I say forgettable affair. I enjoyed the "Minions" best when they were the henchies of the menacing "Gru", but here the whole thing just lacks soul a bit and the normally appealing gibberish - where we try to pick out actual words in any language from their twittering - started to annoy me for the first time as this stretched out what felt like an half-hour television episode into a thinly-spread feature. For some reason, it's told to us via a reflective narration from a museum curator so there isn't even any jeopardy either, and I left thinking it really quite disappointing. Certainly it's a watchable effort and the kids in the cinema did seem to love it, but there's much less for those grown-ups amongst us and it seems to content to rest on it's previous laurels a little too much for me.

author: andrewtislercinephile
content: Illumination made great tributes to Old Hollywood in *Minions & Monsters*. This 2026 comedy film does a great job of exploring the process behind the movies and how they're made, all while delivering funny slapstick comedy, strong character dynamics, incredible animation, an all-star voice cast, and a musical score that blends *Despicable Me*'s signature vibes with a 1920s feel that is charming, intimate, and a loving tribute to an era gone by. I also loved the plot twist at the end of the movie, where it is revealed the whole story is staged and the Minions, James and Henry, were filming the entire movie the whole time, including the studio tour at the beginning. Goomi was a great villain, and the fact you could tell he'd do something evil before he even reveals his true intentions makes his actions all the more devious. People claimed his villainous intent was spoiled too much in the trailers, but Illumination's villains are known for being up front and evil from the get-go, so realistically, Goomi wouldn't be hiding anything. My only complaint is that the movie is too rushed. That is an issue I've always had with Illumination's movies, as it implies that kids cannot sit through something much longer, but Pixar and DreamWorks, among others, have proven that to be not the case. Regardless, this movie was a lot of fun, and I'll happily watch *Minions & Monsters* again soon.

author: Brent Marchant
content: A movie that bills itself as more than it turns out to be has got to be guilty of one of the most egregious sins in filmmaking, and director Michael Showalter’s screen adaptation of this best-selling novel by author Colleen Hoover qualifies on virtually all fronts. Although touted as a dark, erotic psychological thriller, this offering is none of those things. In fact, it barely passes as fare that one might find on the Lifetime cable TV network. When famed novelist Verity Crawford (Anne Hathaway) is severely injured in a car accident, her publisher (K.K. Moggie) looks to hire a ghostwriter to stand in for her to finish several titles in her current book series while (or if) she recovers. Crawford’s husband, Jeremy (Josh Hartnett), recommends the job go to a struggling, little-known aspiring writer, Lowen Ashleigh (Dakota Johnson), whom he inexplicably believes is best capable of mimicking his wife’s prosaic style. Although somewhat intimidated at the prospect of this offer, Lowen nevertheless accepts it and relocates from New York to the Crawfords’ Vermont home, where she has access to the novelist’s extensive notes and research materials. But, once there, the clueless stand-in finds herself embroiled in a scenario full of mysteries, confessions and intrigue involving the Crawfords’ personal and professional lives. What’s more, she unwittingly becomes involved in matters of infidelity (lukewarm though it may be), solving the conundrum of Verity’s true health status, and getting to the bottom of the allegedly accidental drowning of her young daughter (Sienna Kulovitz), a mystery shrouded in details as murky as the lake where it happened. These circumstances also prompt the emergence of new ambitions by all concerned, even if they frequently come out of left field. Potentially speaking, there should have been enough to work with here to make for a steamy noir-esque potboiler or, in the alternative, a deliciously campy romp. Regrettably, though, it’s neither of those things. On the contrary, “Verity” is boring, implausible and lacking in all of the qualities it was erroneously imbued with. The clunky, plot hole-filled writing is the prime culprit here, but the abysmal casting knocks the project down more than a few pegs, too. While Hathaway turns in her usual capable work, it’s vastly overshadowed by the remarkably underwhelming performance of Hartnett and the positively dreadful monotone portrayal of Johnson, who treats her character with the same deadpan, dispassionate handling as she did in the “Fifty Shades of Grey” trilogy (2015-2018). Moreover, were it not for the stunning visuals of the Vermont landscape (particularly in winter) and the stylish appointments of the designer home in which most of the story is set, there’s really not much else to see (or like) in this absolute utter snoozefest. How this title ever got out of pre-production is beyond me, but, if your expectations are low, this just might be to your liking – that is, if there’s nothing to watch on Lifetime.

author: Harish Napa Janakiraman
content:
The psychological thriller sets up an intriguing, twisted premise filled with dark secrets and moral ambiguity. Unraveling the hidden manuscript inside an unsettling household provides genuine suspense, giving the story enough eerie tension to make it a good, engaging watch overall.

Dakota Johnson is absolutely stunning in the lead, bringing effortless allure, quiet curiosity, and sharp emotional vulnerability to her character. Her commanding screen presence anchors the entire film, making her descent into obsession feel captivating even when the narrative begins to drag.

However, the dull screenplay keeps the movie from reaching its full potential. The pacing feels sluggish in key stretches, relying on convenient exposition rather than building sharp psychological dread. While the writing stumbles and fails to deliver a tighter punch, Dakota's magnetic performance and the atmospheric mystery keep it thoroughly enjoyable.

author: CinemaSerf
content: "Lowen" (Dakota Johnson) has just left a sparsely-attended book signing when her agent tells her she might have an opportunity to make some proper cash. That involves her doing a bit of collaboration with the well-established best-seller "Verity" (Anne Hathaway) who has become temporarily incapacitated. She's very anxious about taking on this responsibility, but the poorly author's husband "Jeremy" (Josh Hartnett) - with whom she'd already had an unfortunate encounter en-route to the meeting - convinces her to give it a go and to move in with them at their remote and luxurious Montana home. It's once she is there that she discovers just what is wrong with "Verity" and also a manuscript on a hidden flash drive that provides her with quite a ghastly narrative of the goings-on within this marriage. All the while she is finding herself increasingly drawn to "Jeremy" and their young son "Crew" (Brady Wagner) but the more of the unpublished story she reads, and the more she observes around her, the less she takes on face value and ultimately believes. Is any of this scenario actually real? Given she's barely been off the screen in 2026, it's not too surprising that Hathaway has chosen to spend almost all of her sparing appearances here either in bed or on a chair - she actually contributes really very little to an otherwise rather good-looking but plodding drama that has far too many predicatable tram-lines to follow. When Hartnett was younger and had something of the eye-candy to him, I could see why he was on screen but now he has aged into really quite a bland actor who brings virtually nothing original to his role. Even the usually more reliable, though hardly versatile, Johnson seems content to just go through the motions as we skip along to an denouement that is both rushed and, I felt, contrived to suggest there might be legs in "Verity II". It is trying to be a little more sophisticated a thriller, but sadly it's all just join-the-dots stuff that you may well have forgotten by the time you leave the foyer. I did like the house, though.

author: dumasori
content:
**Brave, emotional, and beautiful**

 I had the opportunity to watch this movie before its official release, experiencing the premiere early. 

The film is gripping, and several scenes had me on the edge of my seat. The direction is excellent, and Brad Pitt's performance is outstanding. Although the story is set in Alaska, most of the shooting took place in New Zealand, showcasing a beautiful wilderness. The emotional scenes were well-executed, making it easy to relate to the protagonist. Not to mention, the dog also did a fantastic job.

Overall, it is a great watch. While the survival concept isn't new, this is one of the most well-executed films in the genre.

author: Manuel São Bento
content:
Check out my full review @ https://www.manuelsbento.com/heart-of-the-beast-2026-david-ayer-finds-his-gentlest-film-yet-in-a-dogs-steady-gaze/

Rating: B

HEART OF THE BEAST sends Brad Pitt and his real-life canine co-star(s) into New Zealand's wilderness for a survival story you've essentially seen before: man and dog, cold and hunger, one obstacle after another. What saves it is restraint. David Ayer lets his camera simply sit with two creatures who trust each other completely, and set against absolutely gorgeous landscapes, that trust becomes genuinely moving. Predictable, formulaic, and I cried anyway.

author: CinemaSerf
content: Anyone remember "One Man and His Dog" on the telly? Well instead of a sheepdog, this introduces us to "Odin" - an highly trained military canine that's clearly had a fairly torrid time and is now in the care of his ertswhile sergeant "James" (Brad Pitt). "James" has his own little Cessna and loves nothing more than to set off into the Alaskan wilderness to get back to nature. He, too, is not without his wartime injuries and it's while he is trying to outfly a storm that his plane ends up in a lake. Now the pair have to make it across sixty miles of inhospitable terrain and avoid some wolves and bears if they are to make it to the nearest road. What ensues illustrates the affection and inter-dependence of both of these characters as they struggle against adversity and injury but I think my problem here was that word "character". We don't really get to know much about "James" at all, and so are largely left with an updated version of "Incredible Journey" (1963) - only with far improved photography of their pristine and unforgiving environment. Oddly enough for a film that can't have had many budget issues, the CGI effects aren't the best and the whole thing just came across as a little too earnest a project for me. Pitt and director David Ayer clearly have points to make and the ethics of using animals as weapons of war, as well as the provision of aftercare for all who fought and returned - traumatised to varying degrees, and who were left to reintegrate into a society for which they are now ill-equipped, are a couple that are raised quite poignantly at times,  but again we are given too little context beyond a few violent flashbacks to put some roots onto their obvious bond. Their constant frying pan-to-fire scenarios also begin to stretch the bounds of plausibility and some of the continuity simply doesn't add up, either. In some ways, I almost wished this were just a documentary of a survival story that we could observe without feeling any need to invest in "James", but instead I found this just a little too short on depth and maybe just a little too sentimental. It does remind us of just how puny mankind is when we are exposed, largely unarmed and un-pampered, to nature on it's terms, and Pitt certainly convinces on the strenuous effort front, but I just wanted a little more story. Sorry.

Given how many endless, empty geometric hallways our main character had to wander through, having Justin Long’s character from Barbarian pop up with a tape measure to calculate the square footage would have genuinely made this a 5-star masterpiece.

Backrooms completely nails the atmosphere in the first half. The grainy, handheld "home video" style shots build an insane amount of tension, and making the entire environment harsh and well-lit instead of hiding in the dark is a brilliant way to capture that pure, unsettling liminal space dread. The sound design is heavy and unrelenting, but the editing kills the momentum in the second half. The audio masterfully amps up your anxiety to a 10, but the actual visual reveals completely flatten out and fail to deliver on the build-up. Still, it's a solid watch on a big screen.

author: Brent Marchant
content: Anointing a young, first-time big screen director as the new filmmaking messiah of his or her particular genre is a risky undertaking, to be sure. Does the fledgling auteur have what it takes to live up to that auspicious title? Is this an ordination that’s truly warranted? It’s serious business, both for box office tallies and artistically speaking. But does the heir apparent truly possess the skills, talent and vision to achieve success on both fronts? That’s something worth considering in light of the debut feature from writer-director Kane Parsons, the force behind this aspiring smart horror release, which is quickly being praised to the hilt and drawing huge numbers in ticket sales. However, I believe that the coronation of this new voice in the genre is far from deserved and entirely premature. While it’s true that Parsons has a keen eye for the aesthetic, that’s only half the challenge when making a movie in virtually any genre. The other part – being an effective storyteller – needs work (and a lot of it). Based on a YouTube adaptation of his immensely popular internet TV series The Backrooms, the film follows a troubled (and largely unsuccessful) seller of cheap furniture, Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor), who’s experiencing difficulties in his personal life and professional calling. His failed marriage and inability to make use of his training as an architect have led him to seek counseling from a high-profile therapist, Dr. Mary Kline (Renate Reinsve). His progress takes a drastic turn, though, when he finds a maze of what appears to be a collection of office suites adjacent to his store’s basement – a discovery he makes by somehow walking through one of its walls. The spaces are seemingly devoid of people but haphazardly strewn with various items from his life, including his past. Has he stepped into a corporeal manifestation of his psyche? An alternate reality? Or something else entirely? That’s what he hopes to learn with the unexpected help of his skeptical shrink. And what will that be? The film’s opening half capably sets the scene, creating a legitimately sinister sense of creepiness. However, about midway into the picture, it becomes repetitive and directionless, as if it’s searching for what to do next. That’s where this offering goes off the rails, turning inexplicable, underdeveloped and outright goofy at times. The alleged scariness of this would-be psychological thriller vanishes, turning tedious, silly and more laughable than frightening. And a last-ditch effort to take the narrative in a redemptive direction involving a mysterious scientific research organization only muddies the waters further, doing little to salvage what has already fallen apart. Many have likened this release to a video game with a protagonist trying to solve the puzzle of the story. Others have said that it’s full of nuanced references to the YouTube series, although that would require an intimate knowledge of the source material to fully appreciate it. And others still have postulated a host of other interpretations given the inherently vague nature of the finished product. For my money, even though it starts out well, it turns into an incoherent cinematic mess that fails to hold attention and left me sighing a big “So what?” What became most apparent to me while sitting through this is just how difficult it is to create an engaging smart horror film, a genre I enjoy immensely but has been plagued by more failures than successes, with this one being yet another entry on that list of disappointments. Indeed, don’t be too quick to reach for that crown just yet. If the filmmaker hopes to assume that title, he’s still got his work cut out for him, beginning with an urgent need to get out of his own “Backrooms.”

author: CinemaSerf
content: Hmmm. Perhaps I just wasn't in the mood, but I really didn't get what the fuss was about with this. "Clark" (Chiwitel Ejiofor) is a recently divorced man who has big dreams but who is reduced to running (and sleeping in) his cheap and cheerful "Ottoman Empire" furniture emporium in small town America. The electrics in his store start playing up and upon investigation he is intrigued by a glimmer of light that appears to be emenating from beneath the basement wall! Investigating, he discovers that there is a mysterious portal into a construction that has something of an Escher drawing straight from the mind of Lewis Carroll to it. He tries to explain this discovery to his sceptical therapist (Renate Reinsve) but she thinks he's lost the plot so he engages the help of two of his employees "Kat" (Lukita Maxwell) and her boyfriend "Bobby" (Finn Bennett) to film his next exploration - and that's when they discover that all in this new dimension is not so very friendly. Meantime, his shrink "Mary" makes a visit to her patient's showroom only to discover the same portal. Is she going to be daft enough to walk through the wall into the unknown? There is some attempt made at the end to tie up the spurious threads but for the most part I found this to be really quite a dull and unmenacing affair that is hand-held filmed in a style of "Blair Witch" to try and immerse us in it's mystery but that more often than not relies on increasingly hysterical dialogue and a great deal of beige paint to create some sense of menace. Kane Parsons presided over a decent idea for about twenty minutes, but thereafter is all just fizzled out into a repetitious short-story of a film that I felt was overstretched.

author: Alejandro Merino Ortega
content:
I'll start by saying I'm not a hater; I wanted to enjoy it, I really did. But I think some scriptwriting decisions were made that really hurt the final result.
I'll begin with the scene where they discover the backrooms. While the opening scene is interesting, the scene where the protagonist finds them is not. Having a clear exit point significantly reduces the tension for him. He controls the space, he's oriented, and he doesn't seem lost or confused by having to take paths he wouldn't choose if fleeing the creature. He quickly finds his way back. This sequence evokes so little fear that the protagonist even goes back to grab a stool. (He's not afraid of the place; he controls it.) For the viewer, this provides a certain sense of reassurance, since this is the character we've been following since the beginning of the film, and he's the one we fear or worry about as viewers.

Regarding the character's development, it's true he displays a certain amount of resentment and simmering anger toward his ex-wife, but the character ultimately commits actions (decapitating Kat) that are implausible given how his psychology had been established up to that point. He isn't portrayed as aggressive, especially not toward others.

I think it would have worked better as an opening film to introduce this place through the eyes of people who had no control over the situation. Perhaps a more slasher-like approach: a group of kids who get lost, become frightened, start fighting amongst themselves, unease and distrust grow, and little by little they are attacked or killed in front of their helpless companions who do everything they can to find a way out.

The character introductions are rather slow, and this doesn't significantly change anything as the plot progresses. In addition, they explain the strange creatures before showing the "final" creature, making it more understandable for the viewer and, at the same time, much less aberrant or terrifying than it could have been. Some things are "planted" in the film, but I think they're underdeveloped, perhaps in anticipation of a sequel or turning it into a saga. I consider this reasonable given the potential of the original idea, but at the same time, I don't think it's the best introduction for viewers unfamiliar with this "universe." That said, I'll add that the version on YouTube seemed a thousand times better; it creates a more disturbing, confusing, and interesting atmosphere than this film. I hope many of you enjoyed it, but for me, it wasn't even half of what I had hoped for.

It fell short.

author: misubisu
content:
**Score: 3/10 — An Engaging Walk to Nowhere**

I don't like movies that go nowhere, don't make any sense, or lack an actual ending. And *Backrooms*? It's the poster child for all three. I feel like I've wasted a part of my life that I will never get back... time that could have been better spent watching a different movie.

The concept is solid. Kane Parsons, the 20-year-old director behind the viral YouTube series, brings the internet's favourite liminal space nightmare to the big screen. Chiwetel Ejiofor plays Clark, a failed architect and struggling furniture store owner who discovers a doorway in his basement to an infinite labyrinth of yellow walled, fluorescent lit rooms. Renate Reinsve plays his therapist, Mary, who follows him in. The production design is genuinely impressive the Backrooms feel unsettlingly real and deeply disorienting.

But that's where the praise ends.

**Having said that, the movie was engaging and I didn't realise that I didn't like it 'til the credits rolled.** I was invested, the atmosphere is thick, the dread is palpable, and Ejiofor's performance is committed. The first 70 minutes deliver exactly what you'd hope: eerie corridors, unsettling silence, and a creeping sense that reality itself is unravelling .

Then the film loses its footing. The momentum shifts, the tension dissipates, and the narrative attempts to add meaning without committing to anything concrete. Clark explains that the Backrooms "misremembers" people, creating imperfect replicas of reality. The monster, revealed as a distorted, pirate costumed version of Clark himself, kills him in a moment that lands with a dull thud. Mary escapes, or does she? The final shot shows a malformed replica of Mary slumped in an interrogation chair, and we're left with ambiguity that feels more like creative cowardice than artistic choice.

It's the kind of ending that thinks it's being clever but is really just being lazy. The film offers no solutions, no rules, no answers, just a mountain of unanswered questions and an audience that's stopped caring. I was left with... well, nothing. No resolution, no catharsis, no desire to ever revisit this world. Many viewers share this frustration, audience reviews are split, with some praising the atmosphere and others decrying the hollow, confused ending.

It earns its 3 points for the production values, which ain't half bad. The set design, cinematography, and Ejiofor's performance deserve some credit. But the story goes nowhere, the ending is empty, and the experience left me feeling cheated. I could have spent those 105 minutes on something that actually respected my time.

author: Vinicius Monteiro
content:
Translating an internet legend to the big screen is a huge challenge, but A24 and director Kane Parsons managed to nail the creepy aesthetic of the famous "Backrooms." By relying heavily on practical effects rather than just green screens, they made the endless yellow maze feel incredibly real, dirty, and deeply claustrophobic. The visual design is the true star here, perfectly capturing that weird liminal space vibe where everything looks familiar but feels fundamentally wrong. Parsons shows surprising maturity as a young director, using steady camera work and patience to build a genuinely oppressive atmosphere right from the opening scene.

The movie’s unsettling vibe is heavily boosted by its brilliant sound design and strong lead performances. The constant, annoying hum of the old fluorescent lights slowly chips away at your sanity, and when the movie suddenly shifts to dead silence, the tension becomes almost unbearable. On the acting side, Chiwetel Ejiofor does some heavy lifting acting against basically nothing, using his body language to perfectly portray a man losing his mind in isolation. Renate Reinsve also shines as his therapist, bringing a much-needed touch of humanity and warmth that contrasts beautifully with the cold, lifeless hallways.

Unfortunately, the movie stumbles hard when it comes to the script and pacing. Stretching a minimalist concept into a two-hour runtime creates a massive drag in the middle, turning what should be terrifying into something kind of boring and repetitive. The film also falls into the modern trap of trying to force a deep, intellectual metaphor about trauma, which just slows the story down. Worse yet, they decided to actually show the threat—a generic CGI monster that completely ruins the mysterious, existential dread the empty rooms had already built up so well. Because the main character isn't given much of a personality, it eventually becomes hard to stay emotionally invested in his survival.

The ending only adds to the frustration, wrapping things up abruptly while clearly planting seeds for future sequels instead of giving us a satisfying, standalone conclusion. It feels a bit like a corporate cash-grab trying to turn a weird, anonymous internet mystery into a predictable movie franchise. Still, even with these glaring issues, the jump from YouTube to a Hollywood feature is an impressive technical achievement. It is definitely worth seeing on the biggest screen you can find, just to experience the incredible visuals and sound for yourself, as the sheer dread of those endless yellow rooms might hit you completely differently.

author: Marco-Hugo Landeta Vacas
content:
(CASTELLANO)

La sensación más inquietante de Backrooms no viene de un monstruo concreto, sino de algo mucho más difícil de explicar: estar en un lugar que parece recordar nuestro mundo sin comprenderlo del todo. Pasillos, muebles, carteles y habitaciones resultan familiares, pero están colocados con una lógica incorrecta, como si alguien hubiera intentado reconstruir la realidad a partir de recuerdos mal conservados. Esa idea me parece mucho más perturbadora que cualquier explicación simple sobre otra dimensión.

Kane Parsons entiende perfectamente el poder del espacio liminal. Lo cotidiano deja de ser tranquilizador porque está ligeramente desplazado: las proporciones no encajan, los recorridos parecen no conducir a ninguna parte y cada objeto conocido genera más desconfianza que alivio. La película consigue que mirar una pared, un pasillo vacío o una iluminación fluorescente pueda resultar más inquietante que muchos sustos convencionales.

Ahí está su gran virtud: la atmósfera. Backrooms no necesita estar atacando continuamente al espectador. Le basta con mantener la sensación de que algo está mal y de que ese error puede aparecer en cualquier esquina. El diseño de producción es extraordinariamente importante porque convierte los espacios en el verdadero centro del terror. Más que atravesar un escenario, los personajes parecen entrar en una memoria defectuosa que se recompone mientras la recorren.

La idea de la reconstrucción imperfecta me parece especialmente potente. Hay algo casi onírico en reconocer un sitio sin poder afirmar de dónde lo conocemos. Como ocurre en ciertos sueños, todo parece correcto mientras no se observa demasiado. Basta detenerse para descubrir que una puerta no debería estar ahí, que una habitación parece demasiado grande o que un detalle pertenece a otro tiempo. Esa lógica de sueño está mucho más cerca del terror que cualquier explicación literal.

Renate Reinsve me funciona muchísimo. Tiene una manera muy natural de transmitir fragilidad, desconcierto y miedo sin caer en la histeria. Su rostro aguanta primeros planos largos y permite que la película repose en pequeñas reacciones. Incluso cuando el entorno se vuelve más extraño, ella mantiene una humanidad que impide que todo se convierta en un mero ejercicio visual. Es fácil preocuparse por ella porque nunca parece una pieza de la mitología, sino una persona atrapada dentro de algo que no entiende.

También agradezco que Parsons no trate de domesticar demasiado el concepto nacido en internet. El peligro de llevar los Backrooms a un largometraje era convertir una idea basada en la sugerencia en una mitología saturada de explicaciones. La película roza ese problema en algunos momentos, pero conserva suficiente misterio como para que los espacios sigan produciendo inquietud por sí mismos.

No todo funciona igual de bien. La narración es bastante más débil que la construcción visual y hay momentos en los que se nota que el concepto podría vivir perfectamente con menos argumento. Algunas partes se estiran y ciertos elementos parecen existir porque el largometraje necesita progresar, no porque el mundo los necesite. Ahí aparece una tensión evidente entre el fenómeno original y las exigencias de una película convencional.

Pero, curiosamente, esa fragilidad narrativa no me molestó demasiado. El verdadero relato está en la exploración, en la sensación de avanzar hacia lugares que reconocemos sin haber estado nunca allí. Es cine de atmósfera antes que de trama, y creo que exigirle una arquitectura narrativa tradicional sería perder parte de lo que la hace distinta.

La película, además, tiene algo melancólico. Esos espacios parecen construidos con restos de realidad, recuerdos, objetos y formas que alguna vez pertenecieron a algo reconocible. Esa mezcla de familiaridad y deterioro convierte el terror en algo casi triste: como contemplar un mundo intentando recordar quién era y haciéndolo mal.

Backrooms me ha gustado mucho más de lo que esperaba. No porque su historia sea especialmente compleja, sino porque consigue algo bastante difícil: crear imágenes y sensaciones que permanecen después de terminar. Puede frustrar a quien necesite explicaciones claras o una trama más robusta, pero como experiencia de terror liminal funciona de maravilla. Y esa idea de estar caminando por una realidad reconstruida desde recuerdos defectuosos es, para mí, lo más inquietante de todo.


(ENGLISH)

The most unsettling thing about Backrooms is not any particular monster, but something much harder to explain: being in a place that seems to remember our world without fully understanding it. Hallways, furniture, signs and rooms feel familiar, yet they are arranged according to the wrong logic, as if someone had tried to rebuild reality from damaged memories. I find that idea far more disturbing than any simple explanation involving another dimension.

Kane Parsons fully understands the power of liminal space. The everyday stops being reassuring because it is slightly displaced: proportions do not quite fit, routes seem to lead nowhere and every familiar object creates more suspicion than comfort. The film manages to make a wall, an empty corridor or fluorescent lighting feel more disturbing than many conventional scares.

That is its greatest strength: atmosphere. Backrooms does not need to keep attacking the viewer. It only needs to preserve the feeling that something is wrong and that the error may appear around any corner. Production design is crucial because the spaces themselves become the true center of the horror. Rather than simply moving through a setting, the characters seem to enter a faulty memory being reconstructed as they explore it.

The idea of imperfect reconstruction is especially powerful. There is something dreamlike about recognizing a place without being able to say where we know it from. As in certain dreams, everything seems correct until we look too closely. Then a door feels misplaced, a room seems too large or a detail appears to belong to another time. That dream logic is far closer to horror than any literal explanation.

Renate Reinsve works extremely well for me. She has a very natural way of conveying fragility, confusion and fear without becoming hysterical. Her face can hold long close-ups and lets the film rest on small reactions. Even when the surroundings become stranger, she preserves a humanity that keeps the film from turning into a purely visual exercise. It is easy to worry about her because she never feels like a piece of mythology, but like a person trapped inside something she cannot understand.

Chiwetel Ejiofor provides a more rational, restrained counterpoint, and that difference helps keep the mystery from becoming completely abstract. The film needs characters who try to understand the impossible, although thankfully it does not spend all its time explaining it. Backrooms is strongest when it leaves empty spaces in our interpretation.

I also appreciate that Parsons does not try to domesticate the internet-born concept too much. The danger of turning the Backrooms into a feature film was transforming an idea based on suggestion into mythology overloaded with explanations. The movie comes close to that problem at times, but preserves enough mystery for the spaces themselves to remain unsettling.

Not everything works equally well. The narrative is clearly weaker than the visual construction, and there are moments when the concept feels as though it could easily survive with less plot. Some sections stretch out and certain elements seem to exist because a feature film needs progression, not because the world itself needs them. That reveals an obvious tension between the original phenomenon and the demands of conventional filmmaking.

Curiously, though, that narrative weakness did not bother me very much. The real story lies in exploration, in the sensation of moving toward places we recognize despite never having been there. This is atmosphere-first cinema rather than plot-first cinema, and demanding a traditional narrative architecture would miss part of what makes it different.

I also liked that the fear depends not only on what we see, but on what we imagine might exist outside the frame. Sounds, distances and the possibility that the space is arranging itself according to its own logic sustain a very primal tension. It is the fear of entering a place where we suspect there may be no normal way out.

The film also has a melancholy quality. These spaces seem built from fragments of reality, memories, objects and shapes that once belonged to something recognizable. That combination of familiarity and decay makes the horror almost sad: like watching a world trying to remember what it used to be and getting it wrong.

Backrooms worked much better for me than I expected. Not because its story is especially complex, but because it achieves something difficult: it creates images and sensations that remain after the film ends. It may frustrate viewers who need clear explanations or a stronger plot, but as an experience of liminal horror it works beautifully. And that idea of walking through a reality reconstructed from defective memories is, for me, the most disturbing thing of all.

Rating: B-

Stepping into the theater for The Mandalorian and Grogu, my anticipation was fueled by the undeniable charm of its main duo, and on a purely sensory level, this leap to the big screen absolutely delivers a blockbuster experience worthy of the largest IMAX canvas. From the breathtaking opening set piece — boasting some of the most brutal, intricately choreographed hand-to-hand action in the modern Star Wars mythos — the film immediately sheds the constraints of its streaming origins. Jon Favreau (Iron Man) crafts a visually stunning flick where the production design feels tangible, dirty, and authentic. The tactile delight of practical creature effects blends seamlessly with CGI elements, creating a visually consistent galaxy that disproves any notion of this looking like a glorified TV episode. Elevating this scale is a thunderous revamping of the musical score by Ludwig Göransson (Oppenheimer), which injects an infectious, epic energy into every frame, while the voice work across the board — including stellar additions from Jeremy Allen White (The Bear) and Martin Scorsese (Shark Tale) — brings an unexpected depth to the ensemble.

Yet, as much as my heart swelled seeing Din Djarin remain a magnetic, stoic anchor alongside a fiercely independent, endlessly cute Grogu, I cannot shake the feeling that the narrative plays it entirely too safe. The story unfolds in a highly cyclical, repetitive structure — accept a mission, face danger, narrowly escape — with jarring transition cuts that practically scream where a TV commercial break or episode boundary should have been. By the time the pacing grinds to a brutal halt in the second half to focus on a quieter, Grogu-centric sequence, the lack of narrative momentum becomes impossible to ignore. It's a lovely, calm breath of fresh air in isolation, but it exposes a frustrating absence of stakes, a revolving door of half-baked villains, and a status quo that leaves our beloved characters exactly where they started at the end of their last season.

It beautifully honors the foundational themes of fatherhood and found family that made us fall in love with this duo, but in refusing to take a genuine narrative risk, it ultimately feels like a spectacular, heartwarming holding pattern. May we always find the courage to venture into unknown territory, for even the most comforting bonds must eventually grow to survive the journey.
