author: andrewtislercinephile
content: *Paw Patrol: The Dino Movie* continues the franchise's streak of fun, action-packed movies about one boy and a team of puppies rescuing people from danger by transporting our furry little friends from the mean streets of Adventure City to an island full of dinosaurs. The visuals, humor, action, and storyline all vibed with me perfectly, with my favorite thing being that Marshall's backstory wasn't about a traumatic reason for him being clumsy, but instead he chose to continue pursuing his goals despite his clumsiness. That's a refreshing take on the clumsy person trope as it shows clumsiness is a choice, not a medical condition that needs to be treated. Keeping Adventure City briefly shown in the opening but still visible ensures continuity between movies, even though it is a little bit sad that Liberty is absent. Having Mayor Humdinger return as the movie's antagonist but actually start out wanting a new, honest life shows a level of growth and accountability that the series previously never used. Before, Humdinger felt like a one-dimensional caricature of a politician with sneaky, conniving motives, but now, he actually feels like a new man, and him relapsing due to the diamonds on the dinosaur island (Dino Island as it is called) is very in-character and shows that growth is not a one-way street. The voice cast-particularly Mckenna Grace as Skye, Jennifer Hudson as Lilian Ledes, and Terry Crews as Alistair Stonewall-were outstanding and delivered some funny, delightful performances. I also really loved the new songs "Bottle Up" by Backstreet Boys and "Work" by Ava Max. Not only do these songs feel like modern bangers any kid would listen to, but they also fit the story's themes very well, with "Bottle Up" serving as a literal expression of how the Paw Patrol is bottling up their emotions in being awestruck by an entire island full of dinosaurs, while "Work" highlights how they have to save the island from being destroyed by a volcano Humdinger activates with a mound of dynamite. My only criticism-and something I've always had with the *Paw Patrol* franchise's movies-is how fast-paced the movie is. Because the movies prioritize the preschool-age audience, they forget that longer pacing can allow for better world-building and stronger character growth. Kid-friendly studios in animation like DreamWorks or Pixar have done this for years and it shows. But overall, *Paw Patrol: The Dino Movie* was a fun, action-packed ride that continued to wow me with a visually spectacular story about resilience and doing the hardest things even when you have a flaw that seemingly holds you back. I hope we get more of these movies in the next 3-4 years or so.

author: Brent Marchant
content: From where I stand, as I have said before, predictability is the cardinal sin of filmmaking. If one can foresee what’s going to happen, there’s little point in watching the movie, now is there? And, unfortunately, such is the case here in the latest release from director Carlson Young. Based on the best-selling novel of the same name (2025) by Anna Todd, the cinematic version of this story is a clinic in formulaic filmmaking, where virtually every plot development is apparent from miles away. Indeed, it’s the kind of picture better suited to the sappy sensibilities of The Hallmark Channel than other less cheesy distribution platforms. “The Last Sunrise” tells the tale of a young Houston-based dancer, Oriah (a.k.a. “Ry”) Pera (Maia Reficco), who’s afflicted with a tumorous condition that causes epilepsy. Her prospects aren’t favorable after she suffers an on-stage accident, prompting her mother, Isolde (Eva Longoria), to take her for a summer’s recuperation on the Spanish resort island of Mallorca, where mom is working on a massive new hotel project for a real estate developer. Isolde’s also anxious for her daughter to see where her mom grew up and to reconnect to her own roots, but, once there, her work keeps her so busy that she and Ry spend little time together. With so much free time on her hands, Ry routinely goes off on her own, a practice that unwittingly takes her to a clothing optional beach and introduces her to Julian (Fernando Lindez), a bad boy with an attitude who, paradoxically, works as a humble fisherman with a passionate ecological agenda. And, of course, they naturally fall for one another. But, as their holiday romance emerges, they each hide secrets from one another (she, her illness, and he, his outstanding debt to a badass loan shark), all of which are piled atop even bigger disclosures of which neither of them is aware. So how will everything play out? Well, as discussed earlier, that shouldn’t be too hard to figure out as all the requisite pieces fall into place neatly on cue. While the narrative shows some improvement as the story progresses, much of it nevertheless follows the standard made-for-TV movie template, with plenty of travelogue-type footage thrown in to exquisitely show off its exotic locale. As for the performances, they represent serious cases of miscasting: Longoria looks bored, tediously walking through her role as if she could have phoned it in; Lindez comes across like a refugee from a designer jeans ad who’s desperately in need of English elocution lessons; and Reficco makes for a stunning, vulnerable ingenue, but it’s difficult to fathom that she’s supposedly as ill as she’s said to be, stretching credibility about as tautly as it can go. Fans of romance novels and film versions thereof will undoubtedly find this effort to be right up their alley, but those looking for something with more substance and a lot less frothy fluff can skip this one and not miss a thing.

author: CinemaSerf
content: Now I know that I'm not really the demographic for this, but I didn't mind the last one from 2023 so had an open mind as it started. Princess 'Peach' is kidnapped by the menacing baby 'Bowser' who is none too pleased that his dad has been locked up. He is determined to use her as leverage to free him, but that is exactly what intrepid and ingenious 'Mario' and 'Luigi' intend to thwart. What now ensues is the thinnest of stories stretched across a messy collection of interstellar scenarios as they bounce from world to world trying to rescue the royal damsel in distress. I always reckoned that the amiable mushroom people belonged more in an Arabian Nights tale than a sci-fi cartoon, but even their innocent cheeriness can't really enliven this rapidly and colourfully edited together sequence of pinball-machine style scenes. There is surprisingly little effort made to characterise either the goodies or the baddies and the frenetic nature of the animation barely leaves us time to draw breath before we ascend to another level and pretty much repeat as before - only with slightly different props and goals. It's not so much that this lacks a beginning, middle and end - it is more that it just comes across as contant sequence of scenes that could all see the film conclude as predictably as the sun coming up. Perhaps very young children might enjoy the sheer buzz of this, but there really isn't anything visually or from the script to entertain the grown ups. I bet the merch merchants are happy, though.

author: datafables13
content:
You know how, sometimes, you get a burger that's so thin, overcooked, and leathery that it stops being a "burger" and starts being "a vehicle for condiments"? That, to me, is Super Mario Galaxy: The story/writing is simply there to deliver Nintendo-brand nostalgia. As someone with deep love and fond memories of Nintendo, I'm okay with this---but I'm not going to pretend that the story is the narrative equivalent of Wagyu beef. 

Contrary to what some of the less charitable critics say, the movie does have a cogent story: Bowser Jr. aims to rescue his father from his imprisonment and bring the dreams they shared when Jr. was young to fruition. To do that, he kidnaps Princess Rosalina, the mother of the stars, to siphon her magic. The gang sets off to rescue the Princess.

A simple enough premise; certainly serviceable. It isn't winning any awards for novelty but not everything needs to be "high art" to be enjoyable. But it fails on even this modest ambition. The execution is riddled with enough _deus ex_ to fill a Greek pantheon. Character motivations are inconsistent without real evolution. There are so many zany little subplots that it's like they worried that the audience's attention span would run out---yet they still made the thing run for over 2 hours.

Fortunately, the metaphorical "condiment" was delicious---like biting into that burger expecting Hunt's ketchup but getting homemade garlic aoli mayo. The quality of the animation made the film's many callbacks enjoyable. I found myself smiling a lot and actually thinking "dang, I really _should_ get around to playing [redacted Mario game(s)]". Which, I'm certain is all Nintendo really hoped for rather than making a genuinely excellent stand-alone cinematic experience.

In sum, it's not something I regret seeing---especially with my family. Though it is something I wish I had saved the video game's worth of money waiting for it to come out on streaming rather than seeing it in theaters.

content:
**It's the thing! It's the thing from the game! Point at the screen and clap!**

I know this is a kids movie, and I feel like if you have a kid that's under 12 years old they'd probably love it... But as an adult, this was a slog. The first movie wasn't a masterpiece but it at least had some heart and some semblance of a story, this one was an incredibly superficial advertisement for anything Nintendo.

Look, it's Yoshi! Look, it's Pikmin! Look, it's Birdo! It's the bee from Mario Galaxy! It's R.O.B.! It's pilot guy! Please clap.

And everything has zero substance. To quote another review: "This movie was like watching youtube shorts about jingling keys stitched together". The voice acting was also so mediocre, I can't get over this Hollywood thing of hiring popular actors instead of anyone talented. Jack Black as Bowser is **abysmal**, he's not even trying anymore. It just sounds like Jack Black. 

The ending... Wow. The movie just _ends._ Nothing is really resolved and everything is pushed under the rug. They defeat Bowser Jr. and the movie just instantly ends one minute later. Remember when Peach was desperate to meet and talk to Rosalina? Or maybe they can add a scene to wrap up Bowser & Bowser Jr.'s story arc? Whatever. Roll credits.

At the very least I can acknowledge the animation is top-notch, Illumination low-key has better artists than Pixar these days.

author: TheFilmCritics.org
content:
A true-crime story this inherently bizarre should not require much embellishment, yet *Primetime* spends so much energy dressing itself up that the actual story gets buried underneath the filmmaking. What could have been a sharp, uncomfortable examination of television, celebrity, and the ethics of true crime instead becomes a frustratingly uneven film that mistakes stylistic excess for substance.

Robert Pattinson gives a pretty good performance as Chris Hansen, bringing enough conviction to make the central figure compelling even when the screenplay does not. The supporting cast is strong as well. Skyler Gisondo makes an impression as the adult decoy pretending to be an underage boy, while Merritt Wever brings welcome dimension as the show’s producer. There are also genuinely interesting ideas scattered throughout the film, particularly in its examination of how media can commoditize real human suffering into entertainment.

The problem is that *Primetime* rarely develops its ideas into a cohesive story. It often feels less like a narrative and more like a collection of scenes placed next to one another. The result makes it difficult for viewers to become invested in what is happening or, more importantly, in the characters involved.

Its aesthetic ambitions are particularly exhausting. The fuzzy mid-2000s look is clearly deliberate, and there is nothing wrong with leaning into the visual language of the period. Here, though, the music, lighting, camera angles, and visual flourishes are pushed so aggressively that the movie starts announcing its artistry rather than letting it emerge naturally. There is a compelling story underneath all the smoke and mirrors, which makes the constant insistence on style feel less like enrichment and more like distraction.

The heavier issue is how much the film dramatizes real events and real people. Using real names and identities while taking substantial creative liberties creates an uncomfortable disconnect, particularly in the portrayal of Hansen himself. The film's portrayal of real-life subjects can make some of its choices feel less like artistic interpretation and more like borderline defamation. Hansen himself has publicly criticized the film, which only makes the question of how responsibly it treats people difficult to ignore. You see how this looks, right?

There are also moments where the dramatization crosses into genuinely uncomfortable territory. The film’s treatment of SA and mental health issues can feel glib and insensitive. For example, the portrayal of the true story of a man who unalived himself while caught in the *To Catch A Predator* investigations is difficult to digest. That was a real human being who faced a genuinely tragic ending, **not** merely a fictional plot device, and the lack of respect taken toward a serious subject matter invites questions that the movie does not seem particularly interested in answering.

Additionally, the creative choice to make the main decoy exclusively male feels conspicuously constructed. The primarily male-on-male encounters feel unrealistic, existing solely to insert the male decoy into the story as a main character.

That is unfortunate because beneath the excess is a worthwhile film trying to get out. *Primetime* has something meaningful to say about the ethics of true-crime entertainment, the machinery of television, and the uncomfortable relationship between public spectacle and private suffering. But its lack of nuance turns complicated questions into an overly tidy division between good guys and bad guys. The satire gets lost in the dramatization, and the film's strongest observations are repeatedly smothered by its need to make everything bigger, darker, and more cinematic.

Ultimately, *Primetime* is a case of flash over substance. Pattinson and the supporting cast do solid work, and there are enough provocative ideas here to make the film worth discussing, but the execution repeatedly gets in its own way. When the real story is already compelling, inventing so much around it feels unnecessary—and, in some cases, ethically questionable.

author: Brent Marchant
content: It’s been said that we often become what we concentrate upon. That’s ironic, because frequently this results in the creation of that which we’re purposely trying to avoid. And, in this third feature outing from director Lance Oppenheim, that’s precisely what happens to its high-profile protagonist, investigative journalist Chris Hansen (Robert Pattinson). In this fact-based satire, the film follows the ascendancy of the reporter on the tabloid TV series *Dateline NBC*, specifically through his work on the show’s *To Catch a Predator* segment (2004-2007) in which he covered stories designed to expose the exploits of pedophiles. Working in conjunction with the website Perverted-Justice, Hansen, his producer (Merritt Wever), and a pair of predator bait decoy actors (Skyler Gisondo, Phoebe Bridgers) orchestrated sting operations aimed at capturing their unsuspecting prey in the act on camera. While it’s undeniable that the intentions with this mission were fundamentally noble, their on-air depictions increasingly took on a vibe of sensationalism, blurring the line between journalism and entertainment. And, as Hansen’s star rose, he relished the personal notoriety and ratings popularity that came with his efforts. However, as the film postulates, his increasingly aggressive reporting tactics and quest for professional glory suggest that he was becoming as much of a predator on the alleged perpetrators as they were on their would-be victims. It might even be said that the methods employed verged on a form of entrapment, an approach that carried significantly murky and curiously ironic consequences. Now, this is not to suggest that Hansen was becoming a sexual predator himself, but, in donning the cloak of self-appointed activist, his personal authenticity was called into question as he became the target of undercover surveillance for a supposed extramarital affair that was threatened to be exposed by *The National Enquirer*. If the foregoing combination of elements sounds like the makings of a cinematic tall tale, you might indeed be correct. Circumstances like those depicted in the film naturally raise questions about the picture’s factual accuracy (Hansen himself has publicly and vocally proclaimed that “Primetme” paints him in an unfairly erroneous light). Moreover, on this basis, this is a picture that won’t appeal to everyone and will likely inspire more than its share of heated debate. However, the purposeful over-the-top approach used here is designed for dramatic effect to reflect the aforementioned question about the blurred lines between journalism and entertainment and the loaded theme of predator chasing predator. And, in doing so, the narrative is not meant to be taken as literal truth as much as it is to be looked upon as a metaphor, a satirical psychological thriller using real-life events and characters as the basis for illustrating its particular viewpoints. This becomes especially apparent through this offering’s insightful script, which deftly fuses wry humor, incisive camp and tense drama to tell its story, quite a writing feat to pull off successfully. In addition, the picture’s superb performances (especially by Pattinson, Gisondo and Bridgers), inventive cinematography and editing, and outstanding original score enhance the story and its various components, combining in a singularly distinctive way suitable for a production with as many diverse elements as are present here. Although this release has a tendency to meander at times, it generally remains faithful to its intents in telling a story with messages and ramifications that go beyond the individual events that make it up – important considerations for all of us to keep in mind in our efforts to create that which we seek and to meticulously avoid that which we don’t.

author: CinemaSerf
content: I'm not really much of a fan of R Patz, but this might be his best effort since "The Lighthouse" (2019). Here, he's a real-life television host who fronts a show that exposes older men who have a penchant for young teens. These men are entrapped by an actor on social media and then lured to an home where they are confronted by Chris Hansen before being surrendered to the authorities. One problem for the show is that their (not always very convincing) decoys tend to find the whole experience fairly traumatic and so don't tend to stick around for long. Perhaps the latest "Dan" (Skyler Gisondo) might endure? Well at the insistence of the producer Andie (Merritt Wever), Hansen goes on a bit of a charm offensive with him and that could end up proving crucial as the show's bosses are falling out of love with their newly promoted primetime concept and he needs to land a big catch else they might be cancelled. Meantime, Hansen turns out to have a peccadillo or two of his own and should that get into the public domain, his career prospects and his marriage might end up going the same way. When "Xavier" (Matthew Maher) on the production team gets what we can only describe as an internet nibble from someone way further up the food chain that they are used to, they have to focus on ensnaring this careful and meticulous fellow. There's a great deal of creative effort gone into the look and the pace of this film and for the most part I thought that worked, but unfortunately director Lance Oppenheim seems to have opted here to focus more on a personification of Hansen rather than on the impact that this "Predator" show had on an unsuspecting American public in an early naughties still largely unaware of the opportunities the web gave to perverts, nor of the vulnerability of many of the young people who used it. I felt that was a bit of a shame because for the most part the individual characterisation isn't so very interesting. Still, this presents us with a really quite salutary lesson in online predation that allows Pattinson to demonstrate he can raise his acting game and signals to the rest of us just how dangerous a tool the web can be. I don't think I will recall this film for long, but it's worth a watch.

author: Dean
content:
As a massive horror fan, I give this latest installment a solid 7/10. While I still thoroughly enjoyed the experience and highly recommend catching it in theaters, it didn't quite reach the perfect 10/10 heights of the previous entries for a couple of specific reasons.

**What Held It Back:**
- **The Shift in Demon Behavior:** In the previous films, the Deadites felt like pure, primal, uncompromising evil. There was no negotiating or reasoning with them—their sole purpose was absolute destruction. In this movie, the demons feel a bit too humanlike. They talk and interact in a way that shifts the tone away from that relentless, otherworldly terror of the earlier films.
- **Out-of-Place Ending Music:** The choice of closing music was a major misstep. Ending a gritty horror experience with a silly French rap song completely broke the atmosphere. A film like this demands an intense, dark, and brooding sonic backdrop—genres like dark ambient or black metal fit this aesthetic perfectly, not modern hip-hop.

**The Verdict:**
Despite these minor gripes, a 7/10 is still a strong rating. The movie delivers great tension, solid horror sequences, and is absolutely worth your time. If you haven't watched it yet, go ahead and check it out—you won't be disappointed!

author: CinemaSerf
content: Things don't exactly get off to a great start for "Alice" (Souheila Yacoub) when her drunken bully of an husband takes off in his car on her birthday and wraps it round a tree. No great loss, you might think, but his dad "Edgar" (Erroll Shand) seems a little upset and so goes to say farewell before he can be cremated. Big mistake - for the not quite deceased "Will" (George Pullar) is determined not be crisped up just yet. You see he is now possessed by an evil that knows that his drippy brother "Joseph" (Hunter Doohan) has inadvertantly discovered the only weapon on Earth that can consign him and his kind back to Hell. Using his dad as a conduit, he now returns to a home where his now widow feels a little unwelcome in the company of his mother "Susan" (Tandi Wright); his brother's gal "Thya" (Luciane Buchanan) and his cantankerous, wheelchair-bound, grandma "Polly" (Maude Davey). The question is, will "Alice" and "Joe" conclude quickly enough what the menacing monster that has invaded their home actually wants and can anyone stay alive long enough to find and/or use it? Predicable, well yes, but I'm not sure that matters. This is much more of a gore-fest in the spirit of the earlier "Evil Dead" movies where the targets for the malevolence assume almost immortal qualities of invincibility - just ask "Joe" and the sharpened contents of the dishwasher - so they can repeatedly bounce off the sanitary wear in the bathroom, or from the top of the building, or from the end of a rather brutal looking garden cutter and return to fight again. On that score, this provides quite a quickly paced and relentless series of gruesome scenarios whilst we can largely ignore the dialogue and, frankly, just about all of the acting. Sure, it has sequel written all over it for much of the second part, but amidst the chaos, cutlery and dentures and by using some lively photography there is fun to be had and to be honest, I found it way more macabre and frightful than almost anything I've seen from this genre this year.

author: The Fixate & Binge Podcast, w/ Joe Curdy
content:
Watching **EVIL DEAD BURN** becomes an ordeal that tests how close the line between the MPAA's R and NC-17 ratings can be pushed like no other horror film seen this year -- and maybe several years before.

Assaulting audiences with tongue-in-cheek, stomach-churning horror has long been the hallmark of Sam Raimi's **EVIL DEAD** franchise since Bruce Campbell first fired up his chainsaw and declared it "Groovy" nearly 40 years ago.

In director Sébastien Vanicek's hands, after Raimi handpicked him for this latest outing following his skin-crawling French-language debut **INFESTED** (2023), there is more humor -- but also far more cruelty than any prior film in the franchise.

As with **EVIL DEAD RISE**, there is a somewhat disconnected intro -- equally horrific -- before the main story settles in, where the central cast (Souheila Yacoub, Hunter Doohan, Luciane Buchanan) experience graphic and disturbing violence that may make some audiences sick to their stomachs.

As the Deadites descend upon a dilapidated, rural family home and a grieving family led by a young widow, the sheer amount of cruelty each of the characters endures is at times overwhelming. In one particular moment, a dinner scene around the family dining table is especially cruel and wince-inducing.

But for the use of some well-timed gallows humor, the whole affair might have otherwise seemed like something out of the blood-soaked dreams of St. Thomas Aquinas.

With a threadbare plot, gnarly vignettes of escalating brutality, fans of the practical effects Raimi first introduced to audiences in 1981 will surely embrace this latest offering for all its coagulated gore.

But underneath the pools of blood and viscera -- is Yacoub's earnest portrayal of Alice, whose ordeal throughout the movie is an empowering example of triumphing over spousal abuse and generational trauma.

When the end inevitably comes -- *but wait! there's more! (a mid-credits scene and a substantial post-credits scene that's worth the wait if you still have the stomach for it)* -- you may leave the cinema drained from the graphic catharsis of enduring this.

If **EVIL DEAD** films have always been about pushing the envelope -- **EVIL DEAD BURN** may get the distinction of pushing it further than any of its predecessors. Erroll Shand, Greta van den Brink, Tandi Wright, and Maude Davey co-star.

author: RetroWill
content:
The film strikes a great balance, delivering clever narrative tie-backs to Evil Dead Rise alongside a subtle, underlying connection to the lore of the original films. Rather than resting on nostalgia, it uses those classic elements to build a story that feels fresh while remaining distinctly true to the franchise's roots. 

The shift in setting works brilliantly here. Moving the terror out of Rise’s cramped city apartment block and into a sprawling, secluded farmhouse gives the film a completely different kind of claustrophobia. The rural atmosphere and isolated location gave off massive Resident Evil 7: Biohazard Baker family vibes. That uncomfortable sense of being trapped with a deeply unhinged, hostile family dynamic long before the supernatural madness even takes over. 

When the Deadites do unleash, the film delivers in spades. Modern Evil Dead entries have really amped up the brutal, relentless nature of the gore, and Burn is no exception. What makes it work so well is the sheer tactile impact of the set pieces. Between the aggressive sound design and a reliance on heavy practical effects over cheap digital tricks, every injury, splash of blood, and horrific transformation feels uncomfortably real and punishing. 

It’s really encouraging to see movies like this succeeding, especially since horror felt like it was going through a bit of a dry spell recently. We’re finally getting a steady stream of inventive, high-quality genre films that actually respect the audience and make the trip to the cinema worthwhile. 

I’d highly recommend Evil Dead Burn to any horror fan. The best way to experience these modern entries is to disconnect them from Raimi’s 80s originals. Those were iconic products of their time, whereas this current era is leaning into dark, visceral, unfiltered horror. Both eras are brilliant in their own right, and Burn proves this franchise still has plenty of gas in the tank.

If you thought the era of Hollywood horror filmmakers using over-the-top gratuitous and totally uncalled for gore and violence on women and girls to cover up for shallow scripts and  lack of creativity, well, you were wrong. author: Brent Marchant
content: Pulse-pounding deadline-based thrillers have become a common source of action-adventure viewing over the years. These largely formulaic offerings are often fairly predictable, with their outcomes frequently obvious well in advance, the only variable generally being the routes their narratives take to arrive at their final destinations. So it is again with this latest effort from director Kevin MacDonald, a typically capable filmmaker who comes up woefully short with this release. When London-based criminal attorney Maia Marten (Gal Godot) goes on her usual morning run before her latest big court case, she’s interrupted in mid-sprint by a cell phone call supposedly from her young son, Noah (Rory Wilmot). However, when she answers, she discovers it’s not from him but, instead, from an anonymous mystery caller (Damian Lewis) who has kidnapped Noah and threatens to kill him unless she follows his instructions to the letter. Specifically, the kidnapper wants Maia to murder a key witness in the case against his former employer, a high-profile mobster accused of killing two young women. But, to ensure that she complies with his directives, the caller says he’s tracking her movements by tapping into the geolocator on her cell phone. This requires her to remain out in the open, on the street, a plan that calls for the former champion pentathlete to run five miles across London in an hour to the hotel where the witness is in protective custody prior to his transfer to the courthouse. This setup thus launches the protagonist into her trek across the city, a journey filled with twists, turns, thrills, spills and the revelation of a variety of highly personal details, including long-held secrets. But is she up to this task? (You get three guesses.) As this scenario unfolds, though, the story is peppered with an array of credibility-stretching implausibilities that not even Wonder Woman herself is realistically capable of pulling off. Indeed, while tales like this typically call for viewers to suspend belief, many of the developments in this plot hole-ridden story are just plain difficult to accept. Admittedly, the narrative is stylishly dressed up in a superbly edited, fast-paced package with some inventive cinematography that shows off street-level London exquisitely, but such window dressing still can’t conceal the plethoric flaws in the script. With better writing and plot scrutiny, “The Runner” might have made for some late summer escapist fun, but it’s hard to fathom it as being much more than a paycheck for the principals involved and yet another in an ongoing string of substandard outings for Amazon Studios.

author: The Fixate & Binge Podcast, w/ Joe Curdy
content:
You've seen this film before.

When it was 1995's **NICK OF TIME** and **DIE HARD WITH A VENGEANCE**, 2002's **PHONE BOOTH**, 2003's **OUT OF TIME**, 2005's **RED EYE**, or even Netflix's **CARRY-ON** (2024) -- well, you get the idea.

Films like **THE RUNNER** do not happen in a vacuum. And the formula is clearly working, as director Kevin Macdonald's film (wisely released direct to streaming on Amazon Prime) is already one of the platform's top films.

Starring Gal Gadot as high-powered London barrister Maia, whose child is held for ransom by a mysterious Caller (Damian Lewis) in exchange for assassinating the star witness of a local mob trial -- it's a premise that sounds increasingly preposterous the more you think about it.

Despite its **RUN LOLA RUN** pacing, with endless clips of Gal Gadot sprinting across every tourist locale in London, from St. Paul's to Canary Wharf, the implausibility of running the London Marathon in 84 minutes strains credulity.

The always-one-step-ahead omniscience of Lewis's character, effortlessly bending hacked technology to his whims, is another worn-out trope that refuses to die.

As diabolical and meticulous as Lewis is, one wonders why he doesn't just carry out the assassination himself instead of putting Gadot through a series of ridiculous time trials during the hustle and bustle of mid-day London.

And while Gadot gamely carries the physical desperation of a single mother trying to save her child, unfortunately, the film leans into her limited range as an actress, with dull dialogue and pointless conversational exposition.

As a tense action thriller, **THE RUNNER** will probably appeal to anyone unfamiliar with any of the aforementioned films in this subgenre. But for anyone else, this is a paint-by-numbers slog through familiar terrain that will do nothing for Gadot's post-**WONDER WOMAN** career.

author: MovieGuys
content:
"The Wrecking Crew" is aptly named. 

This action flick, for me, early on wrecked any chance that I'd actually enjoy this film. I'll put my hand up and say I'm sick and tired of the gratuitous violence oozing out of Hollywood. The light, jokey tone of this film is at odds with oftentimes really ugly violence. Entirely smashing someone's upper teeth against a table in the opening scenes is one such example. It's not funny; it's not okay, its not entertaining, no matter who it's done to.

Regrettably, given how violent US society is, perhaps I should not be surprised, but it's also one of the reasons I don't watch a great deal of US cinema these days.

Beyond that, the actions of the formulaic variety and the bro buddy back story has long since ossified into a cliche.

author: CinemaSerf
content: "Kris" (Hannah Einbinder) has managed to convince some investors to consider funding her attempt to resurrect a dated horror fanchise set at a remote holiday camp. To that end, she has tracked down the woman who was the original damsel in distress in the series's very first outing decades ago. "Billy" (Gillian Anderson) has been fairly reclusive ever since that first success, and has retreated to live at the very camp in which the films were based. Now in the depths of winter, "Kris" braves the snowy conditions to pay her a visit - and her arrival at the eerily silent camp sets in train quite an emotionally and psychologically charged few hours with her enigmatic hostess. I think my problem with this stemmed from the decision of auteur Jane Schoenbrun to put her own experiences front and centre here and rather leave the mysterious substance of the plot to play second fiddle to that. Clearly, this is a film-maker who has had their fair share of struggles to get her often quite eclectically structured (i.e. last year's "I Saw the TV Glow") films funded and made, and so coupled with a sexual fluidity that neither Einbinder nor the underused Anderson are afraid to commit to, this became more of a commentary of a character with whom I couldn't really engage set against an half-baked critique of the repetitious slasher-genre upon which this tries to make it's money. The threads do come together a little more completely towards the conclusion, but I think by exploiting so many of the clichés and photographic tecnhiques of films like "Halloween"; "Friday the 13th" or even the more recent "Black Phone" sequel, and presenting a paucity of meaningful dialogue, this sort of falls into it's own trap of introspective mediocrity rather than "elevating" itself from the more generic quag.

author: Yasmin J. Lee
content:
# Analysis of Jane Schoenbrun’s “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” (2026)

### “I saw ya and wanted to scare ya. It’s only fair, right? You already seen me.”

It is no secret that Jane Schoenbrun (they/them) references pop culture throughout their filmography. The Pink Opaque of *I Saw the TV Glow* (2024) was derivative of *Buffy the Vampire Slayer,* while *Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma* (2026) nodded to slasher flicks ranging from *Peeping Tom* (1960) to *Wes Craven’s New Nightmare* (1994) and *Sleepaway Camp* (1983). Beneath the references and homages, Schoenbrun also engages with time, pushing audiences to stay present in their stories and in themselves. By referencing essential slashers and confronting time, Schoenbrun puts their work in direct conversation with the genre’s aesthetics and flaws, using time as an open door to opportunity and rebirth throughout their latest horror film, *Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma* (2026).

Schoenbrun crystallizes and confronts their love for the slasher subgenre in *Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma* (2026). It is apparent that, while holding slashers in high regard, Schoenbrun is critical of the genre as vastly male-centered. Most, if not all, weapons in slasher films are phallic objects; statistically, a young female character is often the first to die, and women experience significantly more prolonged, graphic, and severe violence on-screen. Rather than criticizing the genre as a whole, Jane Schoenbrun takes on the challenge of queering the genre.

For instance, in *Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma,* the depiction of orifices is prevalent. Little Death’s VHS tape player at the bottom of the lake resembles a vaginal opening. The air conditioning unit on his head is like a portal that still honors the motif of most horror film killers being modeled after blue-collar workers. Little Death even wears a white-vinyl raincoat suit reminiscent of Patrick Bateman from Mary Harron’s *American Psycho* (2000).

> e.g., Jason Voorhees of *Friday the 13th* wears rugged groundskeeper clothes; Michael Myers of *Halloween* wears iconic navy-blue mechanic coveralls; Leatherface of *The Texas Chain Saw Massacre* dons slaughterhouse/butcher work clothes. (MorphCostumes Team, “Why Michael Myers is the Ultimate Horror Costume.”)

In addition to the previously listed images, Schoenbrun also represents orifices as portals. The barn and movie theater openings, the parting of the silver-screen curtains, and the gas station setting all operated as portals into meaningful chapters of the story.

One of the film’s most recognizable female-centered images is the infamous dipping sauce scene. Gillian Anderson’s Billy Presley thumps her pink-painted nail against the dipping sauce flab as Kris Williams (Hannah Einbinder, character pronouns she/they) licks her lips with anticipation. The honey mustard sauce is revealed to the audience before a chicken tender is dipped into its golden wonder. Schoenbrun depicts this otherwise mundane dinner as a ritualistic, orgasmic experience of intimacy between Kris and Billy.

The female gaze is further complicated when Billy recounts her first orgasm to Kris. As helpless slasher-flick victims, the femme characters can see themselves through Little Death’s perspective. This queering of perspective complicates what the camera captures, especially in the slasher genre. Rather than objectifying the lead femmes to the masculine, heterosexual perspective, Schoenbrun’s perspective externalizes their sexual repression. This tension releases when they become both voyeur and submissive participants who are aware of the role they’re playing.

As they shift between voyeur and victim, the film’s thesis emerges in a brief exchange between Kris and Billy about Kris’s debut feature film. Billy states Kris’s film is a remake of Alfred Hitchcock’s *Psycho* (1960) from the perspective of the shower curtain. Initially, Kris is offended by this interpretation, not realizing it’s the key to their entire experience at Camp Miasma.

As Laure Murat once stated in their essay, “What’s Queer about Remy, *Ratatouille*, and French Cuisine?”

> “The spatial transgression of hierarchies and the visual omniscience of \[the character’s\] position confound binary constructions while acknowledging their power.” (p. 138)

The shower curtain is the translucent barrier between the victim and the slasher. Kris, like the shower curtain, occupies a bifurcated space when they subject themselves to the perspective of Little Death while expressing their sexuality.

Upon revisiting the film’s opening, the hack-screenwriter, Kris, enters the gas station with hungry eyes, snagging their favorite candy off the racks. The gas station sits between worlds: both destination and journey. In the third act, having survived the night of terror hosted by Little Death, Kris and Billy return to the gas station to stock up on their gummy candies. These final moments of *Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma* ask audiences to savor their pleasures and desires like candy.

There are no clean conclusions for this tale of gender euphoria and escapism. This natural desire for an ending prompts audiences to ponder the story’s moral, fearing they may have missed it at first.

By enjoying both the film’s ephemeral sweetness, the consumer accepts its conclusion and, hopefully, the moments that pleased them and felt representative of them. Using evanescent metaphors and making the characters cognizant of the passage of time, Schoenbrun presents a conclusion that denotes progress without answers: Time. Time does not give you an answer. It simply measures.

*Enjoyed this review? Subscribe to my Substack (Snowy Reviews, by Yasmin) and give me a follow (@yasminthewriter) on Letterboxd, and see what I review next!*

author: Dean
content:
War Machine (2026) is a standout for anyone who appreciates a straightforward, high-tension film that avoids the typical political traps of the military genre. It delivers a raw experience by focusing on the physical and mental endurance of the characters rather than pushing a specific agenda or narrative.

Alan Ritchson brings a grounded intensity to the role of "81," making the transition from a grueling Ranger selection process to a sci-fi survival scenario feel surprisingly realistic. The film excels because it stays focused on the technical aspects of the situation—how the squad adapts to an unknown threat with limited resources and sheer willpower.

The lack of propaganda is one of its strongest points; it doesn't try to lecture the audience or romanticize the conflict beyond the survival of the men on the ground. It is pure, high-stakes cinema that relies on atmosphere and pacing to keep you invested.

author: Screenopolis
content:
Read at Screenopolis: https://screenopolis.com/reviews/war-machine-burns-hot-goes-nowhere

War Machine is the latest Netflix movie glorifying American tough guys kickin’ ass. The plot is familiar: alien comes to earth, bad-ass soldiers are deployed, carnage ensues, tough-guy outsmarts the alien, ho-rah America!

War Machine has been compared a lot to Predator, not only because the plot is similar, but also because it features current Arnold Schwarzenegger-esque tough-guy Alan Ritchson in the lead role. You may remember this mountain of a human from Reacher on Amazon Prime or the zany The Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare with Henry Cavill.

Ritchson plays tough-as-rocks engineer/soldier 81. He is a number, not a free man. Ritchson’s character never gets a name. He does not need one. It would only distract you from admiring his bottomless reservoir of pain and grit.

You see, 81 had a brother, played by Jai Courtney. His brother was nameless too, so we will call him Bro. 81 and Bro served in Afghanistan. Bro was cocky. He really wanted to be an Army Ranger with 81, who was weary from being so bad-ass. When Bro’s truck pooped out, 81 was deployed from the 101st Rudimentary Foreshadowing Brigade to lecture him on the 2nd Law of Thermodynamics and clean out his gunked-up radiator.

Then the bad guys bombed them. Bro and 81 are hurt. 81 pulls a massive chunk of metal from his knee, grabs his Bro, and tries to get back to base. Spoiler alert, they do not make it. Bro dead, 81 has hurty knee, cue the grit. So much grit.

Guilty from not saving his Bro, 81 signs up for Ranger tryouts, even though he is 20 years too old, badly injured, and has *gasp* facial hair! Pete Hegseth would shit his vodka-soaked pants if he saw this guy in formation.

After numerous skinny white kids get booted from tryouts, the commander, played by a finger-pointy Dennis Quaid, thinks 81 does not have what it takes to cross the finish line and be a Ranger. He thinks 81 is too bad-ass, and sensitive, and deep, and dreamy.

Rather than kick 81 out, they drop him in the forest with a pack of nobodies to prove his bad-assery. Finally, after all this setup, the alien shows up. The ass-kicking proper gets underway.

Now, here is the problem with this movie: who in the hell cares about Bro or the 2nd Law of Thermodynamics, or Ranger school, or finish lines, or any of the setup? I came here to watch explosions, not emotions and grit.

War Machine‘s lengthy setup is unnecessary and ham-fisted. Watch the first five minutes of Predator (split between these two videos below). Predator accomplishes in minutes (and better) what War Machine burns a half an hour to do (and much worse). It also has awesome theme music from Alan Silvestri.

In walks Arnold, he slaps arms with Dillon, fuck yeah! Let’s do this thing. That is all we need. Arnold is bad-ass, Dillion has a dangerous mission, blah blah blah, cue Long Tall Sally. We ain’t got time to emote. Predator does not waste one nanosecond being anything more than it was, a stupid action movie with paper-thin characters (some of whom are sexual tyrannosauruses). The result is a supremely satisfying movie filled with great one-liners.

War Machine desperately needs to stay in its lane. Nobody wants a meditation on the human condition with a stupid flick like War Machine. We want non-stop alien butt-kicking peppered with corny jokes and latent homosexuality.

Nevertheless, once the alien shows up in War Machine, the movie improves. The attacks are relentless, exhilarating, and bloody. The alien robot racks up an impressive body count in short order. It is pretty bad-ass, although not as bad-ass as 81, who is smart and has all those gigatons of grits. Remember that thermodynamics stuff with Bro? Yeah, that is how you kill an indestructible robot from another world. You shove rocks in its nose until it overheats. Boom.

The only way to enjoy this movie is to totally shut down every part of your critical thinking. If you stick to the spectacle, the movie is fine and enjoyable. If you spend any time thinking about this movie, it sucks rocks.

In addition to the terrible setup, this movie has a worthless cast. None of the supporting characters contribute anything of value. They are your standard-issue “military guys” and a lone bald-headed woman (who is mildly bad-ass until she’s not) direct from central casting. Even Jai Courtney’s role felt as limp and lifeless as his character’s body. Dennis Quaid phones in his role as gruff commander who must be within minutes of mandatory retirement age.

However, the most demoralizing part of this movie is the end – yeah I am going to spoil it. It is for your own good. After killing the unstoppable alien machine, 81 gets back to base. He is triumphantly promoted to Ranger. There is a lot of saluting, back slapping, and fist pumping with fluttering American flags. Woohoo!

Then they send the poor sap back out to fight. Congratulations 81 your reward for surviving is to go right back out and die. No rest. No shower. No plate of tater tots. Get to the chopper and fight the unstoppable killing robot – again. 81’s ending is meant to feel rousing and full of even more grit, but it only feels super depressing.

Aww.

If you can shut off your brain, you might like War Machine. I did enjoy the battle scenes with the alien. However, the movie tries too hard to be more than it is. It wants to go somewhere special but ends up going nowhere.

author: CinemaSerf
content: Remember the start of "Galaxy Quest" (1999) when a group of actors are drafted in to help rescue the universe from a nasty megalomaniac bent on intergalactic domination? Well, this time it's poor old "Johnny Cage" (Karl Urban) who's the past his sell-by-date Thespian reluctantly recruited by "Lord Raiden" (Tadanobu Asano) to help save the Earth realm from certain doom. He is to join four other somewhat sceptical fighters, all with various skills, to combat the five soldiers of "Shao Kahn" (Martyn Ford) who has been hitherto indestructable as the princess "Kitana" (Adeline Rudolph) can attest having seen her father slain when her own kingdom fell. Now adopted and trained by this nemesis, and together with her formidable friend "Jade" (Tati Gabrielle), she looks certain to reduce "Johnny" and his cohort to dust. Things become even more doom-laden when an all-powerful amulet is accidentally delivered by Aussie rogue "Kano" (Josh Lawson) into the hands of the khan and getting this sorted out is going to take them all to the perilous netherworld for quite a battle royal. Now this is really quite a good fun action adventure if you take it on face value, and it is certainly no worse than than the first of these Simon McQuoid outings from five years ago, but the dialogue is pretty torrid and even though he looks like his tongue is fixed firmly in his cheek, Urban just hasn't the charisma to pull this off and so he does really rather let this down. That said, along the way there are plenty of homages to other films in this genre; the visual effects are pretty spectactular and there are loads of perfectly choreographed and acrobatically staged combat scenes that are straight out of "Kung Fu Panda" to keep us entertained as the plot heads in a fairly predicable direction. Not great, no - but it passes two hours easily enough.

author: Vinicius Monteiro
content:
Video game adaptations usually struggle, and this fighting franchise sequel is a painful reminder of that fact. Fans naturally expected the movie to fix past mistakes and finally deliver the promised fighting tournament, but it rushes right past it. Instead of focusing on the arena, the story takes a sharp turn into a generic, CGI-heavy fetch quest for a magic amulet. The pacing is ridiculously fast, jumping from one chaotic scene to the next without giving the story any room to breathe. Ultimately, the movie tries to hide its incredibly empty plot behind a wall of extreme physical action and fake-looking digital worlds.

The script doesn't help the situation at all, forcing the cast to deliver cringey, early-2000s style dialogue that makes serious moments feel like an awkward joke. It is honestly frustrating to see martial arts legends like Hiroyuki Sanada and Tadanobu Asano wasted as glorified extras, while the new faces lack any real chemistry or emotional depth. The only actual saving grace here is Karl Urban as Johnny Cage. He completely leans into how ridiculous the whole premise is, delivering a hilarious, self-aware performance that provides some much-needed relief from the rest of the cast's forced, wooden seriousness.

Despite having a noticeably bigger budget, the movie somehow looks and sounds incredibly artificial from start to finish. The sound design is just an exhausting, deafening assault on your ears, where terrible dialogue gets completely buried under non-stop explosions and generic background music. Visually, the heavy reliance on green screens makes the fantasy worlds feel totally empty, and the lighting makes it look like a giant video game cutscene. Even the costumes and weapons look like cheap, plastic cosplay rather than battle-worn gear, robbing the movie of that gritty, realistic edge it so desperately needed to be taken seriously.

Worst of all, the movie completely ruins the one thing people actually came to see: the fights. The director tries to hide the action with dizzying, quick-cut editing and ridiculous amounts of fake-looking CGI blood, which totally kills the brutal impact of the classic fatalities. Instead of letting the martial arts shine, the movie constantly pauses the action just to spoon-feed fans classic catchphrases and forced easter eggs. In the end, this sequel sacrifices a cohesive story and genuine tension just to pander to gamers with cheap nostalgia, leaving us with a hollow and soulless spectacle.

author: CinemaSerf
content: "Robin" (Hugh Jackman) has entered into a sort of solitary retirement, living from a cave and spurning - or worse - any companionship. Then his old pal from the green wood, "Little John" (Bill Skarsgård) turns up seeking his help to reclaim a farm he stole from it's rightful owner years ago so he can reunite with his wife and daughter. That goes smoothly enough, but they don't reckon on the power of old grudges and barely has the sun set on their murderous achievements than the whole place is afire and the wounded "Robin" has been conveyed to an island priory run by "Sister Brigid" (Jodie Comer) and a leper (Murray Bartlett). Prudence dictates that he'd best assume a pseudonym and so "Randolph" is left to recover under her tender cares, but when a young girl arrives, the leper delivers him some home truths and then the enigmatic young "Arthur" (Noah Jupe) arrives with an eye injury, we realise that grievances run deep and that his secret cannot last for long. Indeed, can he? Now this is as far a cry from Errol and Kevin Costner as you're ever going to get, but that needn't have mattered if it had focused a little better on a more substantial story. Instead, it immerses us in an admittedly plausible environment of mud and dirt and brutal weaponry, but it doesn't explain just how we got from the acclaimed "Robin Hood" of legend to this depressed and introspective, almost thuggish, character who appears to have a surfeit of baggage and whose friend "John" will stop at nothing to obtain a stale loaf of bread. Comer seems to have run for cover a little here taking refuge in her early scenes from "The White Princess" (2017) and the second half of the film, including the rather insubstantial contribution from the underused Jupe, descends into something altogether too melancholic. Jackman does impress though, confirming his long established versatility, and there is no doubt that this illustrates a far more realistic Plantagenet England than Hollywood or Pinewood ever have, but in the end I felt it gloomy, plodding and crying out for Enya to come and sing us an haunting ballad. I would still suggest watching on a big screen though, the photography and production design are stylish and really do benefit from a cinema screening, but otherwise I left disappointed.

content: We learn quite quickly that the weedy "Adam" has only just escaped with his life and the sword of power as "Skeletor" (Jared Leto doing his best impersonation of the deceased Alan Rickman) invaded and seized "Castle Greyskull". He (now Nicholas Galitzine) didn't manage to keep hold of the sword for long in his new world, and indeed just ended up in the USA working in HR whilst constantly surfing the internet to track it down before the nasty "Evil-Lyn" (Alison Brie) manages to secure it for her menacing boss. Luckily, and somewhat comedically, "Adam" does manage to find his artefact and then luckily for him his childhood friend "Teela" (Camila Mendes) shows up just in the nick of time to get him back to "Eternia". This is now a decimated world crying out for him to restore the sorceress and the equilibrium of the kingdom. His chances don't look good. His chief enforcer "Duncan" (Sir Idris Elba) has succumbed to the bottle and somewhat neutered his battle robot so it's more adept with a mop than a blaster; and what passes for the rebellion is highly suspicious of this floppy-haired and strangely dressed lad. Now he has to prove himself to just about everyone, including himself, and turn into the "He-Man" they need. The snag with this is that it takes us almost an hour to get back to "Eternia" and so kick start the fantasy elements of the adventure. Once that does get going, I was reminded more of the "Thor" franchise than anything with Dolph Lundgren (who does feature momentarily with some sagely advice). Galitzine does enter into the spirit of the thing, and he's buffed up well but even for a tea-time film, there simply isn't any menace. "Skeletor" barely features until the denouement where there's precisely no jeopardy and we stray perilously closer to soap rather than to peril for me. author: The Fixate & Binge Podcast, w/ Joe Curdy
content:
What a shame that Travis Knight's **MASTERS OF THE UNIVERSE**, at the time of this writing, appears destined to become one of the summer's biggest box office disappointments, struggling to recoup its reported $200 million budget in a crowded theatrical landscape.

Perhaps the economics of supply and demand simply caught up with Eternia. After all, another live-action trip back to the heyday of 1980s cartoon serials hardly seemed like something audiences were clamoring for. The dismal reception afforded the 1987 version—whose failure helped hammer the final nail into Cannon Films' coffin—hardly inspired confidence either.

Yet Knight's film, working from a screenplay by Chris Butler and brothers Adam and Aaron Nee, swings for the fences in an unexpectedly entertaining blend of fantasy adventure and comedy. Tonally, the gamble pays off. These larger-than-life characters inhabit a world where sincerity and camp are not mutually exclusive, and the film wisely embraces both.

Gen Xers (like myself) will appreciate the multiple callbacks to the animated series from over 40 years ago as the film even finds a humorous way to weave in pronouns and a very on brand Dolph Lundgren cameo for the 21st century.

But the biggest question mark entering production was its cast, particularly Jared Leto as Skeletor. Given his recent box office track record, one could be forgiven for expecting the worst. Surprisingly, Leto leans into the character's theatricality and campy absurdity, delivering a performance far better than expected.

More impressive, however, is the supporting cast. Idris Elba is perfectly cast as Duncan, better known as Man-at-Arms, bringing warmth, humor, and gravitas to Eternia's chief weapons master. Alison Brie makes for a delightfully cunning Evil-Lyn, while Morena Baccarin lends genuine mysticism and dignity to the Sorceress.

But the film ultimately belongs to Nicholas Galitzine. In his first true starring role, Galitzine finds all the right marks, balancing swashbuckling action with an easygoing comedic charm that makes Prince Adam instantly likable. More importantly, he understands that He-Man works best when played with conviction rather than irony.

No, **MASTERS OF THE UNIVERSE** is not the fantasy epic that will dethrone THE LORD OF THE RINGS. But as a colorful, earnest, and surprisingly funny adventure, it succeeds far more often than it fails.

That makes its disappointing box office performance all the more unfortunate, as this latest trip to Eternia deserved the opportunity to continue its story in a sequel.

In an era where studios endlessly mine intellectual property for diminishing returns, it's ironic that one of the few adaptations willing to embrace its own goofy, heroic spirit may never get the chance to build a franchise.

author: Vinicius Monteiro
content:
Watching modern cinema try to resurrect 80s franchises has become an exercise in patience and, usually, pure frustration. When a new *Masters of the Universe* movie was announced, the promise was to bring back the grandeur of that world using today's technology. But instead of honoring the original, the studio delivered an exhausting, soulless adventure that feels ashamed of its own roots. Rather than embracing the colorful, campy fantasy of Eternia, the film constantly hides behind worn-out, self-deprecating irony. It’s terrified to take its source material seriously. This heavy reliance on cheap nostalgia and easter eggs might try to pander to older fans, but it leaves newcomers completely lost, resulting in a movie with a massive identity crisis.

Director Travis Knight usually brings a lot of heart to his projects, but he really struggles with an epic of this scale. The direction feels messy, and the shaky camerawork during action scenes makes it almost impossible to tell who is fighting who. Add in a heavy reliance on unfinished green screens, and the movie completely loses any sense of physical weight. You don't feel the impact of a sword strike; you just see a blur of digital lights. The script, written by Chris Butler, Aaron Nee, and Adam Nee, only drags things down further. It's a bloated take on the hero's journey that constantly ruins moments of genuine drama with forced, cynical jokes. To make matters worse, the characters don't actually talk to each other—they just deliver robotic, cringey motivational speeches that kill any chance of an emotional connection.

Originally, this franchise was all about fun, colorful escapism: a giant barbarian fighting a talking skeleton. But the writers insist on forcing dense social commentary and philosophical dilemmas into a plastic universe that just can't handle them. This completely tanks the pacing, especially in the second act, which is bogged down by pointless political subplots that do nothing for the main story. Honestly, the editors could have easily chopped off forty minutes without losing anything important, and we would have had a much tighter, far less tedious movie.

The cast doesn't help either, as they all seem to be running on autopilot with zero chemistry. Nicholas Galitzine tries his best to carry the lead, but Prince Adam is written as so passive and boring that he loses all his classic nobility. We spend way too much time with his angsty human side before He-Man finally shows up, and Galitzine looks visibly uncomfortable delivering his artificial lines. Camila Mendes is also totally wasted. Her version of Teela is stripped of her original bravery and reduced to a bitter character with terrible dialogue, only to be completely sidelined as a spectator in the final act. And seeing an actor of Idris Elba's caliber reduced to a glorified extra as Duncan is tough to watch. He’s just there to dump exposition and drop tired one-liners instead of acting as a meaningful mentor.

Then there's Jared Leto’s Skeletor, which is an absolute disaster. He turns the franchise’s most iconic villain into a hysterical, theatrical joke with a bizarre voice that totally takes you out of the movie. Because he's so over-the-top and never feels like a credible threat, all the tension in the film completely falls apart.

On a technical level, the movie is just as exhausting. The aggressive, guitar-heavy soundtrack never gives you a moment to breathe, often drowning out important dialogue. Visually, instead of a cool mix of sci-fi and medieval fantasy, Eternia looks cheap, sterile, and generic. The costumes look like amateur cosplay, lacking any real grit or wear and tear from a world at war. Everything is so polished and smothered in fake-looking CGI that the big epic battles end up feeling like an outdated video game cutscene, with actors clearly just floating in a green screen room.

In the end, *Masters of the Universe* completely fumbles its chance to be a massive summer blockbuster. Throwing a ton of money at a movie can't buy it a soul. It's frustrating to see a mythology with so much potential reduced to poorly timed jokes and bad CGI because the filmmakers didn't have the guts to just embrace the fantasy. But hey, movies are subjective. What I see as a bloated disaster might be a fun, nostalgic weekend ride for you. If you're curious, grab a ticket and see for yourself—sometimes ripping apart a giant mess of a movie is the best part of the whole experience.

content:
At the beginning of the movie I was really not happy that it was that silly from the get-go. I personally would've really wished to get a "real" in-Eternia movie and not a "real world" thing.

But relatively quickly, the movie did start to work for me. I really enjoyed how fitting the outfits of the named characters were done, especially Trapjaw, Man-at-Arms, Beastman and Mekaneck.

While the "real world" humor was okay for me but not something I would've needed, the humor about some ridiculous parts of the franchise, like how the characters got their names, poses imitating the TV show poses and such, were really done well.

Despite the differences to the cartoon show, it really feels like the people who did the movie actually enjoyed working with the franchise.

The story is fine, a typical "origin story" with some plot-armor and deus-ex-machina events, but contrary to some other movies, these actually fit the "stereotypical warriors of light" theme that He-Man ultimately is.

So, if you can accept that the beginning of the movie has the "real world" shenanigans and humor, I think you'll enjoy it as a fan of the old TV show.\
And it could certainly work as a "prequel" on how He-Man became the "more serious warrior of light" later on.

Needs more Cringer, though!

But yeah, overall, an entertaining movie if you don't take your Masters of the Universe too seriously, many really fun eastereggs, and I hope that, despite the "meh" box office results, we will get a sequel or spin-off at some point.

author: misubisu
content:
**Score: 8/10 — A Bold, Nostalgic, and Slightly Silly Return to Eternia**

After decades of false starts and failed attempts, the live action *Masters of the Universe* has finally arrived, and it's a thoroughly entertaining, if slightly uneven, homage to the beloved 80s cartoon. Director Travis Knight (\*Bumblebee\*) has crafted a film that is **interesting and somewhat brave** in the direction it takes, clearly a love letter to the animated series, with characters that remain quite faithful to their source material. It's bright, breezy, and brimming with heart, even if its jokey tone occasionally undermines the peril.

**What Works: Production, Performances, and Fan Service**

The **production, costumes, and sets are first class**. Eternia is brought to vibrant, Asgardian like life, and the world feels lush and authentic. It's a significant step up from the 1987 version, spending most of its runtime in Eternia rather than on Earth.

The **standout performances** elevate the material. **Idris Elba** is perfectly cast as Duncan/Man-At-Arms, bringing courage, wisdom, and dry humour to the mentor role. **Jared Leto** is a genuine revelation as Skeletor; he's having the time of his life under all that makeup, delivering a villain who is simultaneously menacing, ridiculous, insecure, and genuinely funny. **Alison Brie** rounds out the trio as a compelling Evil-Lyn. **Nicholas Galitzine pulls off He-Man... but only just**. He excels as the bumbling, fish-out-of-water Prince Adam, bringing comedic timing and a relatable vulnerability. However, his "over-reliance on sensitivity" can feel a bit un-He-Man-like, and his performance sometimes feels better aligned with a TV movie than a big budget spectacle.

The film is also packed with fan service, featuring appearances from familiar faces like Cringer, Ram-Man, and Fisto. With **multiple post-credit scenes** including a mid-credits stinger introducing a mysterious woman with a familiar sword (Adora, aka She-Ra), and a final scene teasing Skeletor's return, it's clear they intend to keep the story going.

**What Holds It Back**

The film is **too jokey**. While most of the humour lands, it often undercuts the danger, with even Skeletor aiming for laughs rather than terror. The plot is predictable and riddled with the occasional plot hole, and some of the CGI is distractingly weak. It's a film that doesn't quite have all the power, but it's an infectiously entertaining romp that will be sure to delight both long time fans and newcomers.

**The Verdict**

*Masters of the Universe* is a fun, colourful, and campy thrill ride that embraces its source material with affection and a knowing wink. While its jokey tone and occasionally clunky execution prevent it from reaching the heights of a masterpiece, its heart, production values, and standout performances make it an **8/10**. The multiple post-credit scenes set up a universe with promising potential, and it will be good to see what transpires.

**Watch if:** You're a fan of the classic animated series, enjoy bright and breezy fantasy adventures, or want to see Jared Leto have the time of his life as a wonderfully ridiculous Skeletor.

**Skip if:** You require a serious, grounded fantasy epic or are easily put off by a jokey tone that sometimes undermines the stakes.

author: CinemaSerf
content: If you are looking for something insightful about just how "Oasis" started, functioned or split up as a band, then you will be disappointed with this. It studiously avoids addressing anything contentious beyond acknowledging through some international news reports the impact of their famous barny in Paris and the subsequent fifteen years during which they didn't speak. Then someone, somewhere, realised that the appetite for nostalgia from the public was huge and they were prepared to pay handsomely to wander down memory lane. Not that this documentary suggests quite such an overtly venal rationale behind their reconciliation, but the opening few scenes at the rehearsals suggest that there is nothing whatsoever affectionate between these two siblings and Liam Gallagher looks about as indifferent to the whole enterprise as possible. Then they head to Cardiff for their first night of the much anticipated and sold-out UK tour and we see what all the fuss is about. Nobody needed to care about their tantrums and strops - what we get is a group of musicians who have ninety-odd thousand people in a closed Millennium Stadium eating out of their hands. There's a minimum of chatter with the audience, just nineteen songs rattled off in quick-fire order that have the place enraptured. Away from the on-stage performances, there are a few comments from fans across the world that illustrate just how global they were and remain, and how capable their stinging, poignant and affecting lyrics still are at addressing issues still pertinent to people, of all ages and classes, almost thirty years after they first churned out their very own vision. What comes across clearly here is that age has certainly matured the pair - especially Liam, and that it has also made them realise that when it comes down to it, there are more things to keep them together than were ever there to drive them apart and you also sense that they are now much more in control of not just the entire operation but also of themselves. In the end, though, this is really just a compendium edit of half dozen of their greatest hits compiled a little like they did for David Bowie's "Moonage Daydream" (2022) by combining contemporary with archive images as they sing and when a crowd that size is yelling "Don't Look Back in Anger" or "Wonderwall!" at you, it definitely makes the hairs on the back of your neck stand up. Like or loathe these two men as people, or even as ambassadors of the often derided and chavvy Mancunian music scene, you cannot possibly fail to appreciate that they - and "Bonehead" provided a soundtrack for a generation that will certainly outlive them and their squabbling. It's a couple of hours that flies by; that definitely benefits from cinema sound and is well worth a watch.

author: CinemaSerf
content: “Davis” (Chris Hemsworth) is one of those rare breeds of thieves. He has scruples about violence and so always wants to avoid hurting those whom he robs. It’s a sound policy as usually it is the couriers he is relieving of their diamonds, or watches, or jewels. His latest job didn’t quite go to plan, though, and feeling a bit unnerved he tells his ageing fence “Money” (Nick Nolte) that he wants out. He's not the kind of man to let the job go unfinished, so drafts in his far less scrupulous pal “Ormon” (Barry Keoghan) who is about as subtle as an air raid. When “Davis” hears of the robbery, he confronts “Money” and that’s when the wheels of his well oiled machine begin to come off as the motor-cycling “Ormon” is instructed to turn his attentions on our now disillusioned thief. Meantime, insurance underwriter “Sharon” (Halle Berry) is fed up slaving away under a glass ceiling for her bosses who won’t make her a partner, and so is a ripe target for “Davis” as he continues to plan for his retirement. The question is, can he turn her allegiance to his own advantage and perhaps give her an opportunity to fleece her latest, and most odious, client “Monroe” (Tate Donovan)? “Lou” (Mark Ruffalo) is the cop charged with trying to make headway investigating the robberies and it’s him who concludes that route 101 is crucial to the pattern and that his perpetrator is no ordinary thug. Scene set, what plays out now is a really quite disappointing drama that focuses too much on the characters and not enough on the mischievous intrigues and execution of the heists until the last ten minutes, when it finally comes alive a little. Hemsworth looks the part but doesn’t really embrace it; Berry could have had more of the game but her part is left sadly undercooked; Keoghan just sticks to his tried and tested borderline maniacal role, only this time with dyed blonde hair, and finally there is Ruffalo who could have made for a more formidable foil for Hemsworth had their duel of wits been allowed more prominence. It does look good with Hemsworth looking every inch as if he’d stepped directly out from one of his many luxury goods adverts, but the remainder makes for a routinely charisma-free, car-chase crime caper that I shall never remember. Pity.

author: Brent Marchant
content: It’s been said that crime doesn’t pay, but, as this notion is often portrayed in the movies, that’s only true if one gets caught. Perpetrators skilled in covering their tracks frequently manage to find a way around the law, provided, of course, that they’re truly adept at managing to stay ahead of authorities. That theory gets seriously put to the test in this third feature outing from writer-director Bart Layton, the story of a slick, enigmatic, unassuming Los Angeles jewel thief (Chris Hemsworth) who’s an expert at what he does, successfully pulling off his lucrative exploits without getting caught and without anyone getting hurt. But, in his latest job, wrinkles emerge that prompt him to reassess his circumstances (not to mention his future). These conditions uncharacteristically force him to improvise to stay ahead of those pursuing him, namely, an unconventional but insightful detective (Mark Ruffalo), an incisive insurance agent who specializes in managing the assets of wealthy clients (Halle Berry) and an undisciplined rival thief (Barry Keoghan) tapped by his partner in come (Nick Nolte) when the master criminal appears to be losing his nerve. Everyone here has a stake in how matters play out, both personally and professionally, but knowing how to proceed and who to trust become ever more complicated. In some respects, as this film’s title implies, the narrative underlying this story could arguably be seen as somewhat generic as far as heist movies are concerned. However, there are elements in play here that help to elevate this release above many others in this genre. For instance, the degree of character development is greater than what one typically finds in pictures like this, as virtually all the players here are imbued with more depth and nuance than usual. Then there are the film’s impressive production values, decidedly superior to many comparable offerings in such areas as cinematography, film editing (especially in the riveting car chases) and atmospheric background score. And, of course, the performances of the fine ensemble featured here do much to help set this release apart from its cinematic peers. Admittedly, several aspects of this production could use some shoring up, particularly in the areas of pacing (especially in the middle) and the development of a few of the picture’s less important story threads. On balance, though, “Crime 101” is a cut above what viewers might generally expect out of an offering like this, making for an enjoyable time at the movies, even if it’s not overly original or particularly innovative. But this is one release that successfully finds ways to get away with it – and there’s no crime in that.

author: Livio Andrea Acerbo
content:
Crime 101 takes us along the 101 freeway through sun-bleached Los Angeles, where jewel heists unfold with careful timing rather than scenic views. Chris Hemsworth plays the central figure, a thief who remains untraceable while carrying out these jobs with the exactness of a Swiss watch, leaving the LAPD without leads. The setup keeps the focus on the mechanics of the crimes and the pursuit that follows.

Halle Berry appears as an insurance broker facing a personal crossroads, creating a mix of desperation and chance that intersects with the unfolding events. Mark Ruffalo portrays a detective who senses a pattern and pursues it with steady determination, raising the overall tension in the story.

The film comes from director Bart Layton, working from a Don Winslow novella. It blends familiar elements of the heist genre with occasional surprises that keep things from feeling entirely predictable. While originality can be scarce in this type of Hollywood tale, the movie still finds ways to divert attention and deliver unexpected moments within its two-hour span.

Hemsworth shows range beyond his usual roles, coming across as smooth and calculating enough to make the character engaging. Berry brings depth to her part through layered choices under pressure, and Ruffalo maintains an intense focus that fits the detective's relentless nature.

If the goal is a polished crime story with glamour and suspense, this one delivers on those terms. Those seeking major departures from established patterns might find it less compelling, yet it remains a solidly made example of the form that understands how to execute its premise effectively.
