author: Vinicius Monteiro
content:
My expectations for diving headfirst into a visceral thriller were high when I decided to hit play on Apex, but my time on the couch ended up being a really confusing mix of a racing heart and pure frustration. I was hooked by the promise of a suffocating psychological duel in the middle of nowhere, and the heavy energy of the first few minutes glued me to the screen in a way I didn't expect. But about halfway through this run through the woods, I realized the story itself was tripping over rocks along the way, running desperately without a map. It was one of those exhausting rides that tested the protagonist's limits and, to be totally honest, my patience with writing choices that made me roll my eyes.

I was absolutely glued to the couch during the opening sequence on the Troll Wall cliffs. Seeing Sasha and Tommy (Bana) hanging off that icy abyss set a brilliant tone of urgency right from the first few seconds. The tragedy there actually hurts. And the promise was super obvious: grief was going to be this woman's relentless driving force. Except, after she gets thrown into the Australian jungle, I realized with some sadness that the psychological pain just became an empty plot device. The movie brushes off the mental fallout of that traumatic climb almost immediately. The massive loss doesn't shape her survival tactics in the wild; it just serves as a lazy excuse to justify an isolated trip across the world. I was left with this cynical feeling that they sold me on a complex emotional journey in the interviews, but delivered a shallow drama that gets tossed aside by the end of the first act.

Charlize Theron’s physical commitment is just insane to watch. She carries the film's entire tension on her shoulders, often without saying a word. I didn't see the old invincible action-hero stereotype there; I saw an exhausted woman oozing vulnerability and terror through an almost tangible body language. Her performance creates instant empathy. The painful problem here is that she has to carry this weight all by herself in a total wasteland of good supporting characters. The few locals that show up have no soul. They're just pawns on a board, existing only to die in visually aggressive ways just to prove the villain isn't messing around. And Eric Bana? His blink-and-you-miss-it appearance left a really bitter taste in my mouth. Using an actor of his caliber just as marketing bait to put his name on the poster, reducing him to a narrative pretext who vanishes before you even care about him.

Before the forest closed in on the plot, I felt genuine chills during the buildup of danger at the roadside diner. The script nailed that raw, veiled, and intimidating threat that every woman traveling alone knows all too well. Taron Egerton steps in brilliantly as that toxic "nice guy" archetype, the kind of guy who hides a predatory nature behind an overly polite smile. And he kills it. He shifts from disarming charm to fury in fractions of a second. But as the movie drags on, his character goes downhill fast. The overload of sadistic little jokes and sarcastic one-liners seriously started to get on my nerves. In a setting that called for absolute terror, that performative, almost cartoonish behavior completely broke the heavy atmosphere. It felt like the villain was acting in a dark comedy while the protagonist was suffering in a gritty thriller. The two vibes just didn't mix.

Baltasar Kormákur knows how to create a sense of isolation, I gotta hand it to him for that. The direction understands the need for silence, keeping us tense wondering where the stalker is hiding instead of blowing things up every five seconds. But as soon as the initial adrenaline wore off and the second act kicked in, my patience literally went down the drain. The movie's pacing stalls in an almost inexplicable way. I spent endless minutes watching Sasha wander aimlessly through empty landscapes or crouch behind logs. This sluggishness completely killed the engagement I had built up. And the blind obedience to clichés is infuriating. It follows the survival thriller playbook so exactly that I caught myself guessing which bush the jump scare would pop out of. It lacked the guts to subvert the audience's expectations.

If anything kept me awake during the slower moments, it was the environment itself. The geography doesn't make things easy. We're not just talking about a killer on your tail; we're dealing with deadly rapids, rocks that tear your skin open, and a biting cold that drains the character's sanity. This double layer of threat worked fantastically for me. Watching Sasha being forced to beat the Australian biome before even worrying about Ben's blade gave the movie a very authentic survival weight. The film scores its best points when it treats the forest not as luxury wallpaper, but as a hostile, unpredictable, and living force.

I was genuinely immersed in the claustrophobic cinematography. That invasive camera, focused on the cold sweat on Theron's forehead, creates an insane sense of urgency. Capturing the real locations in Australia commands massive visual respect. But then the digital effects kicked in and ripped my immersion to shreds. In the bits involving the fall into the rapids or the fights on those towering cliffs, the green screen sticks out like a sore thumb in an embarrassing way. The collision of this plasticky CGI with the real mud and the raw acting completely flattens the sense of danger. When I noticed the fake, pixelated water blurring in the background, my fear of the protagonist drowning vanished instantly. It desperately needed some polishing in post-production.

On this front, I applaud without a second thought. The sound design is the true silent star of this movie, masterfully carrying the paranoia on its back. The decision not to shove a dramatic orchestral score down our throats the whole time was a relief. I found myself on the edge of the couch, holding my breath, trying to isolate the sound of a snapping branch or leaves being crunched in the dark. The aggressive amplification of the buzzing flies and the harsh noise of the violent water was unsettling in a good way, dialing up my own discomfort in the room. When the music finally does show up during the direct chases, it rips through with almost tribal beats that make your heart rate sync right up with it.

I love ugly fights. Those instinctual survival brawls where there's no glamour, just the desperation to keep breathing. The movie gets the clumsy tone of the clashes right. The colossal problem, though, is how it was filmed and stitched together. The editing decided to go with the shaky-cam and hyperactive cuts cliché. In the night sequences, it turns into a blur of mud and clothes where it becomes humanly impossible to decipher who's hitting or getting hit. On top of this visual alienation, the script tests your intelligence with its suspension of disbelief. Sasha's initial vulnerability evaporates in the blink of an eye. She takes falls that would turn bones to dust, lets out a groan of pain, and goes right back to sprinting through the woods at Olympic speeds. Wanting the aesthetic shock of a nasty injury but refusing the physical consequences of that same pain ended up killing the authenticity of the conflict.

There came a point in the last act where the lazy writing actually offended me. The tense cat-and-mouse dynamic loses all credibility when the rules of the map just stop existing. Sasha gets swallowed by a fast current for minutes, plunges far away, and then, as if by magic, the villain appears right behind her, laughing and without a scratch. The distance between them shifts depending on whether they need a new jump scare on screen. This heavy reliance on narrative "teleportation" completely destroys the tactical feel of the duel. I lost all desire to think about escape strategies because I knew that, one way or another, the script would make the villain break the laws of physics to catch his prey.

I need to vent about how and where I watched this thing. It is glaringly obvious that the scale of the mountain, the ambition of the sound editing, and the vastness of that isolation demanded a dark room and a massive movie theater screen. Watching all this squeezed into a home setup, fighting off living room distractions, really neutered the impact. The oppression the director tried to create just couldn't bleed out of my TV screen. The strategy of dropping something with this scope straight to streaming ended up sabotaging the very claustrophobic essence the project wanted to convey.

The ending they saved for last managed the feat of being a massive letdown. After spending almost two hours building up anger at the unfairness of the chase and waiting for a soul-cleansing catharsis, things wrap up in a pathetically mundane way. The confrontation ends with a sudden snap, trading a bloody or emotional climax for a lazy, going-through-the-motions conclusion. The psychological journey and the trauma wounds were totally sidelined, rolling the credits with a heavy feeling of "was that it?".

Tackling Apex requires a massive dose of patience. It’s a fractured project that sabotages itself by neglecting a grief subplot with rich potential and resorting to script shortcuts that insult your logic. I was super annoyed by the confusing camera work in the night fights and that fake CGI background blowing up on the screen, not to mention a climax that just left me looking like a fool. But, I can't deny that my heart did race during certain stretches. Charlize Theron’s magnetic presence crawling at the limit of her strength is spectacular, and the jungle's sound architecture delivers the tension that the story loses sight of. If you're having an exhausting day, just looking for some dirty, straightforward entertainment without overthinking the logical details, the momentary adrenaline makes up for it. Just go in without expecting a revolution in the genre.

author: MovieGuys
content:
"Apex" gives the strong impression it hopes the location will carry the film. To be fair, the exotic wilderness of outback Australia is an interesting setting. That said, its window dressing on a film that's lacking in substance and pacing. 

The first shortcoming is Apex's key characterisations feel shallow. You never get any real insight into the mind of the deranged serial killer or, for that matter, his would-be victim. Both remain distant and unknown. This is a major shortcoming. What starts out as a pursuit thriller which supports a more exposition-driven story and bare-bones characterisations quickly turns into a psychological thriller minus the psychological depth it needs to carry it forward. The abrupt finale really demonstrates the confusion as to what Apex is supposed to be. 

Sadly, I can't say a lot of positives about acting either. The lead character's performance feels wooden and forced, which may well be down to character's limtiations in the script. The character of the "Brit/Aussie" serial killer is a little overcooked. He's what non Australian's think Australians are. I can say this wth confidence, as someone who lived in Sydney, for a number of years. 

Action is well done and creative. Both actors have the physicality to carry the outback action convincingly, which does add a sense of realism. 

In summary, whilst not unwatchable, I found myself viewing Apex in stops and starts over a couple of days, which is never a good sign. Its failure to decide what it wants to be, constructing a compelling story that reflects that decision is, in my estimation, its single biggest shortcoming. On the upside, action is well done, and yes, the location is compelling. A marginal 6/10 from me.

author: Martin Oaks
content:
**The return of filmmaking as they used to make it**

What a rare treat it is to be genuinely surprised by a movie nowadays. And how telling it is of contemporary cinema that stumbling upon a gem like this feels more like a stroke of pure luck than the product of routine industry talent.

The year is 1987, at the absolute height of the Cold War. Troy "Assassin" Kelly (Ryan Reynolds), a cocky, reckless US Navy pilot, is shot down over enemy territory during a top-secret reconnaissance mission. Stranded in the brutal Siberian wilderness and hunted by Soviet security operatives, his only hope for survival rests on a completely unexpected ally: Nikolai (Kenneth Branagh), a gruff carpenter and former KGB agent who, ironically, harbors a deep, secret love for American pop culture, Bruce Springsteen, and Hollywood movies (talk about a needle in a Soviet haystack). Together, this odd couple must bridge their cultural divide to forge a chaotic alliance and outsmart the Bolshevik army—one just wants to get home, while the other is looking for political asylum. After all, who wouldn't want to live in the America of Ronald Reagan and George H.W. Bush?

Directors Jonathan Goldstein and John Francis Daley show a real knack for balancing witty humor and high-octane action in "Mayday". They write, direct, and deliver one of the most entertaining rides of the year; a fresh, unapologetic comedy that plays like a nostalgic love letter to '80s buddy movies and the iconic "Top Gun", which gets plenty of nods throughout the film.

There is an undeniable chemistry between the two leads, which, in my book, is mostly thanks to the writers' ability to craft rich characters with actual depth and personality—a concept that sadly feels totally alien in today’s cinema. Will we ever learn a thing or two from the Coen brothers? Reynolds brings his signature comic magnetism and fast-talking wit, while Branagh perfectly captures the rugged communist captivated by the American way of life. Watching them play off each other on screen almost takes you back (and I emphasis "almost") to the classic screwball comedies of Wilder or Lubitsch.

author: The Fixate & Binge Podcast, w/ Joe Curdy
content:
Alfred Hitchcock once declared that filmmakers "should only resort to dialogue when it is completely impossible to tell the story visually" and famously critiqued dialogue-heavy films as merely "photographs of people talking."

However one approaches director Potsy Ponciroli's **MOTOR CITY**, one thing becomes immediately clear: this is a visual story that throws out the rulebook of more traditional action films. 

With nearly zero dialogue -- co-star Ben MacKenzie's character never utters a single word -- and an enviable 1970s soundtrack -- Ponciroli picks up Hitchcock's gauntlet and delivers a crowd-pleasing revenge actioner with one of the most talented casts working in Hollywood today.

Brick shithouse Alan Ritchson fills the screen as John Miller with his hulking, brooding presence, carrying nuance like a kettlebell in scene after gloriously action-packed scene from beginning to end. His love interest -- Sophia (played by Shailene Woodley) oozes thoroughly believable onscreen chemistry with Ritchson. Their happy, blue-collar life is suddenly torn apart with a conspiracy to rival Alexander Dumas's ***The Count of Monte Cristo***.

With telling flashbacks and a **SERPICO**-esque glimpse at police corruption in 1970s Detroit, what happens next will slake the thirst of any action fan, as Ponciroli's film rides hell for leather in a relentless and brutal sequence of revenge.

Co-starring Ben Foster, Pablo Schreiber and Lionel Boyce, and a cameo by Detroit's own Jack White (who serves as one of the 28 executive producers) -- **MOTOR CITY** confirms what most action films dare to risk: dialogue is optional when a filmmaker understands how to tell a story visually.

**MOTOR CITY** is sure to divide critics -- and is likely doomed at the box office for the misfortune of being stuck between a rock and a hard place (released between **THE ODYSSEY** and **SPIDER-MAN: BRAND NEW DAY**) -- yet one hopes it will build on a solid word-of-mouth success and excel once it moves to streaming.

In a "less is more" approach to this revenge actioner -- which is precisely what made George Miller's **MAD MAX: FURY ROAD** and both of Jalmari Helander's much-loved Finnish **SISU** films so great -- **MOTOR CITY** gives audiences a visual feast without holding their hands. 

The principal cast offer standout performances -- especially in one memorable, entirely wordless seductive sequence between Woodley and Foster in a late-night coffee shop rendezvous. This is arguably Woodley's best work. Equally impressive, Ritchson cements himself as one of the most watchable actors in Hollywood today.

author: Brent Marchant
content: Sex is one of those subjects that can be difficult to address on film. It can easily come across as shallow, silly titillation, as bawdy, shameless voyeurism, or as a veiled form of porn euphemistically garbed as a work of erotic art. What’s more, viewers going into theaters to watch offerings about this subject may have expectations that don’t reflect any of the foregoing examples or that don’t live up to what they anticipate, leaving many audience members frustrated and disappointed. But, every so often, a movie comes along that gets things right, as is very much the case with the new comedy from writer-director Gregg Araki. As the film’s title unabashedly proclaims, this release is unapologetically about what it says it is, at least superficially. In actuality, however, there’s much more to this offering than what it suggests, and that’s what helps to make this an insightfully worthwhile watch, sexual considerations notwithstanding. In essence, the film follows the outrageous exploits of an outspoken, freewheeling, perpetually thirsty erotic artist, Erika Tracy (Olivia Wilde), and one of her naïve, sheepish gallery assistants, Elliott (Cooper Hoffman), who engage in a wildly uninhibited relationship ostensibly built just on sex. In many ways, it’s a scenario in which submissive, clueless Elliott finds himself in way over his head. However, as a recent college graduate in need of work, he takes the job, which, despite the considerable demands of his indisputably dominant boss, ironically ends up being quite liberating and erotically fulfilling (especially since his cold, perpetually indifferent girlfriend, Minerva (Charli XCX), frequently leaves him and his needs unattended, prompting Elliott to engage in frequent acts of “self-satisfaction”). As time passes, though, relations between Erika and Elliott start to sour as he begins to take the nature of their relationship seriously (some might even say obsessively), something that she views as completely casual, easily dismissive and lacking in the same emotional intensity as her ever-hopeful would-be suitor. And this, in turn, causes Elliott’s life to fall apart on multiple fronts, even leading to specious suspicions involving murder raised by two perplexed, stone-faced detectives (Johnny Knoxville, Margaret Cho). What’s perhaps most fascinating about this film, though, is the many issues it examines through the lens of sex. The relationship between Erika and Elliott may begin with and be rooted in sex, but it raises questions about such matters as honesty, trust, control and obsession, as well as the relationship dynamics of dom-sub sexuality. The narrative also introduces passing but relevant observations about generational social attributes and how they’re reflected through sexuality, just like virtually all other aspects of life. This makes for an incisive, smartly written movie, one far different from what one might expect (and from conclusions one might draw from its somewhat misleading trailer, which occasionally makes this film look like the second coming of entries from the “Porky’s” franchise). It’s also refreshing to see an offering that isn’t afraid to talk about sex in a frank but humorous context without continually turning its story elements into little more than glorified punchlines. And, even though “I Want Your Sex” is erotically explicit (sensitive viewers take note), it’s never depicted gratuitously or in blatantly bad taste. This is all made possible by the film’s fine script and sustained pacing, backed by the excellent performances of Wilde (what a year she’s having!), Hoffman and the superbly cast ensemble of supporting players, including both those named above and the characters portrayed by Mason Gooding, Daveed Diggs and Chase Sui Wonders. It’s truly amazing how a picture about a topic that might typically be casually cast aside or summarily denigrated can be as thought-provoking as this one. But, as Erika so often astutely observes, sex can open the door to something that is remarkably revelatory in our creativity, our actions and our outlooks – and not just in the bedroom.

author: CinemaSerf
content: "Elliot" (Cooper Hoffman) is working for a renowned artist "Erika" (Olivia Wilde) when she starts to show a little extra interest in him. He's intrigued and more than a little curious, but he is ill-prepared for just what she has in mind when she invites him back to her home - ostensibly for professional purposes - and introduces him to her kinky-side. Meantime, he's been chucked out of his apartment and is taking a break from his studious and physically uninterested girlfriend (Charlie xCx) and so is staying with his sexually fluid colleague "Zap" (Mason Gooding). Now with his sexual boundaries being tested and his eyes (amongst other things) being well and truly opened, his love life becomes something of a rollercoaster to which he is becoming increasingly addicted. The problem might be, though, that "Erika" isn't exactly reciprocating on any emotional fronts. For her, he has a role and a purpose and she seems quite capable of switching on and off at will - much to his chagrin. With his now obvious obsession to her and her power becoming clear, what happens next? The first half hour of this is actually quite ground-breaking; not least because both Hoffman and Wilde throw themselves into their parts enthusiastically and there are some accompanying pithy remarks from the smart-mouthed "Zap", but after that it sort of plateaus into something that runs out of steam before becoming vaguely preposterous - even by battery-powered standards. It's kinkiness is fun, is cringe-making and is innovative but that isn't sustained and with the dialogue never really making that much of an impact on the proceedings, I'm afraid I sort of lost interest. It certainly emphasises that pleasures of the flesh and of the mind are not necessarily restricted to people of the opposite sex, nor to anything even remotely conventional but once that point has been made once or twice, I thought this just became a bit repetitious and the conclusion rushed like Agatha Christie on Ketamine. It'd worth a look for two initially quite quirky performances, but that's about the height of it.

author: CinemaSerf
content: In best Christopher Lloyd style, a man arrives in a busy diner claiming to be from the future. He (Sam Rockwell) also claims that this is the umpteenth time he has been to the place, at the same time, trying to recruit some of the diners to join him on a quest to thwart the ultimate takeover of society by an AI whizzkid. Of course they think he’s a few bricks short of a load, but when he reveals his detonator a few take notice. He already knows whom he wants, and whom he doesn’t and so armed with a reluctant band of “volunteers” and, for the first time, “Susan” (Juno Temple) off they set on a series of adventures that must keep them out of the reaches of the police and get them into the home of the young boy. Rockwell leads this entertainingly, if at times a little over-exuberantly, and he gels well with a Temple who wouldn’t have looked out of place atop a wedding cake. As their quest takes more shape, so does the message it makes no bones about delivering, and for any still sceptical about the manner in which mankind is sleepwalking into an artificially crafted, managed and controlled existence, this serves as a sharply written and potently acerbic critique on just how easy we might be manipulated in the future by the input of one innocent and fully functional young brain and machines that can thereafter write their own rules - for themselves and for us, too. A final plaudit has to go to the unnervingly menacing Artie Wilkinson-Hunt whose sparing contribution at the denouement gives the butter-wouldn’t-melt look on his face a distinctly unpleasant aftertaste. It is a bit long, and occasionally it does lose it’s way as we whittle down the characters, video-game style, but it’s an innovative story that ought to ring alarm bells.

author: Brent Marchant
content: Some prognosticators these days are contending that humanity is headed for a plunge off the edge of a cliff from which there’s no return. Others have even said that we’re already past that point. Either way, it would seem we’re at a critical juncture, a turning point of potentially mammoth proportions. But can anything be done to save us? That’s the question posed in director Gore Verbinski’s latest offering, a wild, whacked out sci-fi satire about the unfolding collapse of mankind and the efforts of a seemingly crazed time traveler from the future (Sam Rockwell) to save humanity. This manic, eccentric protagonist unexpectedly shows up in a present day Los Angeles diner to recruit a team of combatants to help him battle an evil force that will set mankind on an irretrievably unalterable path going forward. The enemy is a nine-year-old computer whiz (Artie Wilkinson-Hunt) who’s about to unleash a malignant form of AI that will lock us into an existence where everyone is hopelessly locked into the distractions of cell phones, social media, virtual reality and fascist AI, a paradigm enforced by relentless attack drones. With the help of seven ordinary individuals (all of them diner patrons who either volunteer or are unwittingly conscripted), the man from the future sets out on his quest to vanquish the enemy before it’s too late – an undertaking that he has apparently unsuccessfully attempted many times before. And, as this bizarre adventure unfolds, viewers are clued in on the back stories of several of these warriors and how their experiences have contributed to the emerging scenario. This includes the recent histories of Mark (Michael Peña) and Janet (Zazie Beetz), high school teachers who are unwittingly (and hysterically) confronted by a zombie-like student body involuntarily controlled by their cell phones, a segment reminiscent of “The Night of the Living Dead” (1968); Susan (Juno Temple), a middle-aged single mother who loses her son (Riccardo Drayton) in a school shooting but who is stunned when he is miraculously brought back to life as a clone (of sorts); and Ingrid (Haley Lu Richardson), a child’s birthday party entertainer who falls in love with a pizza deliveryman (Tom Taylor) who unsuspectingly becomes obsessed with virtual reality. These seemingly unrelated story threads ultimately become intertwined with one another as the film’s unlikely hero seeks to save the day. But can he? If this all sounds highly unusual, you’d be right – this is handily one of the strangest releases I’ve seen in ages. But it’s also one of the funniest, most outrageous tales I’ve ever seen committed to film. Besides the bitingly cynical and immensely creative humor served up here, “Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die” imparts a decidedly important cautionary tale about us and our unknowing surrender to technology that may well end up taking us places we don’t want to go. There’s also an inherently strong metaphysical streak running through the narrative, particularly when it comes to the nature of alternate timelines and probable realities, not unlike themes played out in “Everything Everywhere All at Once” (2022) (but better explored here). Admittedly, this offering is a little overlong (especially in the final act), but, considering everything this title gets right (excellent performances, great special effects, big laughs), that’s easily overlooked. And it’s a fairly safe bet that the frantic nature of the picture and some of its edgy content won’t appeal to everyone. But those looking for something truly fresh, different and over the top while providing much to ponder, this one is clearly right up your alley. Keep that in mind the next time you speculate about the future – or step into your neighborhood diner.

author: Martin Oaks
content:
**When peril feels like a punchline**

The film kicks off with a premise that is as chaotic as it is magnetic in a run-of-the-mill Los Angeles diner—a backdrop that fades into the background when a man armed with a detonator bursts in with an wild claim: he is a time traveler who has failed 116 times before, and this is his last shot at saving the world. His mission is to recruit a group of everyday patrons with no special skills to form a ragtag team whose sole purpose is to stop a rogue AI fueled by the darkest corners of social media.

Verbinski’s ("Pirates of the Caribbean," "Rango"...) visual strengths coexist with the flaws of an overwrought script. Yet, the director proves once again his mastery at choreographing high-octane action sequences and extracting magnetic charisma from his cast. This is especially true thanks to the remarkable chemistry between Sam Rockwell, Haley Lu Richardson, and Michael Peña, who successfully keep the story's comedic momentum alive. Furthermore, the satire on our current technological dependency feels timely and visually stimulating, turning the chaos into a fairly enjoyable piece of entertainment.

However, "Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die" stumbles by trying to wear too many hats at once, shifting abruptly between absurd comedy, dystopian sci-fi, and slight touches of horror (at times, even evoking the grotesque surrealism of Jean-Pierre Jeunet). This tonal clutter dilutes the emotional weight of the climax, making moments of genuine peril feel like a mere punchline. In the end, while the premise relies on a rather conventional and predictable 'unlikely heroes' blueprint, the movie is entertaining and fast-paced, though perhaps too scattered for those of us who expected a social critique with a bit more bite.

author: CinemaSerf
content: Despite the best efforts of the pyromaniacs the creation of “Dr. Frankenstein” (Christian Bale) has survived, and now over a century later is a bit horny. Determined to find himself a companion, he visits the Chicago laboratory of “Dr. Euphronious” (Annette Bening) with his request. Well, it ends up being more of a demand really and so she reluctantly agrees to indulge in a bit of body snatching/reinvigorating. Their corpse? Well we’ve already met “Ida” (Jessie Buckley) before her demise and, personally, I felt death might have been the best thing that could have happened to this vulgar, brash and loud-mouthed creature. Revitalised, she and her new beau “Frankie” set off on some adventures around the city that start to fill in some blanks about both of their lives; involve a gangster kingpin and a dashing Hollywood movie star (Jake Gyllenhaal) upon whom he is fixated. The cops are never far away, especially as their escapades result in even more dead bodies - including a cop or two, so detective “Wiles” (Peter Skarsgaard) and his secretary “Malloy” (Penélope Cruz) are on soon their case and things take a turn for the Bonnie and Clyde. Now, there’s no denying that Buckley, especially, puts her heart and soul into her lively performance here, but I found the characterisation so un-engaging that after about half an hour of the relentlessly paced dialogue accompanying the borderline slapstick comedy I had lost interest. It takes far too long to get up and running and though it’s a grand looking production the thing just never got out of second gear as it quite literally lurched along for a long old two hours. Cruz plays as if she really wanted to be in - or maybe even thought this was - a very wordy “Dick Tracey” movie, and I found that both leading performers seemed more determined to impress us watching rather than present us with anything like a real love story. I suppose the very nature of the science behind this will allow for a sequel, but I think I will just stick with my James Whale collection instead.

Note that the dance-number in the middle is absolutely a nod to Young Frankenstein (which is probably just the better movie, overall).

author: Brent Marchant
content: Life in a post-apocalyptic world is a common theme in movies (especially, if you believe what’s published in the media, the increasing prospect that such an outcome may be coming closer to a reality than any of us might like). In many cases, these films follow the experiences of a resourceful, innovative protagonist who quietly but skillfully struggles to survive, successfully managing to fend off foes while cerebrally wrestling with feelings about what’s been lost. That scenario is apparent once again in this latest release from legendary director Ridley Scott. Unfortunately, however, this is not one of the filmmaker’s better efforts, a blatantly uneven production that gets things right in some regards but woefully misses the mark in others. Based on the 2012 novel of the same name by Peter Heller, the film follows the life of a mechanic and antique Cessna pilot, Hig (Jacob Elordi), who ekes out a comparatively comfortable existence in the Colorado wilderness with his wise-cracking marksman wingman, Bangley (Josh Brolin), in a dystopian future that has been devastated by a deadly virus. Like Hig and Bangley, pockets of survivalists resistant to the pandemic’s lethal impact are scattered across the countryside, but they face constant danger from the encroachment of ruthless scavengers seeking to pilfer whatever they can find for themselves. But, despite the undeniable harshness of this new reality, Hig still pines for a way of life that once was. And he’s convinced of rediscovering that possibility when he receives radio messages from a mystery woman (Allison Janney) in Grand Junction, CO that ambiguously hold out hope for the existence of such a sanctuary. In his quest to find the truth, he embarks on an adventure-filled journey in which he encounters a variety of other survivors, such as Aaron (Bendict Wong), head of a surprisingly thriving Mennonite community, and a hard-nosed gun-toting rancher, Jack (a.k.a. “Pops”) (Guy Pearce), living in a remote and vulnerable locale with his daughter, Cima (Margaret Qualley). But can Hig survive the journey? And what might he find if he ever makes it to Grand Junction? While the premise here is solid, recalling such offerings as “I Am Legend” (2007) and films in the “Mad Max” franchise, the finished product nevertheless occasionally teeters on shaky ground. After a strong but sometimes-slow opening hour, backed by a reasonably commendable closing act, in between viewers are mercilessly subjected to a middle segment that *seriously* defies believability, taking the picture decidedly off the rails, a serious blow to the film’s overall credibility. This is truly regrettable, as this disproportionately out-of-place sequence makes it easy for viewers to quickly lose interest as the project struggles to get back on track before the credits roll. It’s difficult to fathom what the filmmaker was going for in such a ridiculously over-the-top sequence, and it detracts from the elements that truly work well (a terrific cast, gorgeous cinematography, and an emotive soundtrack reminiscent of Scott’s earlier cinematic opus, “Thelma & Louise” (1991)). I can’t help but think that this was a case of failure to “kill one’s darlings,” and, in this instance, that shortcoming nearly undermines all of the audience goodwill the picture amasses before and after it. What’s more, the script is short on its back story elements, leaving one wondering how the narrative ultimately arrived at where it is. Sadly, “The Dog Stars” could have been *much* better, both as a cautionary tale and as a fine work of big screen drama, with some deliberate tweaking. As it stands now, though, the survival considerations addressed here could be just as applicable to viewing audiences as they are to the characters themselves.

THE DOG STARS is a gorgeous, contemplative post-apocalyptic thriller that never fully earns its two-hour runtime. Ridley Scott finds real tenderness in a story about grief, isolation, and the fragile work of learning to hope again, and the ensemble cast sells that journey beautifully. author: CinemaSerf
content: In a world where a flu virus has wiped out most of the human population, mechanic-cum-pilot "Hig" (Jacob Elordi) lives on a remote farm with his world-weary pal "Bangley" (Josh Brolin). He makes occassional sorties with his beloved dog "Jasper" into town (think "Omega Man" - 1971) for supplies and to reminisce at the home he shared with his late wife and unborn bairn but is spotted from the ground as he returns home one day and a violent tragedy ensues. That galvanises him to set off in his plane to find the town of Grand Rapids from where he has had intermittent radio contact over the years. It's at the extreme edge of his range, though, and so it's no great suprise when his aircraft blows a gasket and he finds himself crash-landed in a field. Luckily, that just happens to be adjacent to the home "Cima" (Margaret Qualley) shares with her curmudgeonly dad (Guy Pearce) who promptly gives him his marching orders. That'll be easier said than done as the field has to be cleared of trees and rubble before he can take off - plenty of time for everyone to get to know each other. Pretty swiftly, the question is more about whether he's going to stay or she's going to go - a decision that is made for them and so it's Grand Rapids here we come. What might they find if/when they get there? There is plenty of attractive aerial photography of the Alpine scenery and Brolin does try to bring a little gritty substance to the proceedings as the marauding "reapers" attempt to raid his only functioning fridge in a fifty square mile radius, but there isn't anywhere enough by way of action to sustain this couple of hours and the episodic storytelling strays into all too familiar territory very quickly once Elordi sets off on his adventure. Surprisingly for a Scott film, the continuity isn't the best either - the plane is spattered in blood then it isn't; it's attacked by an axe then - well it wasn't, and the radio aerials are there one minute and not the next, too. That all rather sums up the lacklustre nature of this ponderous opportunity for the charismatic but unchallenged Elordi to travel the lengths of the country in his tiny Cessna hopping from frying pan to fire. It's all perfectly watchable but there's very litle soul to the thing and with each character bogged down with pre-disease baggage it's a bit like swimming through glue at times, too.

author: CinemaSerf
content: “Tommy” (Anson Boon) is an odious cretin of a teenager who bullies, boozes and snorts his way through life until one night he finds himself all alone and somewhat the worse for wear. Next morning, we meet “Rina” (Monika Frajczyk) who has arrived at a remote country house where she is rather perfunctorily interviewed for a cleaning job by “Christopher” (Stephen Graham). On her subsequent tour of their home she is introduced to his borderline catatonic wife “Catherine” (Andrea Riseborough) and their son “Jonathan” (Kit Rakusen) before being taken downstairs to the basement and encountering a lad who is chained to the wall. Yep, that’s our “Tommy” - just as foul mouthed and threatening as before, only now he’s a bit more sober. Oddly enough, that doesn’t scare off “Rina” and so we know that she must have problems of her own as we now follow quite a menacingly bizarre process of what could be called rehabilitation for the angry young man, and possibly for others too. What I did enjoy here was the powerfully charismatic effort from a Boon who genuinely came across as obnoxious as we start out but who becomes someone altogether more shrewd as the dynamics in the house change in a series of quite unexpected ways. Just watch his eyes! Riseborough is also on solid form as her persona deceives effectively and with about half an hour left it’s fairly safe to say that I hadn’t really much of a clue what was going to happen to whom at the end. Stockholm syndrome maybe? Faux-Stockholm syndrome maybe? Watch and see, it’s worth it and I expect to see a lot more of Anson Boon.

author: The Fixate & Binge Podcast, w/ Joe Curdy
content:
Polish director Jan Komasa is emerging as a serious talent worth watching. With **HEEL**, we are given something that initially recalls **A CLOCKWORK ORANGE**, but gradually feels closer to a folk-horror variation on **THE MADNESS OF KING GEORGE** — a psychological tale of confinement, forced rehabilitation, and a very bad boy being coerced into becoming good.

Before we get there, however, **HEEL** opens with what feels like 15 different production-company logos flashing across the screen — an unintentionally hilarious parade that starts to resemble a **FAMILY GUY** gag before the actual movie finally begins. But once the film gets going, it grabs ahold of you and rarely loosens its grip.

Local Yorkshire droog Tommy (played by Anson Boon) is addicted to booze, drugs, sex and violence — wreaking havoc wherever he goes in a whirlwind of debauchery. Like a music video from The Prodigy, Tommy snorts, glugs, and rages aimlessly through life until one fateful evening when, in a drunken stupor, he is separated from his pals after collapsing unconscious in the street.

When Tommy awakes, he discovers himself chained like a dog to a dingy mattress in the cellar of a Yorkshire farmhouse, tended to by Chris (Stephen Graham).

We sense sinister motives behind the kidnapping — though it's hard to feel an ounce of sympathy for the loathsome Tommy — as Chris makes his intentions clear: Tommy will be "corrected" until he can be reformed and welcomed into their family as an older brother to their son Jonathan (Kit Rakusen), and a son to his wife Kathryn (Andrea Riseborough).

Nursing a recent tragedy, Chris, Kathryn and son Jonathan — each broken in their own way — have constructed an unsettling domestic fantasy in which Tommy isn't merely their prisoner, but a replacement piece intended to fill a void that grief has left behind.

Not one to buckle easily, Tommy puts up one hell of a fight, rebelling against his incarceration with abusive language and a torrent of threats that underscore the sheer improbability of this twisted *Pygmalion* experiment. The harder Chris attempts to hammer Tommy into the shape of a civilized human being, the more apparent it becomes that this bizarre rehabilitation may transform everyone involved.

But Komasa's film (written by Bartek Bartosik and Naqqash Khalid) has several surprises in this psychological tale of family, trauma, acceptance and trust that begs the question: can empathy be taught to someone as wayward as Tommy?

With incredible performances by Boon, the always brilliant Graham and Riseborough, HEEL is one of the biggest surprises of the year — a disturbing and unexpectedly moving examination of damaged people attempting to repair one another through deeply damaged means. What begins as a sinister tale of captivity and forced rehabilitation gradually becomes something far more compassionate, suggesting that even in the most unlikely of people, empathy may not simply be innate — it can be learned.

author: CinemaSerf
content: Off the north east coast of Scotland - there lies a small island upon which siblings "Isla" (Gayle Rankin) and brother "Sandy" (Grant O'Rourke) have lived for thirty winters. Entirely self contained and living their lives according to the cult of the gull, they only really have one law. Make sure any interlopers get hoyed over the cliff into the sea! On the mainland, the aspiring "Roz" (Michelle Gomez) has become aware of their existance and so sends the hapless office-boy "Daniel" (Domhnall Gleeson) out to serve them with an eviction notice. Just when it looks like he is destined for the same fate as his predecessors, though, he manages to use the music from his mobile phone and some grand gesturing to convince them he is a wizard. He begins to regale them with a sort of civil service hybrid of JRR Tolkien stories and next thing, they are eating out of his hands. "Isla" is much the more sceptical of the two, but as both gradually fall for their visitor we have to wonder if he might end up going native and staying, or might the ambitious "Roz" have to send in the cavalry - in the guise of her one man army "Callum" (Emun Elliott) to evict and protect? In some ways this has the look of a Mark Jenkin film with some lovely aerial photography of a windswept island that has clearly seen some cottage industries in the past but that is now abandoned save for our two eccentric residents. Thereafter, though, this develops much more of a layered story that combines some genuinely funny Scots humour (you have to be very careful how you punctuate a sentence with "Sam" humping "Frodo" up fifteen flights of stairs!) alongside some mysticism, some local authority form-filling indifference and the effects of isolation on all three of them. She has an interesting relationship with the "Fin Man" (John Hannah doing his own impersonation of a seal - complete with whiskers) that reflects her own issues with not just their current situation but with the memories of her long-absent parents whose backstory is gently but not comprehensively presented throughout. If I'm honest, I didn't really love the denouement but there is plenty of fun along the way and if you've a guid Scots tongue in your heid, you'll appreciate the humour from the vernacular dialogue. It might put you off having a chicken for a while, though - and there are a great many feathers!

author: Brent Marchant
content: The world can be a scary place with its perilous dangers and deceptive temptations, be they real or imagined. This is particularly so for those who have been isolated, with little or no contact with the outside, often buying into misleading superstitions and exaggerated risks. And so it is for a pair of almost-feral siblings, Isla (Gayle Rankin) and Sandy (Grant O’Rourke), the sole human inhabitants on the remote, windswept island of Ork located off the Scottish mainland. These de facto survivalists have resided there for 30 years after the immigration of all of the island’s other residents when lured away by the enticements of the mainland. Their parents, however, chose to stay, telling Isla and Sandy that the island was theirs as long as they protected it from incursions by “incomers” from the mainland. Not long thereafter, however, their parents died, leaving them to fend for themselves. They somehow learned how to survive, but they also developed some unique outlooks and practices, such as beliefs based on fantastic mythic tales involving trickster sea creatures and forging a ritualistic nature cult centered on the island’s only other residents, hordes of aggressive seagulls. Their lives take a sudden turn, though, when they receive a visit from an incomer representing a government agency seeking to relocate them off the island, Daniel (Domhnall Gleeson), a sheepish mid-level bureaucrat who fancies himself something of a closet wizard. Thus begins the clash of two different cultures that each try to influence the other to their way of thinking. In the process, Daniel’s mission becomes derailed as he falls for their rustic existence as Isla and Sandy become increasingly curious about life beyond their island. How will this scenario play out, especially when Daniel’s colleagues Callum (Emun Elliott) and Roz (Michelle Gomez) show up to see what happened to the eviction plan? Such is the charm that makes up this delightful debut feature from writer-director Louis Paxton, a genuine crowd-pleaser full of offbeat, quirky humor, a surprising number of tender (but not schmaltzy) moments, gorgeous cinematography and an intriguing, abstract, eclectic score. There’s much to be said for the trio of principals, too, with Rankin and O”Rourke playing perfect eccentric foils to Gleeson’s deadpan straight man. The picture also makes effective use of monochromatic animation in just the right amounts at just the right points in the narrative to depict the folksy tall tales that help to define the character of this remote and mythic locale, a nice touch that could have become tedious were it not for the filmmaker’s judicious restraint. While a few of the comic bits don’t land quite as effectively as they might have, most of them work well in this multilayered story that plays like an unusual cross between “Local Hero” (1983) and “The Birds” (1963) (yes, you read that right). “The Incomer” is an impressive premiere for a promising cinematic talent, and, fortunately for us and unlike Daniel, you don’t have to go quite so far afield to experience it.

author: CinemaSerf
content: With “Spike” (Alfie Williams) now a captive of “Sir Jimmy” (Jack O’Connell) and his other “Jimmies”, you wouldn't give much for his chances of survival. Terrified and hopelessly out-knived he must face a duel to survive, but even if he wins what awaits him under the control of this megalomaniac who considers himself the direct heir of Satan himself? Meantime, the iodine-coated “Kelson” (Ralph Fiennes) is venturing from his Nissen hut under the ground long enough to try to experiment on the violent alpha whom he names “Samson” (Chi Lewis-Parry). He establishes quickly that morphine will becalm this mighty Jason Momoa lookalike, but what if he tries a cocktail of medication on him? Might he be able to impact on the psychotic behaviour of those infected? Oddly enough, the most psychotic of all in this world is “Sir Jimmy” and when he espies the two talking amongst his towers of bones, he convinces his disciples that “Kelson” is none other than “Old Nick” himself and so a meeting with daddy looms large. Now I did feel that the story of “Spike” was rather lost here. Although we do follow him and get a sense of the fear in which he lives, that storyline’s emphasis shifts more onto the shoulders of the startlingly effective O’Connell whose characterisation mixes intellect with violence so effectively as to get under your fingernails. When we get to Fiennes we get an altogether more humanist thread, peppered by a fair chunk of Duran Duran’s back catalogue, before a rutting of devilish proportions leaves us with a conclusion straight out of Saint-Saëns that could go just about any way you could imagine. Fiennes, in these last fifteen minutes, is at the top of his game and his performance here shows again his huge versatility. This is a great looking take on a dystopia devoid of technology and ruins, but high on humanity’s capabilities for brutality and love, and it’s really well worth a cinema visit.

author: graeaehorror
content:
Back in 2002 an 18 year old sat in her local cinema and viewed one of the best zombie films of her generation. Danny Boyle's 28 Days Later changed the game and kickstarted a true juggernaut franchise. 

Little over 23 years later, a slightly older and still horror obsessed girl sat in a cinema to see the next installment. However this wasn't just a continuation. Nia DaCosta has created a thrilling, dramatic cinematic event that could stand alone in its own right.

This is so much more than a zombie film. The infected remain a threat, yet the true horrors lies in societal breakdown and how survivors navigate this dystopian plane of existence. 

Controversial character choices withstanding, there's no denying Jack O'Connell is the epitome of a true villain with his portrayal of antagonist Sir Lord Jimmy Crystal. In a godless world, the bleakest side of humankind is free to wreak havoc. There are scenes exposing the depths to which the depravity of Crystal and his "fingers" will sink, even against themselves. 

In stark contrast, this movie balances its bleak story with the return of Ralph Fiennes as Dr Ian Kelson. He brings much needed compassion and an optimism for human nature and our ability to exude kindness in a far from ordinary world. Leaning on his medical expertise, he works endlessly to restore this humanity to Samson (Chi Lewis-Parry), our marauding alpha.

The bone temple itself should be horrific but serves as an "ossuary", a memorial to the deceased. It's an embodiment of his memento mori philosophy, a reminder that death is a part of life.

The shining highlight of this film stands within its closing 20 minutes. Set inside the bone temple, we're treated to an absolute masterclass in storytelling, career defining performances (which speaks volumes given the career of Feinnes), and visuals that will live eternally in the minds of its audience. 

The soundtrack is wonderful, using Duran Duran to elevate moments of joy is a much needed mood boost. But the real powerhouse here comes in the form of Iron Maiden's The Number of the Beast. The choice for this to be diegetic is a stroke of genius, providing an injection of drama and elevating the penultimate scene from great to iconic. 

The Bone Temple succeeds where most films mid-trilogy fail. Instead of falling into precarious plot hole traps (ala The Strangers where we know our lead survives for the final film, thus making the second installment redundant), it builds on the existing story, elevating this trilogy to a near unbeatable level.

If DaCosta was not already on your radar of directors to follow, she absolutely should be now. The standards and expectations are insanely high for our final chapter and I for one am excited to see where this goes.

author: Martin Oaks
content:
**The danger of NORMAL-izing the formula**

Ulysses Richardson (once again played by a circumspect and supposedly enigmatic Bob Odenkirk) is a lawman haunted by a turbulent past and deep personal crises who decides to take a temporary gig as acting sheriff in Normal, a sleepy, freezing Minnesota town. Looking for a breather from his marital struggles and inner demons, Ulysses hopes to find some peace in a seemingly quiet community. But, of course, that calm is shattered when he responds to a botched bank robbery, uncovering a massive, violent international criminal conspiracy involving the townspeople, the mayor, and even the Japanese Yakuza. It’s a total plot salad that traps the protagonist in a rat race where everyone wants him dead, forcing the taciturn sheriff to dust off his most lethal skills just to survive.

"Normal" is pure irony: a collision between Midwestern rural slice-of-life and hyper-violent grindhouse nihilism. However, under Ben Wheatley’s direction and with a script by Derek Kolstad (the mastermind behind the John Wick franchise), the movie falls short of its ambitions, delivering a monotonous and boring product. The script shows a blatant insistence on milking the contemporary Bob Odenkirk archetype. From his rise to fame in the "Better Call Saul" universe to his rebranding as an action hero in "Nobody" (2021) and its terrible sequel, the actor has perfected the mold of the middle-aged, reserved, unassuming, and drab guy—the classic neighbor no one would ever suspect, who happens to hide a savage military or criminal past and an alarming capacity for explicit violence.

In "Normal," this trope stops being a surprise and turns into a corporate formula. Ulysses Richardson is, essentially, the exact same character from his previous works: a vessel of apparent small-town calm who, at the first hostile trigger, flips a mechanical switch to start kicking ass and taking names with surgical precision. And frankly, it’s just exhausting. While Odenkirk carries the role with his usual weary, magnetic charisma, the total lack of new nuances makes his character arc feel incredibly predictable and redundant.

Ben Wheatley shows an alarming lack of identity here, though he never quite drops into the absolute dumpster fire that was "Meg 2: The Trench". The director who once blew us away with the dark humor and wickedness of "Sightseers" or the claustrophobic chaos of "Free Fire" seems to be running on autopilot here, serving the rigid blueprint of Kolstad and Odenkirk themselves. The action sequences are decent, but the script chooses to stack up bodies instead of exploring the town’s dynamics or fleshing out subplots that could have given the story more meat. It's a real shame, because the final result is incredibly mediocre and run-of-the-mill.

content: Ok, so I don’t remember going to “Silent Hill” first time around (in 2006), but after this I am certain I will never go again. He’s “James” who meets up with “Mary” (Hannah Emily Anderson) after he managed to hit her luggage with his car. Thereafter they flirt, court, move in together, split up - but as far as this plot is concerned, in no coherent order and only delivered to us by way of flashback. It’s only as he returns to find her again he discovers the town is now the victim of what looks like a nearby meteor strike and the place devoid of all but some curious humanoid creatures that definitely mean him harm. Can he put the pieces of this emotionally confused jigsaw together? Do we care? If this were just to have been a monster film with Irvine in a semi-psychotic fight for survival, then perhaps it might have worked better. It isn’t. The timelines are all over the place; characters appear and the disappear seemingly quite randomly and the psychological impact of the story is so compromised as to render this little better than a mess that looks every inch an incremental video game put onto a big screen. Some of the creativity behind the visual effects is to be commended but the story is completely lacking in either characterisation or substance. It will kill some time on the telly in October, maybe, but otherwise this has little to recommend it to anyone.

author: jackmeat
content:
My quick rating - 4.9/10. Another Bloody Disgusting logo to begin with, so you never quite know what you're going to get. Sometimes that logo means "grab the popcorn," and other times it means "grab your phone". Return to Silent Hill lands somewhere in between.

His disjointed memories and guilt bring painter James Sunderland (Jeremy Irvine) to Room 318 after a handwritten letter from his lost love, Mary Crane (Hannah Emily Anderson) is slid under his door. Seeking closure, he heads to their special place in Silent Hill, now a desolate shell of a town that apparently no real estate agent dared visit in about twenty years. The more James searches for Mary, the more his grief warps the world into a psychological horror show, complete with shifting dimensions and monsters. The more James seeks his lost love, the more it seems to be a setup.

Visually, the film gets a lot right. The grim, darker contrasts of Silent Hill work nicely against the more colorful flashbacks, and the production design leans heavily into the series’ signature oppressive atmosphere. The backgrounds often look downright trippy, and the creatures are genuinely unsettling in that classic Silent Hill way, like someone turned therapy notes into practical effects. I recently fired up Silent Hill 2 in VR and could immediately tell this follows the same story path, though I only played briefly, so I won’t be diving into the endless debate about what the film changed or left out. I’m sure the hardcore fans are already handling that across the internet with surgical precision.

Laura, played by Evie Templeton, is easily the standout. She is wonderfully creepy and unpredictable, and injects some much-needed personality into a film where most of the characters feel like background NPCs waiting for their dialogue prompt. That isn't a knock on Anderson at all, since she has her hands full with multiple characters in this flick and juggles them quite well.

Oddly enough, this reminded me more of Silent Hill: Revelation than the original Silent Hill film. It never wraps up a complete movie, and the plot often feels paper-thin despite some heavy psychological themes. The atmosphere and scenery do most of the hard work, while the story struggles to find a direction. You can see where the film wants to explore trauma and guilt, but the pieces never fit together into a complete picture.

Director Christophe Gans returns after gracing us with the first Silent Hill, but this time he doesn’t quite recapture the same magic. Visually, he’s still on target, but the storytelling feels incomplete, like a puzzle missing just enough pieces to be tossed in the trash.

Then again, if you’ve ever played a Silent Hill game or watched the previous films, this may all feel strangely familiar. Great mood, deliberate pacing, and a journey that never quite clarifies its destination. It isn’t awful. Just another haunting trip through Silent Hill that looks the part but never fully finds its soul.

THE LAST HOUSE is a film of two very different halves — a sluggish, oddly toneless first hour that squanders a genuinely intriguing premise, followed by a back stretch that finally locates the tension and craft the setup always promised, only to rush its way to an ending more interested in sequel-baiting than resolution. Greta Lee and Wagner Moura are doing real work here, and the fully built, physically degrading house is a legitimate technical achievement that elevates every scene shot inside it, but the script never digs past the surface of its own ideas, leaving genuinely rich thematic territory — isolation, technological dependency, what security actually costs a family — almost entirely unexplored. It’s a divisive movie, one that’s likely to frustrate as many people as it entertains, and it’s easy to see why Netflix sat on the embargo until the last possible moment.

author: The Fixate & Binge Podcast, w/ Joe Curdy
content:
Louis Leterrier’s **THE LAST HOUSE** joins a growing list of thrillers seemingly inspired by the post-COVID era. Sure to trigger resentful memories of being forced to shelter in place during the global pandemic, Leterrier’s film is a dampening reminder of how miserable life really was with limited social options.

Then again, being trapped inside a house with your family for years is arguably horror enough without the creatures.

With a screenplay by Matthew Robinson, Leterrier’s film starts off very strong when a major rainstorm inexplicably results in countless occupants being entombed in their homes, but loses steam once the family at the center of the story simply goes about their lives, stuck firmly indoors.

Parents Ann and Jason (played by Greta Lee and Wagner Moura) do their best to hold their two children together against all odds, both psychologically and physically, as the weeks, months and eventually years go by.

(How the family has not succumbed to poisonous black mold over the years spent inside the home is one of the great unsolved mysteries here.)

With diminishing options as the family transitions, worryingly, from thriving to barely surviving, the central mystery as to ***who***, ***what***, ***why***—or even ***how***—this predicament unfolded around the world barely gets the attention it deserves until a hasty final act, heavy on thrills but sodden with explanation, tries to wrap things up.

Leterrier, known for creating engaging spectacle but not always sticking the landing, offers more of the same here as the family stands their ground against creatures who look like a cross between Bill Nighy’s Davy Jones from **PIRATES OF THE CARIBBEAN** and H.P. Lovecraft’s ***Cthulhu***.

More could have been done to explore the mystery of the creatures themselves instead of settling for the feeble “we never saw them again” explanation offered by the narration. It’s the anticlimactic ending no one asked for—especially after Netflix reeled in so much interest with an effective ad campaign that is sure to pay off with streaming records this weekend.

**THE LAST HOUSE** begins with the kind of intriguing premise that promises something far more ambitious than what ultimately arrives. Unfortunately, once the doors close, the film has nowhere nearly as interesting to go.

author: Vinicius Monteiro
content:
What started as a brilliant idea about isolation quickly falls apart in *The Last House*. The premise of a family trapped inside their home by a freak storm had all the makings of a great psychological thriller, but handing the project to action director Louis Leterrier turned out to be a huge mistake. Instead of building quiet, creeping dread, he relies on frantic camera work, cheap jump scares, and loud sound mixing. The movie completely abandons its promised suspense early on, turning what should have been an intimate nightmare into a confused mess that doesn't seem to know what kind of film it wants to be.

If there is one redeeming quality, it is the incredible production design. The house physically rots and decays alongside the family, creating a gritty, realistic atmosphere that anchors the film's few good moments. Unfortunately, the script completely wastes the talents of Wagner Moura and Greta Lee. They act their hearts out trying to ground the couple, but the writing forces these previously smart characters to make laughably stupid decisions—like dropping their weapons or splitting up in the dark—just to manufacture cheap danger. The kids are even worse; they have no real personality and only exist as lazy plot devices to disobey rules and cause trouble, making it nearly impossible to actually root for the family's survival.

The pacing of the movie is also an absolute nightmare. After a solid opening, the story hits a brick wall, dragging the audience through forty minutes of boring, repetitive survival chores that kill any sense of urgency. Then, just when the movie couldn't feel any slower, the third act completely derails. It throws out the psychological dread entirely and suddenly turns into a generic, action-packed monster movie. Swapping out the quiet fear of cabin fever for CGI sea creatures and frantic shootouts is a jarring, ridiculous shift that completely ruins the original vibe.

To top it all off, the story completely ignores its own mystery and delivers a slap in the face with its ending. We never get any real answers about the weird storm or what happened to the outside world, making the whole universe feel like an unfinished rough draft. Then, after nearly two hours of watching these characters suffer, the film just cuts to black right before any real resolution happens. It is a lazy, abrupt ending that proves the writers had no idea how to wrap things up, ultimately wasting a great concept and leaving the audience feeling completely cheated.

author: Manuel São Bento
content:
Rating: C-

Walking into Emerald Fennell's latest venture, I carried a cautious optimism, hoping for a reimagining that justified its existence beyond mere aesthetics. In many ways, WUTHERING HEIGHTS is a triumph of technical artistry; the production design is immaculate, and the costumes offer a masterclass in period detail. Linus Sandgren's cinematography is particularly arresting, utilizing gorgeous silhouettes and immersive visual callbacks that frame the story with a haunting, pristine beauty. When paired with a cathartic, sweeping score from Anthony Willis, the feature's craftsmanship becomes undeniable. However, this film serves as a sobering reminder that technical brilliance cannot salvage a hollow foundation. It's the most recent case  against the notion that striking imagery can compensate for a broken narrative, as WUTHERING HEIGHTS ultimately feels like a style-over-substance exercise that prioritizes visual vamping over the raw, psychological gravity required for such a legendary tale.

As a viewer who often isn’t familiar with the source material, I'm typically the first to advocate for a filmmaker's creative liberty. Yet, the choices made in this adaptation are bafflingly contradictory. The story, ostensibly centered on a monumental love, quickly devolves into a repetitive cycle of toxic behavior and juvenile vengeance, with protagonists who navigate their world without a shred of morality. WUTHERING HEIGHTS strips away the spiritual obsession that defines the original bond, replacing it with a prolonged, almost demonic montage of physical encounters that makes their connection feel carnal rather than soulful. Fennell leans so heavily into a  maximalist tone that the thematic weight is completely gutted, leaving a gaping hole in Heathcliff's character evolution and making the circular, frustratingly redundant dialogue feel like an endurance test.

Ultimately, WUTHERING HEIGHTS is a visually sumptuous yet emotionally hollow experience that forgets that for any adaptation to truly resonate, it must preserve the beating heart of the story it seeks to tell.

author: Brent Marchant
content: Poking fun at the supposedly sacred can sometimes be a source of perverse glee, particularly when targeted against works of art and literature that many might consider off limits and untouchable. Undertakings like that, however, were made for writer-director Emerald Fennell. As a filmmaker with a reputation for unapologetically telling stories with outrageous narratives, she was the perfect choice for the assignment of skewering Emily Bronté’s classic 1847 novel Wuthering Heights. Long considered one of the best works of English literature, this Gothic romance with a tawdry underbelly has long passed itself off as a respectable piece of writing thanks in large part to the carefully managed protection afforded by literary purists. However, in this latest cinematic adaptation of this time-honored tale, the filmmaker holds nothing back in bringing its kinkier aspects to light, all presented with a deliciously wicked sinister grin. While the film admittedly takes considerable license with the original narrative, its core characters and much of its basic storyline have been spared, albeit with a twisted approach in doing so. The film basically follows the exploits of ambitious social climber Cathy Earnshaw (Margot Robbie) who comes from a once-moneyed family now experiencing diminishing financial means. Cathy’s smitten with an orphan boy whom her father (Martin Clunes) rescues from the streets whom she has named Heathcliff (Jacob Elordi) in honor of her deceased brother. Cathy and Heathcliff grow up together, almost like siblings, but there’s an undeniable attraction between them. But, for Cathy, giving in to her romantic impulses would be imprudent in light of her ambitions to become socially respectable. And, as a consequence, she abandons her love for Heathcliff in favor of Edgar Linton (Shazad Latif), the landed owner of a neighboring manor, a move that breaks Heathcliff’s heart, who subsequently flees in despair. But, when Heathcliff returns several years later as a wealthy man, Cathy’s hormones stir to life once again, especially since her love for him now has money to back up the considerable pheromones he exudes. Thus begins a tale of erotic intrigue involving this romantic triangle, a deliciously campy romp brought to life and further seasoned by the maneuverings of Cathy’s longtime (and supposedly trusted) servant, Nelly (Hong Chau), who has a vested interest in how affairs ultimately unfold. The filmmaker thus spins a pulpy web on par with the best plots found in classic 1980s prime time soaps, suitably peppered with witty one-liners and hilarious sight gags. These antics are sufficiently facilitated by the superb performances of Robbie, Elordi and Alison Oliver as Edgar’s naïve sister Isabella (who’s not nearly as innocent as she seems, especially when she takes a shine to Heathcliff upon his triumphant return, adding more spice to the stew). While some viewers may not take to the deviations from the novel’s original story, and despite some tonal inconsistencies on the part of the filmmaker. “Wuthering Heights” is nevertheless a delightfully juicy guilty pleasure. It’s not meant to be taken as seriously as previous cinematic versions of this work, but there’s nothing wrong with that, as it’s intentionally following a different approach from those earlier offerings. And, in this case, Fennell’s version isn’t afraid to brazenly expose the hitherto-cloaked dirty little secrets of those iterations. I can’t imagine any other filmmaker capable of taking on the task of telling this story in this particular way. The outrageousness that the director unabashedly brought to the screen in previous works like “Promising Young Woman” (2020) and “Saltburn” (2023) is again present here (though handled far more skillfully this time), deftly combined with top-shelf production values in areas like cinematography, costuming, art direction and set design, not to mention the aforementioned spot-on performances. This release definitely won’t appeal to everyone, especially among those who prefer their adaptations of classic literature unadulterated. But viewers who have a pronounced mischievous streak in their movie preferences will no doubt revel in this release’s refreshingly bawdy frankness and clever tongue-in-cheek humor. This is truly a cup of tea with a hefty shot of a potent potable added to it, so, if that’s your taste, by all means drink up and enjoy.

author: CinemaSerf
content: I’m not sure, with the exception of “Barbie” (2023), that I’ve ever seen a film with Margot Robbie and really understood what all the fuss was about. Even there, that was more to do with Ryan Gosling knowing how to entertain whilst looking good. This time, she relies on Jacob Elordi for that support and if possible, he is even more wooden than her. Sure, he’d look good in a wet shirt contest, but that rather sums up this terribly disappointing adaptation of Emily Brontë’s novel. “Cathy” is the daughter of the wealthy but temperamental “Earnshaw” (Martin Clunes) and ever since she was young has had a close relationship with his ward “Heathcliff”. Thing is, though, as her father is guzzling his way through what little cash they have left she has to think on her feet. Perhaps the newly arrived velvet millionaire “Edgar” (Shazad Latif) might just offer a solution? Snooping on him one evening, she manages to sprain her ankle and so ensure an invitation to stay and recuperate with him and the ribbon-collecting “Isabella” (Alison Oliver). Narked, before we know it the smouldering one has pinched their only horse and gone off in the huff. It’s some years before he returns, a wealthy man, during which time she has married and is expecting a bairn - but can they continue to keep their hands off each other now they are in similar social classes? So much of the original story is in the gentle but powerful development of both the characters and the pulsating, seamy and evocative story, set against the bleakness of the Yorkshire landscape. This, on the other hand, over-relies on what we can see and what we might already know about the characters and so leaves us with something really quite shallow. It does look as if effort has gone into the look of the production but the screenplay has been stripped back to something barely recognisable and when there are opportunities for it to grab us by the throat, we default to some Enya-esque songs from a Charlie XCX who might actually be the most creatively influencing here. I’m sorry, but this was a real missed opportunity to update one of the most enduring and toxic love stories in the English language, but instead we have something that is so much style over substance. More withering than wuthering, and no heights at all here for me - no wonder they have been promoting it so heavily.

author: Sierbahnn
content: It's quite clever to put a shark movie in a dark cave. It does save a lot on the effect budget when you don't have to show the main antagonist with any degree of clarity. The characters are fun enough, even though they aren't very engaging, and they all get picked off one by one by a very angry fish just doing fish things. What I did like about this is that the fish isn't actually malicious or supernatural or vindictive, it just does fish things and that's pretty cool. For a cave movie this doesn't rate very high and as a shark movie, it doesn't rate much higher. It isn't a bad movie, but it isn't really all that special.

author: HaremCinema
content: More of a Public Service Announcement or maybe an After School Special than this is a real movie review. I'm not going to say "Don't Watch This Movie' because, if you picked up a watery, Teen-Chop-A-Thon like this then I think you'll probably be perfectly satisfied with watching this flick. I'm writing this 'advisory' because I wish someone had done the same kindness for me. It would have saved me the sour taste this left in my mouth. You see, the first half of The Devil's Mouth is above average when it comes to this kinda movie. That's what made the second half hurt so much. If the first half hadn't spent the time developing real characters with some depth, characters that were actually interesting, then the disappointment of the second half wouldn't have been so.....well, sourly disappointing. Don't get me wrong, this isn't a bad movie. It starts with some teens who can keep your attention with their shrieking & screaming & fleeing in terror. That's why we watch these movies, right? But the second half pulls the ol' bait n' switch on us. SPOILER WARNING! It shifts from a bunch of victims desperately fleeing, trying to escape & stay alive, it changes into a 'let's fight that shark!'.....why? Look, if you've ever been trapped in a cave system with a vexed bull shark, & which of us hasn't? then you know the choice to go fistacuffs with an apex predator on it's home turf is just a dumb idea. Wow is it dumb. Anyhoo, enjoy the first half but know what's coming. I honestly believe that this warning will improve your viewing experience as you won't feel duped like I did. I genuinely hope this helps you. If it did, please let me know.
